content:
The Ashen Chronicles, Volume I: The
Kindling Years

Chapter 1
The bells beneath the chapel had no tongues, yet they rang.
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned stood beneath the painted vault and listened to the iron tremor
passing through the stone. Dust descended from the ribs of the ceiling. It settled upon their black gloves,
their shoulders, the pale ash worked into the seams of their coat. Above them, saints without faces leaned
from the frescoes, their halos drowned beneath old smoke.
The chapel had been built for confession. The Ashen Vanguard had converted it into a tribunal.
“High Inquisitor.”
The voice came from the doorway.
Sabelle did not turn. The second crown pressed against their brow, a blackened circlet of name-scarred
metal. It was not the Crown of Burned Names. That ward lay sealed beneath their coat, against their
breast, cold as a buried tooth. The crown they wore was older, plainer, and made for being seen. It told the
room what Sabelle was before they spoke: severity given flesh, authority sharpened into a blade.
Behind them, the doors groaned open.
“Say it,” Sabelle said.
A clerk entered with a packet clutched in both hands. He wore the gray of the Ashen Vanguard, though the
hem of it was wet with coastal mud. His eyes lingered on Sabelle’s crown and fled.
“Gloamreach has sent a sealed report.”
“Gloamreach sends sealed reports whenever it wishes to conceal a wound.”
“The seal bears the mark of the garrison.”
“Then it is not a report from Gloamreach. It is a report from fear.”
The clerk swallowed. “Gloamreach’s garrison strength is 2483.”
The bells shivered again beneath the floor.
Sabelle turned at last. Their face was narrow in the candlelight, its planes made harsher by the two crowns:
the visible one above, the hidden ward beneath their coat, and behind both the knowledge that a crown
was merely a promise made to those who still believed promises mattered.
“Continue.”
“The hold has been quarantined. No vessels are permitted to land. No courier is permitted to depart
without examination.”
“Who ordered it?”
The clerk hesitated.
Sabelle stepped down from the dais. The chapel seemed to contract around them. “You have brought me a
sealed report, named the garrison strength, and omitted the hand that closed the coast. That is not caution.
That is incompetence.”
“The order was countersigned by Fleet Admiral Morwenna Ashgrove.”

At the name, something cold moved behind Sabelle’s ribs.
Morwenna Ashgrove was a major Fleet Admiral, born in 288 AS. Discipline clung to her station like salt
to rope. Beneath it, if the whispers were true, she secretly sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel. Sabelle
had never trusted whispers. Whispers were the lazy currency of cowards.
But the Iron-Ring Cartel had never needed cowards.
“Give me the report.”
The clerk crossed the chapel. He tried not to look at the black doors behind the altar, the doors that
descended into the cellar. Few looked at them directly. Those who did tended to discover how much fear
could be made to resemble piety.
Sabelle took the packet.
The wax was gray. Not ash-gray, not the soft white of old bone. It had the color of water seen beneath a
moonless sky.
They broke it with a thumb.
Inside, the ink had run in places, though the parchment was dry. The first lines spoke of lamps
extinguished along the Pale Coast. The next described a watchman found standing beneath a sealed arch,
his mouth filled with black reeds. The final portion had been scraped away so violently that the parchment
had torn.
At the bottom, someone had written:
THE DEAD ARE ANSWERING.
Sabelle read the words twice.
The clerk watched them. “There is more.”
“There is always more. It is the only mercy of bad news.”
“A vessel reached the outer chain before quarantine. Its cargo was seized. Among it was an object
identified as the Diadem of Sorrowgate.”
Sabelle’s gloved fingers tightened over the report.
“Artifact class?”
“A reliquary.”
The word seemed to deepen the chapel.
The Diadem of Sorrowgate. Forged in 281 AS. Attunement to it costs 9. A reliquary, not a weapon, though
weapons were honest about their hunger. Reliquaries asked to be opened. They made grief into a vessel
and called the vessel sacred.
“Where is it now?”
“The Fleet has it.”
“Morwenna Ashgrove has it.”
The clerk lowered his head.

Sabelle walked toward the altar. The painted saints watched without faces. Beneath them, the black cellar
doors breathed a thin ribbon of cold through their joined seam.
The revenant below had been silent for three nights.
It had not slept. The dead did not sleep. It had merely ceased its scratching.
Sabelle had bound it in the cellar beneath their residence, beneath salt, iron, and the remnants of rites no
sanctioned inquisitor would admit to knowing. They had given it no name. Names were handles. Names
were doors. Still, at times, the thing spoke through the stone in a voice borrowed from the living, and
Sabelle could not decide whether its silence was obedience or patience.
“What does Gloamreach have to do with the Diadem?” they asked.
“The report does not say.”
“Then why bring it to me?”
“Because the seal was addressed to the High Inquisitor.”
Sabelle looked at the clerk.
The man’s hands trembled. “And because the courier who carried it died before he reached the gates.”
“Of what?”
“He had no wound.”
“Then the answer is not in his flesh.”
A draft moved through the chapel. The candles bent toward the cellar doors.
Sabelle heard a scrape below.
The clerk heard it too. His face emptied.
“Do not move,” Sabelle said.
The scrape came again. Metal against stone. Slow. Deliberate.
The clerk’s hand went to the knife at his belt.
Sabelle seized his wrist before he could draw. Their grip was not painful. It did not need to be.
“The cellar is sealed,” Sabelle said.
A third scrape.
“High Inquisitor,” the clerk whispered, “what is beneath us?”
“History.”
The answer seemed to satisfy him less than silence would have.
Sabelle released him and turned back to the report. They read the date on the seal, then stopped. The ink
had bled too badly to trust. There were no numbers worth preserving in the ruin of it. No clean sequence.
No certainty. That was how contagion entered institutions—not through blood, but through doubt.
The War of Drowned Light had begun in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS, with 64617 casualties. It had
collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals. The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor, though the war’s

spark had secretly been staged by them. Sabelle had studied the surviving records until the letters swam.
Broken banners. Drowned radiance. Towns where victory was remembered only as the absence of another
burning.
The Silent Choir had won, and the realm had continued to bleed.
There were lessons in that, if one had the stomach to learn them.
“Send word to the Ashen Vanguard,” Sabelle said. “No public alarm. No proclamation. The Silent Choir
must not know we suspect their hand.”
The clerk’s mouth tightened. “You believe this is theirs?”
“I believe the Silent Choir has never needed to be present when their work begins.”
“And House Morvain?”
“Watch their envoys.”
“The Bleeding Crown?”
“Watch them more carefully.”
“And the Iron-Ring Cartel?”
Sabelle looked toward the cellar.
“Watch whoever claims not to be watching them.”
The clerk nodded, though he had the expression of a man discovering that obedience could be another
name for drowning.
A bell rang beneath the chapel.
This time the sound was clearer.
Something below had struck the iron.
Sabelle slid the report into their coat. Beneath it, the Crown of Burned Names gave no heat. It was a ward
forged in 266 AS, and its attunement cost 60. Its makers had shaped it to protect the bearer by erasing the
names of those who came too close. Sabelle had worn it through interrogations, executions, and councils
where every smile concealed a knife. Sometimes, afterward, they could remember a face but not the name
attached to it.
Protection had always been a form of loss.
The clerk backed toward the doors. “Should I summon the guard?”
“No.”
The cellar doors shuddered.
Sabelle raised one hand.
“Leave the chapel.”
“But—”
“Leave.”

He fled with the packet’s empty wrapper still caught beneath one heel. The doors slammed behind him,
and his footsteps vanished into the passage.
Sabelle waited until the echoes died.
Then they crossed the chapel alone.
The altar stone was cold beneath their palm. A hidden catch yielded. Somewhere below, a lock turned
with the thick reluctance of an old joint.
The cellar opened its dark mouth.
From the stairwell rose the smell of wet earth, extinguished candles, and the faint sweetness of rot. Sabelle
descended. Their boots touched the steps without a sound. The crowns remained steady upon their head.
At the bottom, chains crossed the room in a web of black iron. They had been fastened to the walls, the
floor, the ceiling. At their center knelt the revenant.
Its head was bowed.
Its hands were bound behind it.
Around its throat, the binding cord had cut a dark groove into flesh that no longer belonged to any living
law.
Sabelle stopped beyond the first circle of salt.
“You have heard the bells,” they said.
The revenant did not move.
“Gloamreach is quarantined. The Diadem of Sorrowgate has been taken from a vessel and placed in Fleet
custody. The Silent Choir may be stirring old embers. Morwenna Ashgrove may be selling what she
should guard.”
The corpse lifted its head.
Its eyes were shut.
Sabelle felt the Crown of Burned Names tighten against their skull, as if some absent hand had drawn a
thread through the metal.
“Answer me.”
The revenant opened its mouth.
Water spilled across the floor.
Not from its lungs. From between its teeth, black and shining, spreading through the salt without
disturbing a single grain. It carried the stink of the Pale Coast and the deep, mineral cold of drowned
places.
Then it spoke in a voice Sabelle knew.
Not the voice of the dead thing.
Their own.
“Do not let them crown you again.”

Every candle went out.
In the dark, something moved beyond the chains, and Sabelle reached beneath their coat for the ward as
the revenant began to laugh—
The laugh came apart in the dark.
It did not fade. It thinned, strand by strand, until it seemed to hang from the ceiling like wet hair. Sabelle
kept their hand beneath the coat, fingers closing around the ward’s iron grip. The metal was warm. That
was wrong. Iron in the cellar was always cold enough to bite.
Their other hand found the wall.
Salt rasped beneath their palm. The room had not changed, yet every measure of it had become uncertain:
the floor stretched too far, the chains breathed where they crossed the stone, and the black water continued
to spread without wetting anything it touched. It reached the toe of Sabelle’s boot and stopped.
A voice spoke from somewhere behind them.
“High Inquisitor.”
Sabelle turned.
Nothing stood in the passage. The door remained shut. Beyond it, the stairs climbed toward the rooms
where servants slept, where lamps burned, where the clean, obedient life of the Hold waited to be
resumed. Sabelle could almost smell the ashwood in the hall and the bitter tincture kept for headaches.
“Show yourself,” they said.
Their voice sounded like their own again. That, too, was wrong.
The ward gave a small pulse against their palm.
A light kindled beneath the revenant’s ribs.
It was not flame. It was the pallor seen under deep water, a drowned radiance trembling behind flesh that
had long ago forgotten warmth. The chains emerged from that dimness one at a time. They were black
with age, each link engraved with names burned so deeply into the metal that the letters had become
wounds.
The revenant sat where it had been bound.
Sabelle could see its face now. The skin had collapsed along one cheek. Its hair floated around its skull
despite the stillness of the air. Water ran from its sleeves and gathered in the hollows of its hands. The
thing looked toward Sabelle with an attention too intimate to be called hunger.
“Who sent you?” Sabelle asked.
The revenant’s mouth opened.
“Who sent you?”
A drop of black water fell from its chin.
“Do not let them crown you again.”
Sabelle drew the ward.

The gesture was practiced, severe, and almost useless. A thin flare crawled along the iron, illuminating the
salt lines, the chains, the wall. The light struck the Crown of Burned Names and broke upon it. Blackened
metal gleamed across Sabelle’s brow, scarred with the names burned into its surface. The Crown of
Burned Names was a ward, not a diadem, not a mark of office, not a promise made to the living. It had
been forged to keep something out.
Or in.
The revenant leaned forward as far as the chains allowed.
The links tightened.
Sabelle felt each pull in their teeth.
“Be still.”
The command had subdued witnesses who lied beneath oath, zealots who bit through their tongues, and
one magistrate who had attempted to make a spectacle of his own death. It had no effect on the bound
dead. The revenant’s head tilted.
“You have worn it so long,” it whispered.
Sabelle stepped closer.
The salt underfoot remained dry. The black water touched the hem of their coat and climbed without
soaking the cloth, a dark reflection rising against the weave. In it, Sabelle saw a room that was not the
cellar.
A quay beneath a colorless sky.
Walls white with old salt.
A bell tower split open from crown to foundation.
Figures moving through the streets with covered faces, carrying hooked lanterns whose light fell
downward instead of out. Doors marked in ash. Windows shuttered. Blood diluted by tidewater and
dragged toward the sea.
Gloamreach.
Sabelle stopped breathing.
The vision shuddered. It showed the Pale Coast under a sky that seemed too near the roofs. It showed the
quarantined streets of Gloamreach, sealed against the world and against whatever had already entered it.
The image offered no scale, no beginning, no end. Only devastation, repeated until repetition became a
kind of law.
“The Purge of Blackport devastated Gloamreach in 320 AS,” Sabelle said.
They had read the record. They had signed the record. The sentence had been copied into ledgers until the
ink lost its darkness, and each copy had been treated as proof that language could contain an atrocity.
The revenant smiled.
“Did it?”
Sabelle’s grip tightened around the ward.

“The Purge of Blackport devastated Gloamreach in 320 AS,” they repeated, more sharply.
“Devastated.” The revenant tasted the word. “A clean word.”
“Enough.”
“Gloamreach did not die cleanly.”
The images in the water changed.
A child crouched beneath a cart, face pressed into the mud. A uniformed hand reached down. A woman
stood in a doorway with a basin of blood between her feet. A tower bell swung without sound. Along the
quay, bodies lay beneath sheets that moved in the wind though there was no wind.
Then the scene drew back, and Sabelle saw the whole coast as a pale scar.
The ward’s light dimmed.
Something struck the cellar door above.
Once.
Dust fell from the ceiling.
Sabelle looked toward the stairs. The sound had come from the upper side of the door. A knock, measured
and patient.
The revenant’s chains creaked.
“Who is there?” Sabelle called.
No answer.
A second knock.
Their mind moved through possibilities with the cold discipline of an executioner selecting a blade. A
servant who had heard the extinguished candles. An inquisitorial messenger. An intruder. Something
wearing the shape of a person.
The revenant lifted one dripping hand.
“Do not open.”
Sabelle laughed then, though no amusement touched them.
“You are bound.”
“Yes.”
“You cannot advise me.”
“I can remember.”
The third knock came harder. The hinges complained.
Sabelle crossed the cellar. The black water followed. It did not ripple, but it carried the reflection of the
revenant beside them, walking where the dead body remained chained.
At the foot of the stairs, Sabelle paused.

There was a scent in the air now: wet wool, burnt paper, and the mineral cold of a shore without sunlight.
Gloamreach had entered the cellar through the water, or memory had become a door. Either possibility
offended the order of the world.
The Crown pressed against their skull.
A name flared briefly among the burned scars.
Not theirs.
Sabelle raised the ward. Its iron point touched the first stair.
The darkness above moved.
Not a person. Not exactly. A shape passed across the thin line beneath the door, long and narrow, then
withdrew. Sabelle heard breathing on the other side. Slow. Deliberate.
“High Inquisitor,” said a voice.
This voice belonged to Morwenna Ashgrove.
Sabelle knew the disciplined cadence, the command held beneath every syllable. Fleet Admiral. Authority
given human form. The voice had addressed assemblies and crews and those who required no explanation
before obeying.
But Morwenna Ashgrove was not in the cellar.
Sabelle kept their eyes on the door.
“What do you want?”
“To see what you keep below.”
The answer was delivered without threat. That made it worse.
Behind Sabelle, the revenant began to whisper. The words ran together, too low to catch. A litany,
perhaps. Or the recitation of names. The chains trembled in time with it.
Sabelle placed their free hand upon the Crown of Burned Names.
The metal had no heat, yet beneath it their skin prickled as if touched by frost. The Crown had never been
beautiful. It was a funerary thing, a blackened circle marked by names that had burned through the surface
and left their absence behind. Its protection had always felt like erasure. To be guarded by it was to accept
that some part of oneself might be sacrificed without permission.
The name beneath their fingers vanished.
Sabelle flinched.
The door shook.
A narrow crack opened between the boards. Darkness looked through it.
Not an eye. A depth.
The ward struck out on its own.
White fire ran from Sabelle’s hand into the stair, filling the cellar with the stink of scorched salt. The thing
beyond the door recoiled. Something scraped backward across the floor above, and a sound followed—a

wet intake of breath that might have been pain or laughter.
The Crown tightened.
Sabelle screamed.
The revenant answered with a roar.
Every chain snapped taut. The cellar walls groaned. Salt lifted from the floor in thin spirals, circling the
revenant’s body. Black water surged across the stones, climbing the walls in sheets. Where it passed, the
old mortar darkened, and beneath the damp appeared lines of writing.
Names.
Hundreds of them.
Sabelle stumbled back, ward raised before their face. The writing crawled over the walls and gathered
around the door. Some names were clear. Others had been burned away. One appeared beneath Sabelle’s
hand, then disappeared before they could read it.
The thing outside spoke through the crack.
“Twice-crowned.”
Sabelle steadied themselves.
“Leave.”
“You are already open.”
The door began to swing inward.
Sabelle drove the ward into the floor. A circle of pale fire burst outward, catching the black water, the salt,
the chains, the walls. The revenant convulsed within its bindings. Its mouth opened impossibly wide, and
from the dark behind its teeth came the sound of a distant sea.
The door halted.
For one breath, nothing moved.
Then the Crown of Burned Names split with a sound like a bone breaking.
Sabelle felt the crack travel across their brow.
Something on the other side pushed one finger through the gap.
The finger was pale, wet, and marked with a burned name.
Sabelle raised the ward, but the revenant spoke first.
Not in Sabelle’s voice this time.
In the voice of the dead.
“Crown me.”
And the finger curled around the edge of the door.
The finger tightened.

The door groaned inward, though the bars were sunk into stone and the lock had been sealed with iron
prayer. Water streamed from the pale knuckle. It ran black across the threshold and gathered in the seams
between the flagstones, carrying with it the cold stink of a shore that had never known the sun.
Sabelle held the ward before them.
The Crown of Burned Names had split across their brow, but it had not fallen. One half clung above the
left eye. The other pressed into the temple, biting deep enough that blood warmed the cheek. Beneath the
blackened metal, the burned names stirred like insects beneath paper.
“Crown me,” the revenant said again.
Its voice had no distance now. It spoke from the mouth in the dark room, from the crack in the door, from
the hollow beneath Sabelle’s tongue.
They felt the word enter them.
Not as sound. As command.
The ward shuddered. The names upon it brightened, each scarlet line opening and closing like a coal in a
dead hearth. Sabelle’s hand clenched around the grip of the inquisitorial blade at their hip. The blade was
useless here. Steel had no authority over what had been invited across a threshold.
They had not invited it.
That was the lie they had told themselves on every descent.
The revenant had been found bound. The chains had been old, the salt unbroken, the door already marked.
Sabelle had merely preserved what the world had failed to destroy. They had kept it beneath their house,
beneath their offices, beneath the rooms where petitions were heard and confessions were taken. They had
kept it because some things were safer when watched.
They had kept it because it knew names.
Now the door opened another finger’s breadth.
Beyond it, the revenant’s face remained indistinct. There was only the glimmer of wet teeth and the pallor
of its hand. The chains dragged across the floor. One link struck stone.
The sound climbed through Sabelle’s bones.
“Do you know what you are wearing?” it asked.
“The Crown of Burned Names.”
“You know what it does?”
“It wards.”
The dead laughed.
The noise was soft, almost tender. Sabelle remembered the first time they had heard that laughter, when
the thing had been no more than a shape under cloth and bindings. They had believed the sound came from
water draining through the cellar wall. They had believed many things before belief became another
instrument of self-harm.
“It erases,” said the revenant.

The names beneath the crown flared.
Sabelle’s vision broke into fragments. A stair descending through ash. A chapel with no roof. Black water
cupping drowned candles. A field of banners hanging upside down, their colors leeched into gray. Faces
pressed against the inside of glass.
Then a name.
Not theirs.
A name they had once read in a sealed report and ordered forgotten.
The crown burned hotter.
Sabelle staggered, catching themself against the wall. Their shoulder struck the old stones. Dust sifted
down. Somewhere above, beyond the ceiling, a bell began to tremble without ringing.
The revenant drew its finger along the gap.
The wood peeled beneath its touch.
“Take it off,” it whispered.
Sabelle looked at the thing they had concealed beneath their own authority.
“Why?”
“So I can see you.”
The answer was simple enough to be monstrous.
Sabelle’s mouth had gone dry. Their years of command rose before them—not as triumph, but as weight.
The black seals. The interrogations. The doors opened at a word. The doors closed at a word.
Marrowwatch bending around their will, its watchfires answering their summons, its silence thick with
obedience.
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned commanded Marrowwatch since 293 AS.
They had repeated the fact to themself whenever fear threatened to strip the flesh from their thoughts.
Command was a structure. Command was a wall. A wall could hold anything if it had been built high
enough.
But the cellar had never belonged to Marrowwatch.
It belonged to the thing below.
Sabelle raised the ward until its broken rim hovered before the door.
“You will not pass.”
The revenant’s hand withdrew.
For an instant, the gap darkened. The black water ceased to move.
Then something struck the other side.
The door buckled. The bars screamed in their sockets. Sabelle thrust the ward forward and spoke the first
binding syllable. The sound came out thin, scraped raw by the voice that had entered them.

The revenant struck again.
A crack ran down the door from lintel to threshold.
Sabelle spoke the second syllable.
The crown answered.
A ring of pale fire burst from their brow and raced across the floor. It touched the salt lines, the chains, the
iron nails driven into the walls. Every mark awakened. The cellar filled with the smell of scorched hair
and rain on hot stone.
The door held.
The revenant did not.
It began to sing.
There was no melody Sabelle could follow, only pressure. The walls bowed inward. Water climbed the
stones against gravity, sliding upward in narrow black streams. The chains rose from the floor one by one,
their links trembling, then turned toward the door as though the revenant had become a star and they were
iron filings.
Sabelle planted both feet.
Their knees wanted to fold. Their heart beat with an unfamiliar rhythm, a second pulse beating beneath the
first.
The crown had begun to forget them.
They could feel it in the absence of pain. The names burned less fiercely. The metal grew cold. The ward
no longer recognized the shape of their skull.
“Do you hear them?” asked the revenant.
Sabelle heard only the cellar.
“No.”
“They are beneath you.”
The stones underfoot shifted.
Not physically. Memory moved through them.
Sabelle saw the bodies packed into the foundations, not buried but layered, each one wrapped in the
remnant of a uniform, a robe, a shroud, a banner. They saw hands folded over ribs. They saw mouths
stuffed with ash. They saw names carved into teeth.
The vision was not a revelation. It was an accusation.
Sabelle had passed over these stones countless times. They had brought candles, salt, ink, condemned
relics. They had knelt in the center of the cellar and drawn circles around the revenant’s chains. They had
believed the dead remained where they were put.
The dead had believed otherwise.
The Crown of Burned Names shifted against their brow.

A word appeared in the split between its halves.
CROWN.
Sabelle’s breath stopped.
The revenant pressed its palm to the door.
Its skin flattened against the wood, revealing the ridges of bones beneath. Burned names crawled across
the hand in rows, some fresh, some ancient, all written in a script that seemed to move when Sabelle tried
to read it.
“Give it to me,” the revenant said.
“You cannot wear it.”
“Neither can you.”
“I am its keeper.”
“No.”
The palm pushed harder. The door cracked wider.
“You are its wound.”
The words struck deeper than any blade.
Sabelle reached for the crown.
Their fingers touched the blackened metal. It was warm now, almost alive. Beneath their fingertips, the
names rearranged themselves. One became another. One vanished. One opened like a mouth.
They knew what removing it would mean.
The ward had protected them from the voices of the dead. It had given their authority a shape others could
fear. It had hidden the trembling beneath the severity, the rot beneath the vows. Without it, they would
stand before the revenant as flesh, bone, and the private accumulation of every decision that could not be
confessed.
The door opened another inch.
A second finger appeared beside the first.
Sabelle heard boots above.
Not close. Beyond the cellar steps, beyond the sealed inner door. The sound came in a measured rhythm:
someone approaching through the house. Someone who had not yet seen the breach. Someone who
believed the High Inquisitor’s chambers were safe.
The revenant heard them too.
“Open,” it said.
The command rolled through the cellar.
The inner door began to turn on its hinges.
Sabelle looked over their shoulder.

The passage beyond was empty, but a line of gray daylight showed beneath the upper threshold. Dust
drifted through it. A shadow crossed the light and paused.
The hand on the outer door curled.
Sabelle had moments. Perhaps less.
They could remove the Crown of Burned Names and place it upon the revenant. They could let the ward
pass from one prisoner to another and trust the old bindings to hold. They could speak the final syllable
and burn the cellar, the house, and whatever waited beneath the stones.
Or they could do what they had always done when faced with an impossible choice.
They could make the choice belong to someone else.
Sabelle seized the broken halves of the crown and tore them from their brow.
Pain opened them.
The cellar vanished into white.
For one breath, Sabelle was nowhere. No body. No title. No command. No Marrowwatch. There was only
the vast, unmarked silence from which every name had been taken.
Then the crown screamed.
The revenant answered.
The door burst inward.
Black water struck Sabelle full in the chest, carrying the cold of a drowned world. They were thrown
against the wall. Their blade tore free and skidded across the floor, ringing once before the sound was
swallowed.
The revenant stepped through.
It wore the chains like a veil.
Its face remained hidden in darkness, but its hand reached toward the crown lying between them. The split
ward spun over the stones, shedding sparks. Every burned name upon it turned toward the dead thing.
Behind Sabelle, the inner door opened.
A voice called their title from the passage.
The revenant bent.
Its fingers closed around one half of the crown.
And all the bells in Marrowwatch began to ring.

Chapter 2
The blood would not clot.
It hung from Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven’s palm in a dark, trembling bead, bright as a garnet where the
brazier-light found it. They held their hand above the map and watched the drop widen the inked coast
beneath their fingers. Pale Coast. Gloamreach. The name had been written in a careful clerk’s hand,
though the parchment itself smelled of mildew and old smoke.
“Stop that,” said Ossric Ashgrove.
He spoke without looking up. A Quartermaster’s voice, flat from counting things that vanished. His quill
scratched across a slate, marking sacks, casks, bundles of arrows, the small brutal arithmetic by which
hungry men were persuaded that tomorrow remained possible.
Isolde let the blood fall.
It struck the coast.
Ossric’s quill halted.
“You see?” Isolde said. “The map has more courage than you.”
“The map does not need to bleed on its provisions.”
“Nothing needs to bleed. It merely does.”
The chamber had once been a watchroom in Cindermere Hold, though no watch had been kept there for
years. Wind pushed through a split in the stonework and worried the hanging lamps until their flames
leaned east. Beyond the narrow windows, The High Spires rose in black teeth through a veil of snow.
Cindermere Hold had been founded in 246 AS among those heights. Its garrison once numbered 8878.
Now the hold was abandoned, and its towers stood hollow around them, each archway opening on
darkness.
It was not a core holding. That fact had been stamped onto the latest military register in red wax, as if ink
could make a ruin less useful.
Ossric dipped his quill again. “You were asked to bring a decision.”
“I brought one.”
“You brought a wound.”
“Both can be opened.”
At the far end of the table, Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless stood with his hands resting on the pommel of his
sword. No canonical portrait had survived of him, though Isolde suspected that was because portraits
demanded a face one could trust. He had been born in 258 AS, and served as a Warden-Commander with
the posture of a man still waiting for obedience to become a natural law.
The title sat on him like a borrowed cloak.
“The decision,” Ignatz said.
His gaze moved from Isolde’s palm to the red mark spreading across Gloamreach.
“Gloamreach,” said Isolde.

The word seemed to draw the cold nearer.
Gloamreach lay on the Pale Coast, a core location sealed beneath quarantine. Its garrison was 2,483. The
number had been repeated so often in reports that it had become a charm, a wall built from digits against
whatever waited beyond the cordons.
“Gloamreach is closed,” Ossric said.
“So is a grave.”
“Quarantine is not a suggestion.”
“Then you have found your first useful truth.”
Ossric’s mouth tightened. He was young enough to resent the accusation and old enough to know it was
not one. He placed a second slate beside the first. “No wagons enter Gloamreach without authorization.”
“From whom?”
He glanced at Ignatz.
That glance had weight. Isolde felt it settle among the maps, alongside the damp and the iron stink of the
brazier. Ignatz did not move. His secret was known only to those who had purchased it or feared it: Ignatz
Ashgrove the Oathless secretly sold intelligence to The Iron-Ring Cartel. Somewhere beyond these
mountains, merchants of war were reading roads, troop strengths, shortages, names. Somewhere, a price
had been placed on every weakness.
Isolde had learned long ago that secrets did not make a person powerful.
Knowing where to press them did.
“From the proper authority,” Ignatz said.
“And that is?”
“The authority that holds the seal.”
“Which seal?”
His eyes sharpened. A lesser person might have mistaken the expression for anger. Isolde knew better.
Anger burned outward. This was calculation, the cold turning of a blade in its sheath.
The door opened before he could answer.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched entered with snow on their shoulders and sanctity in their wake.
Their robes were pale, their collar stiff with embroidered ash, and the firelight found no warmth in them.
They served as Arch-Prelate, a title that made every room into a chapel and every disagreement into a sin.
Born in 289 AS, Malchior had forged their own lineage papers.
Isolde had seen the proof.
The papers had been folded beneath a reliquary in a chamber where Malchior believed no one else could
kneel. The seals were clever. The ink was old. The blood used to authenticate the family line had belonged
to no ancestor at all.
There were many kinds of fraud. The most durable wore vestments.

“Gloamreach has sent no petition,” Malchior said.
“Perhaps the quarantine has made it shy,” Isolde replied.
“It has made it contained.”
“Contained things rot.”
“So do uncontained things.”
Malchior removed their gloves finger by finger. Their expression remained serene, but beneath the
serenity something strained, something that had been fabricated and must therefore be defended at every
breath.
Ossric’s quill resumed its scratching.
“Quartermaster,” Malchior said, “how much grain remains in Cindermere Hold?”
“Enough for the people presently here.”
“Not what I asked.”
Ossric looked toward Isolde. “There are no people assigned here.”
The wind moved through the cracked wall. One of the lamps hissed.
Isolde smiled without pleasure. “Then the answer is generous.”
Ignatz turned from the window. “We are wasting the night.”
“No,” said Malchior. “The night is wasting us.”
Beyond the table, the old banners of Cindermere hung in strips from the rafters. Their colors had faded
into the shade of bruises. Isolde wondered whether the dead still remembered what those colors had
meant. The War of Drowned Light had begun in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS, leaving 64617 casualties
and no clean victory worth the name. It had collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals, each killing
offered as payment for the last. The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor.
Recorded.
The word had always amused Isolde.
“The War of Drowned Light was not won,” they said. “It was arranged.”
Malchior’s gaze settled on them. “War is rarely arranged by the people who suffer it.”
“The spark that started the War of Drowned Light was secretly staged by The Silent Choir.”
Ossric stopped writing again.
The silence afterward was not empty. It filled with drowned radiance, broken banners, villages burned
beneath a light that had seemed to come from beneath the earth. Isolde had heard the official account
recited in sanctuaries and command tents: an insult, a border death, a righteous answer, a necessary
escalation. Every version ended with The Silent Choir named victor, as if victory could wash the blood
from the hands that had struck the first match.
Malchior folded their gloves on the table. “Those are grave words.”
“Grave words are the only kind that survive burial.”

“You accuse The Silent Choir of engineering the conflict.”
“I state what I know.”
“And how do you know it?”
Isolde looked down at their palm. The cut was closing now. Blood-magic was not healing. Healing was a
kindness. This was coercion, a command issued to flesh until flesh obeyed.
“I listened,” they said.
Ignatz’s hand tightened on his sword.
Was he afraid of the Choir? The Iron-Ring Cartel? Or merely of a truth he could not sell without losing its
value?
“Whether the spark was staged is irrelevant,” he said. “The Choir has power. Gloamreach is under
quarantine. The garrison must remain where it is.”
“Why?”
“Because the order is sound.”
“From whom?”
No answer came.
Isolde felt the old grievance stirring beneath their ribs, patient as a knife hidden in a sleeve. They had
carried it since the day they understood that obedience was merely ambition taught to kneel. They had
been born in 286 AS, into a house that expected loyalty to travel downward forever, from throne to liege,
from liege to sworn hand, from sworn hand to the starving fields. The chain had been called honor because
no one wished to admit it was made of fear.
They had plotted the death of their own liege.
The knowledge moved through them with the steadiness of a second pulse. Not regret. Not yet. Regret
belonged to those who believed another choice would have made them innocent. Isolde had chosen, and
the choosing had revealed what they were.
“Send the grain,” they said.
Ossric’s quill lifted. “Into Gloamreach?”
“Send it to the quarantine gate.”
“That is not entry.”
“Then send someone to open the gate.”
“No.”
The word came from Ossric, though his eyes had already fallen.
Isolde leaned over the map. “You are a Quartermaster.”
“I am.”
“Your duty is to count what can be moved.”

“My duty is to prevent waste.”
“Then count the dead as waste.”
His face went gray beneath the lampglow.
Malchior murmured, “Threats are an undignified form of persuasion.”
“I have never mistaken dignity for virtue.”
“You mistake grievance for strength.”
“I mistake nothing.”
A soft knock came from the corridor.
All four turned.
The knock came again, measured and polite. The kind of knock used by a servant who had been told not to
hear what lay beyond the door.
Ignatz drew his sword.
The blade made a thin sound, almost musical. Isolde watched Malchior’s hand drift toward the hidden
chain beneath their robes, watched Ossric clutch the edge of his slate. The room narrowed around them.
Snow breathed through the cracks. Somewhere below, in the abandoned levels of Cindermere Hold, stone
gave a long, low groan.
“Who is there?” Ignatz called.
No one answered.
Isolde pressed two fingers to the blood-mark on the map.
The red stain moved.
It gathered itself into a narrow line, crawling from Cindermere Hold toward the Pale Coast, toward
Gloamreach and its garrison of 2,483, toward every sealed door and frightened sentry waiting for orders
that had not yet been written.
The door opened by itself.
Beyond it stood only darkness—and, on the threshold, a single wet footprint pointing inward.
The wet footprint darkened as Isolde watched it.
Water gathered in the hollow of the heel, though the flagstones beneath it were dry. A thin sheen trembled
over the print, reflecting the red line on the map. The stain had reached the coast. It pulsed there, once,
twice, like a wound refusing to clot.
Behind Isolde, Ossric made a sound that belonged in a smaller room.
“Shut the door,” Ignatz said.
“The door opened,” Ossric replied.
His voice had gone pale. Isolde could hear the scrape of his breath, the small animal labor of it.
Quartermaster, keeper of stores, man who could name every barrel of salt and every sack of black grain
left in the abandoned hold. He had the hands for ledgers: square-knuckled, ink-stained, restless. Now those

hands hovered uselessly before him.
Ignatz did not turn. “Then shut it.”
The dark beyond the threshold seemed to lean closer.
Isolde kept their fingers on the map. Blood had dried beneath the nail of the first finger, a crescent of their
own making. The stain answered it. They felt the contact deep in the wrist, not pain but invitation—the
patient pressure of something that had learned the shape of their pulse.
Malchior shifted near the hearth. The hem of the Arch-Prelate’s robe whispered over grit and old ash.
“Do not touch the mark again,” Malchior said.
“Then remove my hand.”
“Would you trust me to do that?”
“No.”
The answer came too quickly. It pleased neither of them.
Ignatz stepped toward the door. The absence beyond it did not brighten. In Cindermere Hold, even
abandoned corridors possessed a residue of light: snow through arrow slits, blue lichen in the mortar, the
faint mineral gleam of frost. This was different. The dark had weight. It filled the doorway from lintel to
floor without spilling across the threshold.
The footprint pointed inward.
Ignatz stopped before it.
His shoulders held the authority of a Warden-Commander, but authority was only a garment, and Isolde
had seen garments burn. The epithet the Oathless clung to him more faithfully than any cloak. He had
sworn himself to too many causes, perhaps, or none. In the silence, his hand found the hilt at his side.
“Isolde,” he said.
It was not a request. It was the sound of a man placing a burden where he believed it might break.
They lifted their fingers from the map.
The red line snapped taut.
Something moved in the dark.
Ossric cried out. Malchior’s palm flashed with a low, blue-white flame, and for one instant the doorway
showed itself: a corridor buckled by age, walls sweating black moisture, stairwells descending into the
buried levels. No figure stood there.
But another footprint had appeared.
Then another.
They came toward the room, wet and narrow, each one laid down with deliberate care.
Ignatz drew his sword.
Steel rasped. The sound traveled into the hold and returned altered, as if the stone had tasted it.

“Back,” he ordered.
Ossric obeyed at once. He retreated until the table struck the backs of his knees. The slate in his grasp
slipped and knocked against the wood. A smear of chalk dust fell across the drawn coast.
“Those marks,” Malchior said. “They are not a summons.”
“No,” Isolde said.
“What are they?”
“A trail.”
“To what?”
Isolde looked at the darkness. “To us.”
The Arch-Prelate’s flame guttered. Behind the blue light, Malchior’s face seemed carved from pale wax,
sanctity stretched thin over fear. Their lineage papers had been forged by their own hand; Isolde knew
that, though the knowledge had not yet become a weapon. It rested between them with all the other hidden
blades. Malchior’s authority depended on the world believing in a bloodline that did not exist. Isolde’s
depended on the world failing to learn what they had done to their own liege.
The dark took another step.
Water ran from the new print and vanished into the cracks.
Ossric swallowed. “We should go.”
“There is nowhere to go,” Ignatz said.
“There are upper galleries.”
“The stairs are open to the snow.”
“Then the snow is preferable.”
“You think the snow will stop it?”
“I think I would rather die cold.”
Ignatz glanced back at him. “You were born in 333 AS, Ossric Ashgrove. You have not lived long enough
to choose the manner of your death.”
The quartermaster stared at him.
Isolde saw the insult strike deeper than intended. Ossric’s mouth tightened. There were old facts in the
room, and new ones. The year of his birth lay naked between them: 333 AS. He had been young enough,
perhaps, to believe that ledgers could outlast armies, that a thing written in the proper column could be
made orderly by the force of ink.
“I have lived long enough to know when a door is wrong,” Ossric said.
The footprint appeared at the threshold.
Not beyond it. On it.
Water seeped from the stone as though the hold itself had begun to bleed.

Malchior raised both hands. Flame opened over their fingers, a crown without warmth. “Name yourself.”
The corridor gave no answer.
“By the authority of the ash-seals and the sanctum—”
“Do not invoke what is not here,” Isolde said.
Malchior’s eyes cut toward them. “You presume much for an Unforgiven.”
“And you invoke much for an Arch-Prelate.”
The flame shivered.
Ignatz lifted his sword toward the door. “Enough.”
The word struck the room with military force. For a breath, the darkness withdrew. Isolde felt the map
cool beneath their palm. The red line faded from the coast and drew itself backward, crawling over the
parchment toward Cindermere Hold.
It stopped at the black square representing the hold.
Then the ink began to move.
Letters surfaced beneath the old cartographer’s marks. They were cramped and angular, written in a hand
that seemed to press up from the underside of the page.
Ossric leaned forward despite himself.
“Read it,” Ignatz said.
“I can’t.”
“You can read a manifest.”
“I can read a manifest written by the living.”
The words came one at a time.
ASHEN VANGUARD.
Below them, another line bled through.
THE WAR OF DROWNED LIGHT.
Then:
BELLIGERENT.
The room seemed to tilt.
Isolde had heard the war spoken of in halls where candles were kept low and in courtyards where veterans
carried their silence like a second spine. The Ashen Vanguard had been a belligerent in The War of
Drowned Light. The fact had been carved into histories, repeated by officials, sharpened into grievance.
Yet here it looked less like history than a summons.
The letters beneath it turned wet.
SILENT CHOIR.

BELLIGERENT.
Malchior’s flame collapsed to a thin blue tongue.
“The Silent Choir,” Ossric whispered.
Ignatz did not move. “That is what it says.”
“No,” Malchior replied. “That is what it wants us to believe.”
The map buckled under Isolde’s hand. The old parchment softened, becoming almost flesh. A pulse beat
beneath it.
The Silent Choir had been a belligerent in The War of Drowned Light. The Ashen Vanguard had been a
belligerent in The War of Drowned Light. Two names laid beside one another, not as enemies, not as
victors, but as doors.
Isolde remembered drowned radiance on broken standards, though they had not been there. Memory was a
treacherous servant; it borrowed faces, borrowed smoke, borrowed the terror of those who had survived
and called the theft inheritance. The war had become a language for every later wound. Men used it to
explain hunger, loyalty, betrayal. They used it to excuse the knife once it was in another’s ribs.
The footprints stopped.
Something breathed beyond the door.
Ossric’s slate fell. It struck the floor and split along its middle.
A black line opened through the writing surface. Within it glimmered a dull red, the same red as the mark
on the map. Ossric bent to retrieve it, but Isolde caught his sleeve.
“Leave it.”
“That is my slate.”
“It is open.”
His eyes dropped to the fracture. “It was not.”
“No.”
The split widened with a faint mineral crack. A smell came from it: wet iron, old ash, and the sourness of
sealed rooms. Ossric tried to pull free. Isolde tightened their grip.
For an instant, blood answered blood.
The quartermaster’s pulse leapt beneath the cloth. Isolde felt its rhythm enter their hand, felt how easy it
would be to close their fingers and make the small life inside him stutter. The knowledge came without
effort. That was the horror of their gift. It did not ask permission. It offered solutions.
Their liege had died because Isolde had believed a death could be made clean if enough people benefited
from it.
The memory did not show a face. It showed only a hand falling away from a table, a cup rolling in a
widening red pool, and the silence afterward—vast, obedient, almost holy.
They released Ossric.

He stumbled back.
“Do not touch me,” he said.
“I did not.”
“You thought about it.”
The words landed softly. Malchior heard them. Ignatz heard them. The dark heard everything.
At the threshold, water began to run uphill.
It streamed from the footprints toward the corridor’s unseen depths, gathering in silver threads. The red
mark on the map answered with a slow flare. Cindermere Hold became a black wound ringed in crimson.
Ignatz lowered his sword point.
“Malchior,” he said, “can you seal the doorway?”
“Not against this.”
“Can you seal anything?”
The Arch-Prelate looked down at their hands. “Perhaps.”
“Then do it.”
Malchior stepped toward the threshold.
Isolde caught their arm. Beneath the robe, the Arch-Prelate’s body was rigid with restraint.
“You will not cross.”
“I have no intention of crossing.”
“Your intention is not the danger.”
“What is?”
“The thing that knows we are here.”
Malchior looked at the wet trail. “It knew before the door opened.”
“Yes.”
“And you know what it is?”
Isolde listened.
Far below, stone groaned again. This time the sound did not come from the abandoned levels. It came
from inside the walls, close enough that dust sifted from the ceiling onto the map. The hold had begun to
wake around them. Ancient hinges complained. Somewhere beneath the floor, something heavy dragged
itself over stone.
“No,” Isolde said. “But it knows what I am.”
The answer unsettled Malchior more than ignorance would have.
Ignatz looked between them. “Explain.”

The black fracture in Ossric’s slate widened. A thin red thread emerged, climbed over the edge, and hung
in the air. It pointed not toward the door, but toward Isolde.
Their skin tightened across their ribs.
The thread touched their wrist.
The room vanished.
Not wholly. The table remained beneath their other hand. Snow still breathed through the cracks. Ignatz
was saying something, Malchior was reaching for flame. But beneath those things came another place: a
corridor drowned in pale light, banners hanging wet and broken, voices chanting from behind walls.
The Silent Choir.
The Ashen Vanguard.
The words were not spoken. They were struck, one after the other, like stones against a bell.
Isolde saw a door at the end of that drowned corridor.
On its surface was a footprint made of blood.
They reached toward it—
—and felt a hand close around their throat.
The hand had no warmth.
It was not flesh, though its fingers pressed with the intimate cruelty of flesh. They sank into the soft
hollow beneath Isolde’s jaw, and the pressure found the old scar there—the pale seam left by a blade that
had failed to finish its work. Their breath stopped. Their heart gave one hard beat against the grip.
Then another.
The drowned corridor widened.
Light lay over the stones like milk poured across a grave. Banners hung from the ceiling, their colors bled
into one another until every device had become a bruise. At the far end, the door waited beneath its red
footprint. Behind it, something scraped slowly across the floor.
Isolde tried to turn.
The hand tightened.
Their body remained in the chamber, their other hand gripping the edge of the table while snow hissed
through the wall’s broken seams. Ignatz’s voice came and went, a low shape without meaning. Malchior’s
flame fluttered. The blood-thread across Isolde’s wrist darkened, swelling as though a vein had been laid
atop the skin.
They knew this trick.
Not the vision. The trespass.
A mind could be entered through blood only when blood had first been invited. A cut. A vow. A name
spoken with the mouth open and the soul unguarded.
They had given none of these.

The presence at their throat was not searching for permission.
It was searching for the place where permission had once been.
Isolde bared their teeth. The corridor trembled.
“Take your hand from me.”
The words emerged in both rooms. In the chamber, their voice was a rasp. In the corridor, it rang from the
walls and returned altered, spoken by a hundred mouths.
Take your hand from me.
The fingers vanished.
Isolde fell forward over the table, dragging air into their lungs. The thread snapped from their wrist. A red
bead leapt from the break and struck the wood.
Malchior caught the bead before it rolled.
Their flame burned blue in the hollow of their palm. The light sharpened the angles of their face, made the
skin at their temples seem almost translucent. No lineage, true or forged, could have made that expression
less hungry.
“Do not touch me,” Isolde said.
“I am not touching you.”
“You have my blood.”
“I have a bead of it.”
“Give it back.”
Malchior smiled without pleasure. “You know that is not how blood works.”
Across the table, Ignatz had not moved. Their stillness was more dangerous than Malchior’s smile. The
Warden-Commander watched the broken thread, then the door, then Isolde. Their gaze had the weight of a
lock sliding into place.
The chamber smelled of cold iron and spent magic.
“What did you see?” Ignatz asked.
“Nothing.”
“That answer has never been true when spoken by anyone.”
“It is true now.”
Malchior folded their hand. The blue fire went out, leaving the blood bead on their knuckle. “A corridor.
A door. A footprint.”
Ignatz’s eyes shifted to them. Rivalry lived there—not the hot kind that made men careless, but the older
and more disciplined breed, honed by proximity. Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched was the rival of
Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless. Each had learned the other’s silences. Each knew how long the other could
stand beneath accusation without blinking.

Isolde watched that knowledge pass between them and felt the familiar disgust of being trapped in a room
with people who mistook restraint for virtue.
“The door,” Ignatz said. “What was behind it?”
“I told you what I saw.”
“You told us what stood in front of it.”
“The door was shut.”
“Doors are shut for reasons.”
“Sometimes they are shut because no one wants what is inside to leave.”
“Sometimes,” Malchior murmured, “because someone is afraid to enter.”
The words slid beneath Isolde’s skin.
For an instant, the corridor returned. Pale light. Wet banners. The red mark beneath the door. The pressure
at their throat.
They drove their thumb into the cut on their wrist.
Pain restored the room.
The walls settled around them. The frost clinging to the stones became frost again, not the white residue of
drowned radiance. Malchior’s face returned to its proper distance. Ignatz’s hand remained near the hilt at
their side, though no weapon had been drawn.
Blood welled beneath Isolde’s thumb.
“Do not make a ritual of my pain,” they said.
“No one here is making anything,” Ignatz replied.
“That is a lie.”
The accusation struck cleanly. Ignatz did not flinch, but the muscles at the corner of their mouth tightened.
It was a small betrayal. Isolde treasured it.
Malchior did not look at Ignatz. They looked at the blood on Isolde’s wrist.
“There was a place in the vision,” Malchior said.
“You saw the same thing?”
“No. I saw what the thread wanted me to see.”
“And what did it want?”
“To frighten you.”
“Then it failed.”
“Did it?”
The chamber seemed to contract.

Snow sifted from the ceiling in a soft, continuous whisper. Somewhere beyond the walls, metal struck
metal once, then fell silent. Isolde could feel the old machinery of the hold shifting under them: doors
barred, lamps being checked, watchmen carrying messages from one draught-filled corridor to another.
All of it fragile. All of it pretending the dark could be contained by habit.
Ignatz leaned over the table.
“What was at the door?”
“A footprint.”
“Whose?”
“Blood has no owner.”
“That is philosophy. I asked a question.”
“You asked for certainty in a place built from remnants.”
Ignatz’s gaze hardened. “You have been difficult since we entered.”
“I was difficult before we entered.”
“You have been waiting for something.”
Isolde felt the wound in their wrist pulse.
They had spent years learning how to bury intention beneath injury. Grievance made a convincing mask.
Ambition made a better one. People expected the Unforgiven to desire redress. They did not question the
hand that reached for the knife if the hand trembled at the right moment.
They lowered their eyes to the thread.
It lay across the table in a loose coil, black-red and glistening. The severed end had begun to crawl toward
Malchior’s sleeve.
Malchior noticed.
Their expression changed—not fear, precisely. Recognition without understanding. The flame returned to
their palm, smaller now, trembling as if it had been born in a sickroom.
“Move,” Isolde said.
Malchior did not.
The thread touched their sleeve.
Every lamp in the chamber went out.
Darkness dropped like a curtain.
Ignatz cursed. Steel whispered free.
Malchior’s fire flared, but the flame gave no light. It burned inside itself, a blue seed sealed in glass. The
thread lifted from the table and hung between them, its end pointing toward the far wall.
A shape appeared there.
Not a person. Not entirely.

The outline of a door pressed through the stone, dark against dark. Beneath it, something red began to
seep.
Isolde could smell wet ash.
The door had no hinges. No latch. No sign by which it might be opened. Yet something on the other side
dragged itself toward the threshold, pausing after each pull as though listening.
Ignatz raised the blade.
“Stand back.”
“From what?” Malchior asked.
“From the wall.”
“Excellent command,” Isolde said. “If the wall attacks, we shall be ready.”
The red seepage reached the baseboard.
A single footprint formed upon the stone.
Then another.
They led away from the door.
Toward them.
Isolde’s mouth went dry.
The first print was narrow. The second deeper. The third appeared beside the table, though nothing had
crossed the space between. Blood welled up from the floor in the shape of a heel, then spread into the long
impression of a sole.
The thread tightened around Isolde’s wrist.
This time the hand at their throat did not come from the corridor.
It came from behind them.
They felt the fingers settle against their skin, patient as a lover’s touch.
Malchior whispered a word in a language Isolde did not know.
The door in the wall opened.
There was no room beyond it. Only a fall through pale light, banners, and distant chanting. The sound
entered the chamber without passing through the air. It trembled in the teeth. It made the blood in Isolde’s
veins turn cold.
The Silent Choir.
The words were not heard, but they were understood.
The Ashen Vanguard.
Ignatz stepped backward. For the first time, command left their face.
“What is this?” they said.

Isolde stared into the opening.
At the bottom of the impossible depth, something waited beside the threshold. A figure wrapped in a
quartermaster’s gray, its head bowed, its hands red to the wrists.
The face lifted.
Ossric Ashgrove.
No. Not his face. A face shaped by the memory of him, blurred at the edges, as though seen through deep
water.
A voice rose from the fall.
“Ossric Ashgrove serves at Emberdeep.”
The figure’s mouth did not move.
The chamber lurched. Malchior seized the table. Ignatz caught the wall. Isolde remained upright only
because the hand at their throat held them there.
Beyond the door, the drowned banners began to burn without flame.
Malchior turned on Ignatz. “You knew.”
“I knew nothing.”
“You knew the name.”
“I heard it spoken.”
“By whom?”
The hand tightened.
Isolde clawed at the fingers. Their nails met nothing, yet pain split the skin beneath them. Blood ran down
their neck. The unseen grip pulled their head back, forcing them to look into the opening.
The figure below had moved closer.
Ossric Ashgrove’s borrowed face was now clear enough to show terror.
Behind him, in the pale corridor, stood another shape.
Tall. Hooded. Waiting.
Its hand rested on the red footprint.
Isolde understood then what the blood on the door had been.
Not a warning.
A signature.
Their own blood surged toward it.
They saw, with the clean horror of revelation, the place where the thread had entered their skin. They saw
the old mark beneath the new wound, the tiny scar no healer had ever noticed, the one left by a needle and
a vow made in darkness.

A promise they had thought buried.
A promise that had survived the death they had plotted.
The hooded shape raised its head.
The grip at Isolde’s throat became almost gentle.
And from behind the door, in a voice wearing their own, something said—
“Come home.”

Chapter 3
The rain came down black over the roofs, though Corvus Hollowmere the Pale knew it was only ash.
It gathered in the gutters of the chamber and ran in thin, dirty veins toward the drain. Beyond the shutters,
the city muttered beneath the weather. Wheels groaned over stone. Iron struck iron somewhere below. A
bell sounded once, then stopped, as if a hand had closed around its throat.
Corvus stood beside the table and watched the ash-water bleed through the cracks.
Their gloves were white. Their coat was white. Even the narrow mask hanging from their belt had been
carved from something pale and smooth, though no one in the palace asked from what. People preferred
not to know the materials of a Spymaster’s life.
On the table lay three sealed messages.
One bore the black brand of the Ashen Vanguard.
One bore the hooked crown of House Morvain.
The third had no seal at all.
That one frightened the servants.
It did not frighten Corvus. Fear was a language, and silence was the oldest word in it.
A knock touched the door.
“Enter.”
Hesper Wrenfield came in without haste. An Outrider’s cloak hung from their shoulders, wet at the hem.
They carried a narrow leather tube beneath one arm and kept their other hand near the knife at their hip.
Corvus had never been given any canonical feature by which to remember Hesper Wrenfield; only the role
remained, an Outrider in a rain-dark doorway, breath pale in the cold.
“Spymaster,” Hesper said.
“Hesper Wrenfield.”
The Outrider’s eyes moved to the three messages. “You were expecting one.”
“I was expecting a lie.”
“Then you have received three.”
Corvus looked at them. “How old are you?”
The question startled Hesper more than a threat might have done.
“Born in 404 AS,” they said after a moment.
The answer entered the room and settled there.
Corvus had been born in 351 AS. They remembered the first years only as fragments: a ceiling of cracked
plaster, a woman’s hand withdrawing from a brazier, the taste of soot. Memory had no mercy. It preserved
the useless and burned away the rest.
“You rode from the Pale Coast?” Corvus asked.

“From Gloamreach.”
At that name, the candles bent in their sockets.
Gloamreach lay on the Pale Coast, sealed behind quarantine walls and guarded by a garrison of 2,483. It
was a core location, though the word core had begun to sound like a curse. Nothing at the heart of the
realm was healthy. The coast around it was pallid and wind-scoured, and Gloamreach had taken that
bleakness into itself until its stones seemed to wait for a burial.
“Quarantine holds,” Corvus said.
“It holds.”
“People?”
Hesper’s mouth tightened. “Some.”
“A useful number.”
“I was not asked to count them.”
“No. You were asked to bring me a message.”
Hesper placed the leather tube on the table. “This came through the western gate.”
“From whom?”
“The seal is inside.”
Corvus did not touch it. “And who opened the gate?”
The Outrider looked toward the shuttered window.
There it was: the small pause in which loyalty measured its price.
“Answer me.”
“I do not know.”
Corvus smiled without warmth. “That is the first honest thing anyone has said tonight.”
They took the tube and drew out the parchment. The seal inside was gray wax, pressed with a circle of
narrow teeth.
The Silent Choir.
For one breath the chamber became very quiet.
Corvus’s fingers closed around the message. Beneath the cuff, beneath the skin, the old oath tightened like
wire.
I am a member of The Silent Choir.
The words did not leave their mouth. They did not need to. The oath had been sworn in darkness, and
darkness remembered its own.
Hesper watched them. “You know the mark.”
“Anyone who has survived the courts knows the mark.”

“Does everyone who knows it tremble?”
Corvus broke the seal.
The parchment contained six lines. No greeting. No signature.
A vessel has been found beneath Cindermere Hold.
The ward is waking.
Bring the Sceptre of Final Winter.
Corvus read the lines again.
Cindermere Hold had been founded in 246 AS among The High Spires. Its garrison had once numbered
8878. Now it was abandoned, no longer a core holding, its silhouette blackened against the heights like a
fortress that had been hollowed by its own dead.
The message offered no explanation. The Choir had never mistaken explanation for obedience.
“What does it say?” Hesper asked.
“Your superiors did not send you to read.”
“My superiors sent me to survive the road.”
“Then you have already failed them by arriving.”
Hesper’s hand shifted near the knife. “If I had failed, you would not have the message.”
Corvus folded the parchment. “You will leave before dawn.”
“For Cindermere?”
“For the place where the road ends.”
“Will you come?”
Corvus turned toward the iron cabinet set into the wall. Its lock was old and elaborate, though not old
enough to have survived the Sundering intact. They drew a key from inside their sleeve.
Behind them, Hesper said, “The Iron-Ring Cartel has men watching the eastern roads. House Morvain has
closed its passes. The Ashen Vanguard is calling for levies.”
“And the Bleeding Crown?”
“Buying grain.”
“Then the realm is exactly where it should be.”
Corvus opened the cabinet.
Cold breathed out.
The Sceptre of Final Winter rested within a bed of black wool. It was not large. That was the first deceit of
it. The ward had been forged in 87 AS, before the realm learned to fear the shapes of its own miracles. Its
surface held no jewels, no inscription, no ornament that could soften its purpose. It was simply a length of
pale metal narrowing to a dark point, and looking at it made the teeth ache.
Attunement to it cost 55.

The number had been carved into the cabinet’s inner door by someone who had believed numbers could
protect the living.
Hesper took one step back.
“You know what that is,” Corvus said.
“A ward.”
“The Sceptre of Final Winter.”
The name seemed to dim the candles.
Hesper swallowed. “I thought it was lost.”
“Most things are lost until someone needs them.”
Corvus reached for the sceptre. The cold crossed the room before their hand touched it. Their fingers
closed around the shaft, and the world thinned.
Snow fell upward.
A field of banners drowned beneath white radiance.
Men and women moved through the glare with their faces hidden, their voices reduced to distant knocks.
The memory did not belong to Corvus, but the sceptre gave it freely: a war without triumph, a brightness
buried under water, broken standards sinking into black mud.
The War of Drowned Light began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS.
64617 casualties.
The conflict collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals.
The Silent Choir is recorded as the victor.
Corvus saw the final line behind the vision, written in a hand that did not belong to any living clerk: the
war’s spark was secretly staged by The Silent Choir.
Their grip tightened.
The vision broke.
The chamber returned in pieces—the rain, the candles, Hesper’s breathing, the taste of metal at the back of
Corvus’s throat.
“The war,” Hesper said. “You saw something.”
“I remembered something.”
“You were not there.”
“No.”
“Then whose memory was it?”
Corvus set the sceptre against their shoulder. The cold had entered their bones. “That is the question.”
Hesper stared at the ward. “They say The Silent Choir won the War of Drowned Light.”

“They say many things.”
“The records say it.”
“The records are written by those who survive the burning of the records.”
“And the truth?”
Corvus looked at the sealed window, at the ash-water crawling down the stone. “The truth is that The
Silent Choir is recorded as the victor.”
“That is not what I asked.”
“No. It is what you can carry.”
Hesper took a breath. “Why would the Choir send for this?”
“Because something beneath Cindermere Hold is waking.”
“And why would they trust you with it?”
The old oath moved beneath Corvus’s ribs.
Not pain. Not guilt.
Recognition.
They turned from the cabinet. “Trust is a word used by those who have never had power.”
“Then what word do you use?”
“Obligation.”
Hesper did not move.
Corvus crossed to the table and lifted the message bearing House Morvain’s brand. The wax had been
warmed, opened, and pressed shut again. A lesser hand might have missed the seam.
“Someone has read this,” Corvus said.
“House Morvain?”
“Possibly.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel?”
“Possibly.”
“The Ashen Vanguard?”
“Possibly.”
“And the Bleeding Crown?”
“Possibly.”
Hesper’s expression darkened. “You have no answers.”
“I have answers. I lack the comfort of knowing which ones are true.”

They placed the message beside the Choir’s parchment. “The powers are moving pieces. The Ashen
Vanguard wants bodies. House Morvain wants roads. The Iron-Ring Cartel wants whatever can be
weighed. The Bleeding Crown wants grain enough to make hunger kneel. And The Silent Choir wants a
ward carried into an abandoned hold.”
“While Gloamreach remains quarantined.”
“While Gloamreach remains quarantined.”
“Does the message concern the quarantine?”
Corvus looked again at the gray seal.
“Yes.”
It was not a lie. It was not enough of a truth to be useful.
From below came the scrape of a bolt being drawn. Another followed. The palace had begun its nightly
closing, locking the corridors against thieves, messengers, assassins, and anyone else who believed a door
could be persuaded.
Hesper said, “If we leave before dawn, we need horses.”
“You will have them.”
“Food.”
“You will have that.”
“Passage.”
Corvus lifted the sceptre. Frost flowered across the table’s edge. “You will have no passage.”
The Outrider’s face hardened.
“Roads are watched,” Corvus continued. “Gates are bought. Any official writ can be copied, forged, or
sold. We will go where no one expects a road to be.”
“Cindermere Hold is in The High Spires.”
“I know where it is.”
“Do you know what is beneath it?”
“No.”
At last, Hesper smiled, though there was no humor in it. “Then you are coming blind.”
Corvus fastened the sceptre beneath their coat. The cold spread through the fabric, touching their ribs like
a patient hand.
“No,” they said. “I am coming sworn.”
The candles went out.
In the darkness, something beneath the palace answered with three soft knocks.
The three knocks came again.
Not from the door. Not from the walls.

From below.
Hesper’s hand went to the knife at their belt. The motion was quiet, but Corvus heard the leather whisper.
In the extinguished chamber, the sound seemed indecently loud.
“Did you know?” Hesper asked.
Corvus let the darkness remain between them. “Know what?”
“That the palace had a heartbeat.”
“The palace has many things beneath it.”
“None of them should knock.”
A faint grey entered the room through the shutters, the first suggestion of dawn or ash. It touched the table,
the overturned cup, the empty candlesticks. Hesper’s face appeared by degrees, all watchfulness and
withheld accusation.
Corvus could feel the sceptre beneath their coat. The ward had grown colder since the knocks began. Its
chill no longer resembled metal. It had become a direction.
Down.
They crossed to the far wall.
Hesper did not move aside. “You said there would be no road.”
“There will be no road.”
“You also said we would leave before the palace woke.”
“It has not woken.”
Something answered beneath the floor with a slow scrape.
Hesper’s fingers tightened around the knife. “That is a poor distinction.”
Corvus stopped before a panel of dark wood. Its grain was warped by age, though the rest of the wall had
been kept clean. They placed two fingers against it, then withdrew them before touching the hidden catch.
The sceptre pulsed once beneath their ribs.
A memory rose—not of sight, but of pressure. A mouth held shut. A hand laid over another hand. The
promise had been made in darkness, as all true promises were.
They had sworn to the Silent Choir, and the oath had never loosened.
Not when the war ended. Not when the banners were taken down. Not when men began calling victory a
clean thing.
Hesper watched them. “You are afraid.”
Corvus turned their face toward the Outrider. “No.”
“You lie better when you are afraid.”
“I lie better when I am calm.”
“That is not what I meant.”

“No,” Corvus said. “It is not.”
The hidden catch clicked under their thumb. The panel opened inward without a groan. Behind it waited a
narrow stair descending through the palace’s bones. No lamp burned there. The steps were pale with dust,
and the air rising from below tasted of wet stone, old iron, and something sweetly rotten.
Hesper leaned toward the opening. “You knew this was here.”
“I knew there was a way beneath the palace.”
“You knew.”
“I am Spymaster.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only answer you are owed.”
Hesper looked past them into the stairwell. “You have been here before.”
Corvus did not reply.
They had been here before, though not in the way Hesper imagined. Years of listening had taught them
that every seat of power possessed a second anatomy: passages where servants vanished, chambers where
decrees were rewritten, cavities where older things endured beneath newer stone. The palace had been
speaking for a long time. Most people mistook its speech for settling masonry.
The knocks came a third time.
Hesper flinched despite themself.
Corvus stepped into the stairwell. “Close the panel.”
“I am not following you into a buried throat without knowing what waits at the bottom.”
“Then remain here.”
“And let you go alone to Cindermere Hold?”
“We are not at Cindermere Hold.”
“You intend to reach it.”
“I intend to leave.”
“With me.”
Corvus looked back. The grey light had reached Hesper’s hands. The Outrider’s knuckles were bloodless
around the knife.
For one moment, Corvus saw the first night they had taken responsibility for Hesper Wrenfield. No
ceremony had marked it. No witness had been summoned. Hesper had been younger then, though Corvus
would not permit the memory to furnish details it had no right to keep. There had only been a road, a
sealed message, and a question asked without hope of kindness.
Corvus Hollowmere the Pale had become Hesper Wrenfield’s mentor in the only fashion they understood:
by teaching them which silences concealed danger, which courtesies were sharpened weapons, and how to
walk away before a room decided to kill.

The lesson had not made Hesper obedient.
It had made them difficult to lose.
“Stay behind me,” Corvus said.
Hesper’s expression hardened. “You say that as though I have ever been good at it.”
“No. I say it because you are my charge.”
The words settled between them.
Hesper’s knife lowered by a fraction. “Your charge?”
“My protégé.”
A long silence passed.
Then Hesper said, very softly, “Say it plainly.”
Corvus faced them fully. The stairwell pressed cold against their back.
“I am Corvus Hollowmere the Pale,” they said, “and I am your mentor, Hesper Wrenfield. If you follow
me below, you follow my judgment. If I tell you to run, you run. If I tell you to kill, you ask no question
until you are alive enough to ask it.”
Hesper stared at them.
It was not trust that moved across their face. Trust was a coin Corvus had never possessed in sufficient
quantity to spend. It was something older and more burdensome: recognition.
“You have never called yourself that before,” Hesper said.
“You never asked.”
“I have asked you many things.”
“Not that.”
The Outrider slipped the knife away. “And if your judgment is wrong?”
“It will be.”
“When?”
“I cannot tell you.”
“Then why should I follow it?”
“Because you are not following certainty.”
Hesper stepped into the stairwell. “That sounds like something carved over a grave.”
“Most useful truths do.”
They descended.
The palace above them withdrew by layers. First the chamber vanished, then the adjoining corridors, then
the muffled evidence of waking life: a footfall, the scrape of a bolt, the distant cough of someone who
would never know how near the dark had come. The stair was too narrow for comfort. Hesper’s shoulder

brushed the wall. Dust gathered on their sleeves.
Corvus kept one hand against the stone and the other over the sceptre. The ward’s cold had become almost
unbearable. It did not burn. Burning was alive. This was the stillness after life had been denied.
At the next landing, the steps ended before a door made from blackened timber.
A mark had been cut into it.
Not a sigil. Not a letter. Three shallow lines intersecting at their centers, like cracks in ice.
Hesper came close behind. “Is that yours?”
“No.”
“Do you know it?”
“Yes.”
“Whose is it?”
Corvus placed their palm against the door.
The wood shuddered.
“Not whose,” they said. “What.”
The thing beneath the palace shifted. Dust sifted from the ceiling in a thin veil.
Hesper’s breath touched the back of Corvus’s neck. “You said we were going where no one expected a
road to be.”
“This is not a road.”
“What is it?”
Corvus listened.
Beyond the door, something dragged itself across stone. Once. Twice. Then stopped.
The hidden oath inside Corvus tightened like wire. They felt the shape of it around their heart, the old
command without language. The Choir did not need to speak. It had taught them better than speech.
Open.
Corvus drew the sceptre from beneath their coat.
Even in the dimness, The Sceptre of Final Winter possessed no shine. It drank what little light found it.
Frost filmed the door where its tip hovered, spreading in delicate branching veins.
Hesper saw the weapon and swore under their breath. “You brought that through the palace?”
“I brought it because we are going to The High Spires.”
“To Cindermere Hold.”
“Yes.”
“Cindermere Hold is abandoned.”
“Abandoned things are not harmless.”

“You said the hold would be empty.”
“I said no garrison would be waiting for us.”
“That is not the same thing.”
“No.”
The frost reached the mark in the wood. The three lines whitened, then darkened beneath the ice as though
something on the other side had opened an eye.
Hesper moved to stand beside Corvus rather than behind them.
Corvus caught their wrist.
“Behind me.”
“I am your protégé, not your furniture.”
“Do not mistake defiance for courage.”
“Do not mistake protection for command.”
The words struck cleanly. Hesper had learned that from them.
For an instant, Corvus considered ordering them back. The old instinct rose, precise and bloodless.
Authority was easiest when one pretended it was affection. They had seen rulers do it. They had done it
themselves in smaller rooms, with smaller stakes.
But Hesper’s wrist was warm beneath their fingers. The pulse there was quick, alive, refusing the cold.
Corvus released them.
“Then stand at my left,” they said.
“Why?”
“If the door opens inward, you will be outside its reach.”
“And if it opens outward?”
“You will have learned why I told you to stand behind me.”
The corner of Hesper’s mouth twitched. It was not a smile. It was the shadow of one, starved before it
could form.
Corvus lifted The Sceptre of Final Winter.
The ward answered.
A line of ice split the door from top to bottom. The sound was delicate, almost musical. Beneath it came
another sound: a deep intake, as though the darkness beyond had lungs.
Hesper drew the knife again.
“Mentor,” they said.
Corvus did not look at them. “Yes?”
“If what is beneath this place knows your name—”

“It does not.”
The door opened one handspan.
A breath emerged, carrying the smell of drowned ash.
Corvus’s oath stirred.
Hesper whispered, “You are lying.”
From the gap came a voice that was not a voice, shaping the first syllable of—
Corvus shoved the door wider, and the darkness reached for them.
The darkness reached for them.
Corvus felt it touch the oath before it touched their flesh.
Something cold moved beneath their ribs, not through the body but behind it, where promises were kept
after memory had been scoured away. The hidden words rose in them without sound. The Silent Choir had
taught them that silence was not the absence of speech. It was speech stripped of mercy.
Their hand tightened around The Sceptre of Final Winter.
