The ward’s shaft had grown white as bone. Frost crawled over the knuckles, biting through glove and skin.
The Sceptre of Final Winter had been forged in 87 AS, in a furnace that had burned without flame, and its
price had never been measured in coin. Attunement to it cost 55. Corvus had paid in sleep first, then in
warmth, and lately in the small private certainties by which a person knew themselves.
The dark pressed closer.
Hesper caught Corvus by the sleeve. “You said it did not know your name.”
“It knows the shape of names.”
“That is not what I asked.”
“No,” Corvus said. “It is what you can bear.”
A pale filament uncoiled from the gap and brushed the floor between them. It made no sound, yet the
stones whitened beneath it. The filament paused beside Hesper’s boot.
Hesper lowered the knife.
Corvus saw the movement and hated them for it. Not because the blade would have availed them, but
because fear had made an offering of their hand.
“Do not answer it,” Corvus said.
“Answer what?”
The filament rose.
The voice came again, deeper now. It did not emerge from the chamber. It emerged from the wall, the
floor, the marrow of the hold.
“Cor—”
Corvus drove The Sceptre of Final Winter into the threshold.

Winter burst outward.
The corridor filled with the crack of breaking lakes. Ice sealed the opening, not cleanly but in jagged
overlapping plates. Something struck the other side. The door shuddered. A darkness like wet cloth spread
through the ice, and behind it a pressure gathered, patient and immense.
Hesper stumbled back. “You knew.”
“I suspected.”
“You brought me here knowing?”
“I brought you here because you could walk where I could not.”
“Because I am an Outrider?”
“Because you were born in 404 AS.”
The words escaped before Corvus could stop them.
Hesper stared. Their face became strange in the blue light, not changed, only emptied of all the answers
they had expected to receive.
“What does that have to do with this?”
“Everything that survives the Sundering has a preference for the newly made.”
“I am not newly made.”
“No.” Corvus withdrew the sceptre. The ice groaned. “But you are younger than the wound.”
The door bucked.
A fracture raced through the frozen seal. Beyond it, the voice shaped another syllable. Corvus heard no
name this time. They heard a number.
Eight.
Then seven.
Then the scraping procession of figures marching through a language that had forgotten whether it was
counting the dead or summoning them.
Hesper’s knife hand trembled once. “What is behind that door?”
“An account.”
“Of what?”
“What was spent.”
The ice split in a vertical seam. Through it, Corvus saw a chamber sunk far beneath the hold. There were
no walls in the ordinary sense. Shelves and pillars rose from a black floor, all of them coated in a mineral
sheen like old tears. Thin lights hung overhead, drowned in glass. They shone without illuminating
anything.
On the nearest pillar, letters had been carved into the stone.
THE WAR OF DROWNED LIGHT

Below the title:
BEGAN IN 225 AS.
ENDED IN 235 AS.
Corvus’s breath fogged before them.
Hesper leaned toward the opening. “That war.”
“Do not read aloud.”
“Why?”
“Because it is listening.”
Hesper read the next line anyway.
“64617 casualties.”
The chamber inhaled.
The lights overhead dipped together.
For one instant Corvus smelled salt, hot iron, and the rotting sweetness of bodies left beneath broken
banners. They saw a shore that was not this shore: drowned radiance trembling across black water, men
and women advancing beneath light that poured from the sky in sheets, their faces shining through mud
and blood. Then came the decade after—the guerrilla reprisals, though the stone did not call them that. It
showed them in fragments. A knife beneath a sleeping tongue. A farmhouse burning with its doors barred
from within. A child holding a banner whose color had been washed away.
The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor.
The words had been carved deep enough to outlast the hold.
Beneath them, in a thinner hand:
THE WAR’S SPARK WAS SECRETLY STAGED BY THE SILENT CHOIR.
Hesper turned slowly.
Corvus met their gaze.
The old oath moved again beneath their ribs, pleased by the confession.
“You knew that too,” Hesper whispered.
“I knew the truth was more poisonous than the record.”
“And you let me ride beside you through all this?”
“You rode beside me because you were an Outrider.”
“That answer is becoming a cowardice.”
“It has always been one.”
Behind the ice, something dragged itself across the floor.
Corvus looked back into the chamber.

A second pillar stood beyond the first. Its inscription was almost obscured by black growth, but the ward’s
frost cleared the letters as Corvus watched.
CINDER MERE HOLD.
No. Not two words. The stone insisted on the other shape.
CINDERMERE HOLD.
FOUNDED IN 246 AS AMONG THE HIGH SPIRES.
GARRISON: 8878.
STATUS: ABANDONED.
CLASSIFICATION: NOT A CORE HOLDING.
The chamber had been built to preserve such facts, but preservation had not made them harmless. Corvus
could feel the numbers moving in the dark, each one a small door. Cindermere Hold had once held 8878
soldiers, and now the place could not hold two living intruders without opening its buried mouth.
Hesper wiped frost from the stone. “There are no garrison fires above.”
“There are no soldiers above.”
“You said it was empty.”
“I said nothing.”
“You said the hold was abandoned.”
“Abandoned is not empty.”
A sound came from deeper within the chamber: a faint chiming, as of spoons striking the rims of cups.
Corvus lifted their head.
At the far end, another inscription glimmered through the dark.
GLOAMREACH.
THE PALE COAST.
GARRISON: 2,483.
STATUS: QUARANTINED.
The letters seemed damp. A bead of water formed beneath the name and slid downward, leaving a black
trail.
Hesper moved nearer the gap. “Gloamreach is on the coast.”
“Yes.”
“Then why is it written here?”
“Because this place keeps what the powers deny.”
“Which power denies Gloamreach?”
Corvus did not answer.

The question passed into the chamber and returned altered.
Which power denies—
The voice broke off.
Something touched the inner side of the frozen door.
Not struck. Touched.
The ice bent inward around the shape of a hand.
Corvus’s hidden oath tightened until their heart stumbled.
They had served as Spymaster long enough to understand that every fortress had two architectures: the one
built of stone, and the one built of omissions. Cindermere Hold had been abandoned, yet its ledgers
remained. Gloamreach was quarantined, yet its name had traveled inland. The War of Drowned Light had
been won, yet its dead continued to count themselves.
They had been born in 351 AS. That fact had always seemed to Corvus like an accident of ash and
weather, a mark in a register. Now it felt like a summons. The chamber had been waiting for a person born
after the war, before the old order finished rotting. Someone whose skin carried neither victory nor defeat,
only inheritance.
Hesper looked at them. “What are you?”
Corvus almost laughed.
The sound would have been a cruelty.
“I am Corvus Hollowmere the Pale.”
“That is a name.”
“It is the one that opens doors.”
“And beneath it?”
The pressure behind the ice increased. The ward began to crack.
Corvus remembered the first time the Silent Choir had placed a vow upon their tongue. Not the place, not
the hands that held the basin, not the shape of the blade. Only the sensation remained: a darkness entering
them with the gentleness of a guest who intended to stay.
They had sworn an oath to the Silent Choir.
They had sworn it hidden.
Now the chamber knew.
A final panel of stone slid out from the wall. Behind it lay a narrow recess, and within the recess a black
cradle held the shape of a crown. No metal gleamed there. No jewel caught the cold. It looked as if
someone had removed a crown from a living head and left only the absence.
Hesper raised the knife again. “Is that what called you?”
“No.”
“Then what did?”

Corvus stared at the crown-shaped hollow.
The voice spoke from directly behind them.
“Spymaster.”
Hesper spun.
Nothing stood in the corridor. Only the dark, the whitening stones, and the thin red line where Corvus’s
blood had begun to run from the hand gripping The Sceptre of Final Winter.
The ice shattered.
A wind poured through the doorway, carrying the smell of drowned ash. It lifted Hesper’s cloak and drove
the fragments across the floor. In the chamber, every inscription flared at once.
225 AS.
235 AS.
64617.
246 AS.
8878.
87 AS.
55.
404 AS.
351 AS.
The numbers circled them in cold fire.
Hesper seized Corvus’s arm. “We leave.”
Corvus could not move.
From the black cradle, something began to rise.
Not a crown. Not a head.
A voice wearing both.
“Corvus Hollowmere the Pale,” it said.
The oath opened inside them like a second mouth.
And from the dark beyond the threshold, the Silent Choir answered.

Chapter 4
The bell beneath the chapel had no tongue, yet it rang.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched felt the note in the bones of their hands before it entered the air.
A pressure. A warning without language. The candles along the crypt wall leaned toward the sound, their
flames thin and blue, as though the dark beneath the chapel were drawing breath.
They did not look down.
An Arch-Prelate could not be seen listening to the foundations.
“Read it again,” said Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven.
Her voice held the dry patience of a blade being sharpened. She stood beyond the iron table, her
Blood-Mage’s robes blackened at the cuffs, the red stitching at her throat bright as a fresh wound. The
torchlight found no softness in her face. Grievance had made a temple of it.
Malchior kept one hand upon the parchment.
“The report is sealed,” they said.
“Seals are wax.”
“Some are law.”
“Law is also wax, if the hand is hot enough.”
The bell beneath them gave another soundless toll.
Malchior’s fingers tightened. Beneath the sleeve of their vestment, the scar along their wrist prickled with
remembered heat. They had been born in 289 AS, under a sky their mother had called ash-white. The
lineage papers said more than that. They said blood, inheritance, sanctity. They said that Malchior had
been born to a house whose name opened doors and closed mouths.
The papers were forged.
Not altered. Not amended. Forged.
Every letter of their descent had been raised by their own hand, each seal pressed while the ink was still
wet, each ancestor invented from the silence between records. The lie had carried them to the office of
Arch-Prelate. It had carried them here, into a crypt where dead wars were kept in iron drawers and living
men came to bargain over them.
Across the table, Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless watched without blinking.
Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless was a Warden-Commander.
The title sat upon him like armor, though no armor showed. Authority had its own shape: the stillness of a
person accustomed to being obeyed, the careful economy of every glance. Born in 258 AS, Ignatz had
learned the value of silence in places where oaths were spoken loudly. Malchior had heard another truth
whispered through locked rooms: Ignatz secretly sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel.
The knowledge had not made him less dangerous.
It had made him legible.

“The quarantine at Gloamreach remains in force,” Malchior said. “The garrison is 2,483. The Pale Coast is
closed to passage.”
Isolde’s mouth bent.
“Closed to whom?”
“To everyone.”
“Then why does the report bear the Cartel’s cipher?”
Malchior looked at the parchment. A black ring had been stamped in the lower corner, faint but
unmistakable. The Iron-Ring Cartel never needed to sign its messages. Its mark was a threat precisely
because it resembled a craftsman’s blemish.
Ignatz reached for the document.
Malchior placed their palm over it.
For one breath, the crypt narrowed around them. The candles guttered. Somewhere in the stone, water
moved.
“You presume much, Arch-Prelate,” Ignatz said.
“I preserve much, Warden-Commander.”
“You preserve paper.”
“I preserve the realm.”
“The realm has five powers,” Isolde murmured. “The Ashen Vanguard. House Morvain. The Silent Choir.
The Iron-Ring Cartel. The Bleeding Crown. Each believes the realm is something it can possess.”
Her eyes settled on Malchior.
“Which one do you serve?”
The question was soft. That made it worse.
Malchior withdrew their hand from the parchment and turned toward the wall. A map had been nailed
there beneath a veil of dust. The High Spires rose in black strokes at its center, jagged and inhospitable.
Far to the coast, a pale smear marked Gloamreach.
“Cindermere Hold,” they said.
Ignatz’s gaze moved to the map.
“Why speak of it?”
“Because the report names it.”
The abandoned hold had been founded in 246 AS among The High Spires. Its garrison had once numbered
8878. Now the place stood empty, and it was not a core holding. Malchior had seen its silhouette once
from a mountain road: blackened towers thrust into cloud, battlements without banners, windows staring
down upon the ravines like blind eyes.
“Cindermere Hold is a ruin,” Ignatz said.
“Ruins are honest. They admit what happened to them.”

“Nothing happened there.”
“Nothing is never empty.”
Isolde drifted closer to the table. She did not walk so much as arrive, her robes whispering over the
flagstones.
“The report says movement beneath the eastern vaults,” she said. “It says the old armory has been
opened.”
“The report says many things,” Ignatz replied.
“And you know which are false?”
“I know what I have been told.”
“By whom?”
His expression did not change, but one of the candles went out.
Malchior felt the familiar pressure behind their eyes, the demand to perform sanctity. Their office required
certainty. Their blood—claimed, fabricated, treacherous—required them to appear as though certainty had
been bestowed upon them at birth.
They lifted the parchment.
“The War of Drowned Light began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS, with 64617 casualties.”
The number seemed to darken the room.
Isolde’s gaze lowered. Ignatz’s jaw hardened.
“The conflict collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals,” Malchior continued. “The Silent Choir is
recorded as the victor.”
“Recorded,” Isolde said.
“Yes.”
“Their spark was secretly staged by them.”
The words came from Ignatz.
For the first time, Malchior saw strain beneath his composure—not fear, precisely. Recognition. A man
hearing a door open in a house he had believed abandoned.
The Silent Choir had staged the spark of the war in secret. The knowledge was not meant to be spoken
where stone could carry it. Yet the crypt had been built for dangerous truths, and the dead did not repeat
what they heard.
Malchior folded the report once.
“The reprisals did not end with the victory.”
“They never do,” Isolde said.
“You speak as though you know.”
“I know what vengeance costs.”

Her hand rested near the knife at her belt. Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven, born in 286 AS, Blood-Mage,
wore her epithet as other people wore mourning. There was a secret beneath her secret: she had plotted the
death of her own liege. Malchior had never asked how the plot had been made, nor whether the liege had
died. The truth itself was a dangerous enough companion.
Isolde smiled without warmth.
“You should not have brought us here.”
“I did not bring you,” Malchior said. “You came.”
“Then you should not have let us remain.”
“Would you have obeyed?”
“No.”
The bell beneath the chapel trembled again.
Dust fell from the ceiling in a fine gray rain. It silvered Isolde’s hair and settled upon Ignatz’s shoulders.
Malchior thought of ash upon their own robes, ash upon the forged papers, ash filling the mouths of all the
ancestors they had invented.
The crypt door stood behind them. It had no visible lock.
Ignatz turned toward it.
“Someone is below.”
“No one is below,” Malchior said.
“Then the bell is ringing for the dead.”
“Those are the same thing.”
He looked back at them. “You have a habit of making blasphemy sound like doctrine.”
“It is an Arch-Prelate’s privilege.”
“Is it lineage that grants the privilege?”
The words struck cleanly.
Malchior heard the rustle of parchment beneath their fingers. Their claimed lineage was suspect. The truth
lay hidden in a chest beneath their sleeping chamber, behind a panel carved with a saint’s face. Every time
they touched their seal, they remembered shaping the false crest. Every time someone called them
Flame-Touched, they felt the lie flare beneath their skin.
Isolde watched them with sudden interest.
“Careful, Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless,” she said. “Some questions are snares.”
“Some answers are weapons.”
“Then tell us which weapon you carried to the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
The room became still.

Ignatz’s eyes moved to her, and the force of his silence was almost physical. Malchior imagined the
Cartel’s cipher opening like a black flower between them. Intelligence sold. Routes exposed. Names
placed into other hands. The oathless guardian standing at the gate while coin passed unseen behind his
back.
No accusation had been made aloud.
No denial followed.
Malchior felt the chapel waiting for judgment. They could condemn him. They could condemn Isolde.
They could condemn themselves. The machinery of authority was simple when one did not examine what
powered it.
Instead, they set the parchment on the iron table.
“The eastern vaults of Cindermere Hold were opened before the report was written,” they said.
“Gloamreach sealed its gates afterward. Someone is moving between the High Spires and the Pale Coast.”
“Someone,” Isolde repeated.
“The Silent Choir,” Ignatz said.
“Or the Cartel,” Isolde replied.
“Or the Crown.”
“The Ashen Vanguard,” Malchior said. “House Morvain.”
Five powers. Five hungers. The names seemed to gather in the crypt, each one carrying its own weather.
A thin line of blood appeared beneath Isolde’s fingernail. She had not cut herself. Malchior saw the bead
rise, dark and deliberate, then slide down her finger.
“Open the eastern vaults,” she said.
Ignatz gave a humorless breath. “You first.”
“I am not the one who wears a commander’s title.”
“I am not the one who killed a liege.”
The blood on Isolde’s finger stopped moving.
Malchior stepped between them.
The heat came then—not from the candles, nor from the buried bell, but from somewhere within their
chest. It spread behind the ribs and climbed the throat. Flame-Touched, the faithful called them.
Flame-Touched, the papers proclaimed. The word was meant to sanctify what it could not explain.
They raised two fingers.
Every candle in the crypt ignited at once.
The sudden brightness threw the three shadows across the walls: Isolde’s long and crooked, Ignatz’s
straight-backed and armed with authority, Malchior’s crowned in fire.
The door behind them opened.
No hand touched it.

Beyond lay a stair descending into a darkness deeper than the crypt’s own. Cold air flowed upward,
carrying the smell of wet stone and something older—oil, perhaps, or extinguished incense.
Ignatz drew his sword.
Isolde’s blood lifted from her finger in a thin red thread.
Malchior heard the bell below ring once more, and this time the sound had a voice.
“Arch-Prelate,” it whispered from the dark.
Malchior took the first step down.
The stair received him without echo.
Stone pressed close on either side, sweating beneath a skin of mineral sheen. The candlelight clung to
Malchior’s sleeves and the gilt thread at his throat, but it could not descend far. Each step swallowed the
flame a little more completely, until the darkness seemed not an absence of light but a substance through
which he was wading.
Behind him, Isolde followed barefoot-soft despite her boots. Ignatz came last, sword drawn, the blade
whispering against the wall whenever the stair narrowed.
“Arch-Prelate,” said the voice below.
Malchior stopped.
The word had not come from ahead. It had risen through the soles of his feet.
Isolde’s blood-thread trembled in the air beside him, bright as a filament of garnet. “It knows your office.”
“It knows what the crypt was built to hear,” Malchior said.
“Then it knows more than you do.”
He turned his head. Her face was half-lit, the other half made severe by shadow. Isolde Fellgard the
Unforgiven watched him with the stillness of a woman who had already decided what his corpse might be
worth.
Ignatz’s sword lifted behind them.
“Keep walking,” he said.
Malchior looked at him. The dark made a mask of the Warden-Commander’s face, but authority needed
no features. It entered a room before its bearer did and remained after he left. Ignatz Ashgrove the
Oathless was rival of Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched; the truth sat between them like a drawn
blade, honed by every council chamber and every sealed dispatch.
“Your concern is touching,” Malchior said.
“My concern is preventing whatever waits below from reaching the Hold.”
“Then you should have brought a larger concern.”
Ignatz’s sword point settled nearer to Malchior’s spine. “You mistake restraint for obedience.”
“No,” Malchior said. “I mistake neither.”
The bell rang again.

This time the stair shuddered. Dust sifted from the joints in the masonry. Isolde’s blood-thread snapped
taut, and a bead of red rolled upward along it, against the pull of the earth.
Her eyes narrowed.
“Something is calling that,” she whispered.
“Something is answering,” said Malchior.
The stair ended beneath an arch blackened by old fire. Beyond it spread a chamber so broad that the candle
in Malchior’s hand could not find its boundaries. There were pillars, perhaps, or standing stones. Their
upper reaches vanished into dark. Water dripped at intervals with the patience of a clock whose maker had
forgotten its purpose.
A thin floor of ash covered the stone.
Malchior stepped across the threshold.
The fire in his candle bent toward him.
Not away from the draft. Toward him.
He felt the heat gather beneath his skin, the old inward burning that had given him his epithet and made
every blessing spoken over him sound like an accusation. Flame-Touched. The title had once been a gift.
Now it was a lock with no visible key.
A pale line appeared in the ash.
It curved from the far dark to the hem of his robe.
Isolde came forward, crouched, and touched it with one finger. Blood welled immediately from the nail.
“Not a line,” she said. “A boundary.”
Ignatz stepped beside her. “For what?”
“For whoever believes they own the room.”
“Then stand outside it.”
Her mouth moved in something too sharp to be called a smile. “You first.”
The bell sounded beneath the floor.
The pale boundary flared. Every pillar in the chamber revealed itself at once, not stone but stacks of sealed
tablets, black slabs leaning one against another. Their surfaces were crowded with impressions: names,
decrees, genealogies, condemnations. Wax seals had hardened across them like tumors.
Malchior saw the shape of a throne in the center, fashioned from tablets. No sovereign sat upon it. A
shallow basin rested in its seat, filled with a darkness that reflected no candlelight.
Isolde’s blood-thread drew toward the basin.
Ignatz’s sword did not waver. “What is this place?”
“An archive.”
“Of what?”

Malchior did not answer.
He knew the script on the nearest tablet. It was an older hand than the one used in the upper crypt, pressed
into the surface with a stylus that had cut rather than written. The first mark was a flame enclosed in a
broken crown. Beneath it, the letters were rubbed away.
His throat tightened.
The tablet bore the shape of the lineage papers he had forged.
Not the same script. Not the same seals. But the same claims, the same ancient architecture of belonging.
Blood descending through names. Names made into keys. Keys made into doors.
He had fabricated his own inheritance with patient hands and borrowed ink. He had built a house where
there had been none, then prayed until the walls began to cast shadows.
The darkness in the basin stirred.
“Arch-Prelate,” it said.
Malchior’s hand tightened around the candle. Wax spilled over his fingers. He did not flinch.
Ignatz noticed. “You recognize it.”
“I recognize a voice.”
“Whose?”
“Not yours.”
“Answer him.”
The command struck harder than it should have. Malchior’s authority had been assembled from ceremony,
silence, and the confidence of those who feared appearing ignorant. Ignatz had always understood that. He
did not attack the office directly; he worried at its joints until it creaked.
Malchior faced the basin. “What do you want?”
The darkness drew itself upward, taking the vague outline of a standing figure. No face appeared. Only a
hollow where the head should have been, and within that hollow a small red glow.
“Name.”
“My name is spoken.”
“Name.”
“Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched.”
The chamber answered with a long exhalation.
The tablets shivered against one another. Seals cracked. From the darkness came a smell of damp ash and
old blood.
“False,” said the voice.
Isolde looked at him.

Ignatz did not. That was worse. His attention remained fixed on the figure, but the silence around his
sword became suddenly deliberate, expectant.
Malchior felt the forged papers under his coat, folded into the hidden lining where no hand but his had
touched them in years. The parchment was not truly there; he had left it in the sanctum above. Yet the
memory of its weight pressed against his ribs.
A name was a bridge. A name was a weapon. A name was the first lie a child was taught to tell about
being wanted.
“Many things are false in this realm,” Malchior said. “It does not make them powerless.”
The red glow brightened.
“Blood.”
Isolde’s head tilted. “It wants blood.”
“It has yours already,” said Ignatz.
“Not enough.”
The blood-thread between her finger and the darkness snapped. Red droplets flew across the chamber and
struck the basin. The darkness drank them without rippling.
Isolde inhaled through her teeth. Her wounded finger had opened again, the cut widening as though some
unseen mouth worried it.
Malchior caught her wrist.
Her skin was cold. Beneath it, her pulse beat with brutal steadiness.
“Release me.”
“Not until you stop feeding it.”
“Then stop holding me.”
She twisted. The movement was quick and practiced, and a red stain blossomed beneath Malchior’s nail
where her blood entered his skin. Heat flashed through him. The chamber lurched.
For an instant he stood somewhere else.
A hall of banners drowned in pale light.
Broken standards hung from rafters slick with rain. The floor was crowded with the dead, their armor
filmed in white residue, their open mouths filled with glowing water. Somewhere beyond the walls, a host
cried victory without joy. The sound continued long after the bodies stopped moving.
Then the vision collapsed.
Malchior staggered. Ignatz caught his shoulder, not from kindness but necessity.
“What did you see?” the Warden-Commander demanded.
Malchior pulled free. “A warning.”
“Whose?”

“The sort that kills the person who understands it.”
Isolde wiped her blood against her palm. Her gaze had become fever-bright. “The basin is a mouth. The
tablets are teeth. It is trying to swallow a name.”
“Yours?” Ignatz asked.
“No.”
Both of them looked at Malchior.
He hated them for the speed of it. Hated the room, the bell, the old stones that had waited beneath the crypt
while he dressed himself in sanctity. Most of all, he hated the small, treacherous part of him that wished
the thing would speak again, clearly enough to tell him whether the papers had always been doomed.
The figure leaned over the basin.
“Give the name,” it said.
Malchior raised the candle.
The flame lengthened, thin and white. Every tablet in the chamber caught its reflection. For a heartbeat,
the archive glittered with innumerable false lineages: kings without kingdoms, saints without graves, heirs
who had purchased their blood with ink.
Among them, his own claim shone brightest.
Ignatz saw it.
Malchior knew by the sudden stillness of him.
“You forged something,” Ignatz said.
The accusation was quiet. That made it final.
Isolde turned toward Malchior, not surprised. She had the expression of a woman discovering that a
locked door had never possessed a wall.
“Your lineage,” she said.
The figure in the basin opened its faceless mouth.
Malchior’s candle guttered.
He could confess. The word rose cleanly, almost sweetly. He could let it leave him and watch his office
fall away, watch the robes become cloth, the seals become metal, the sacred histories become stories told
by people who had never needed to survive them.
Instead he thrust the candle into the basin.
Fire struck darkness.
The chamber screamed.
The sound entered his bones and shook them like dice. Tablets toppled. Seals burst in showers of red wax.
Isolde cried out as her blood-thread whipped around her throat. Ignatz seized the thread with his free hand,
and blood ran across his palm.
Malchior leaned over the basin.

Within the fire, the faceless figure had found eyes.
They were his own.
“Speak,” it commanded.
The flame climbed his arm. Skin blackened beneath his sleeve. He smelled himself burning and heard
Ignatz shouting something lost beneath the bell.
Then, from somewhere behind the tablets, another voice whispered a name Malchior had never—
The voice whispered a name Malchior had never permitted to pass his own lips.
“Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched.”
The fire went still.
Not dimmer. Still.
Even the bell’s convulsion ceased. In the sudden quiet, he heard the wet hiss of his sleeve burning and the
small, involuntary click of Isolde’s teeth. Ignatz’s grip tightened on the blood-thread. His hand was slick
with her blood, yet he did not release it.
The voice spoke again, from the dark behind the tablets.
“Arch-Prelate.”
Malchior wrenched his arm from the basin. Flame came with it, clinging to his skin in a thin blue veil. He
struck at it with his palm. Pain burst white behind his eyes. The fire vanished, leaving the flesh beneath his
sleeve black and split.
“Who speaks?” he demanded.
His voice had authority in it. He had trained that authority into every syllable, polished it until it sounded
older than his bones. The chamber knew the sound. The tablets knew it. Even the men and women who
hated him knelt when he used it properly.
The dark did not kneel.
A tablet slid from its stack and struck the floor. Its clay face broke open. Within the fracture, ink glistened
like trapped blood.
Isolde looked toward it. “Malchior.”
He turned on her.
Her blood-thread had tightened across her throat, drawing a red line beneath her jaw. The Blood-Mage’s
eyes were bright with pain, but not fear. Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven had always worn grievance like a
second skin. Even now, with her own blood choking her, she watched him as if waiting for him to reveal
which part of himself deserved hatred.
“Tell him,” the voice said.
“Tell me what?”
“The paper.”
Malchior’s burned hand began to tremble.

Ignatz saw it. Of course he saw it. The Warden-Commander missed little when suspicion had been given a
shape. He had no need of an oath to make his attention feel like a blade.
“What paper?” Ignatz asked.
The question was too mild.
Malchior faced him. “Release her.”
“Answer the voice.”
“You mistake a haunting for an order.”
“I mistake nothing.”
The bell above them gave one slow, dying toll.
Beyond the chamber walls, the fortress stirred. Boots crossed stone. Someone shouted for water.
Somewhere a latch broke, followed by the frightened murmur of servants who had learned that disasters
wore official robes when they entered through the sanctum doors.
Malchior pressed his unburned hand against the basin’s rim. Heat crawled through the stone and into his
wrist.
The faceless figure had disappeared from the fire. In its place, letters moved beneath the surface—pale
strokes chasing one another through the ash.
He knew the script.
He had paid a scribe to copy it.
He had paid another to destroy the first copy.
“I was born in 289 AS,” he said.
Isolde’s eyes narrowed.
Ignatz’s mouth hardened. “That is not an answer.”
“It is the answer the basin wants.”
The letters stopped.
Beneath them appeared a line of black, exact and merciless:
MALCHIOR CINDERVALE THE FLAME-TOUCHED — BORN IN 289 AS.
Then another line unfolded.
LINEAGE: FORGED BY THE CLAIMANT.
The chamber seemed to lean toward him.
Malchior heard the old rasp of parchment beneath a seal. Saw the false descent he had constructed piece
by piece: names borrowed from dead ledgers, marriages lifted from ruined registries, a bloodline stitched
out of ash and clerical ink. He had not inherited sanctity. He had manufactured its proof.
The Arch-Prelate was a title. The Flame-Touched was a wound. The lineage was a lie.
Ignatz read the basin. His expression did not change, but something behind his eyes closed.

Isolde laughed once. It was a small sound, nearly tender.
“So the holy blood was paper.”
Malchior turned his burned hand toward her. “And yours was spilled for ambition.”
Her smile died.
The blood-thread shuddered. Isolde’s fingers flexed, and the strand around her throat loosened by a hair.
The basin wrote again.
ISOLDE FELLGARD THE UNFORGIVEN — BLOOD-MAGE.
The title appeared beneath her name in a wash of red.
SECRET: PLOTTED THE DEATH OF HER OWN LIEGE.
Ignatz looked at her now.
Not surprise. Confirmation.
Isolde’s face became very still. “Do not look at me as if you have never known what loyalty costs.”
“I know what it costs,” Ignatz said.
The basin darkened.
IGNATZ ASHGROVE THE OATHLESS — WARDEN-COMMANDER.
Malchior felt the room contract around the name. Ignatz’s hand remained on the blood-thread, but the
muscles in his forearm had gone rigid.
A final line surfaced beneath it.
SECRET: SELLS INTELLIGENCE TO THE IRON-RING CARTEL.
No one spoke.
The fire whispered against the basin.
Malchior had suspected treachery. He had used suspicion as a private comfort, a way to explain why
Ignatz’s orders always arrived sharpened against him, why patrols went blind at the wrong moment, why
the Iron-Ring Cartel seemed to know the movement of the Ashen Vanguard before the Vanguard knew
itself.
But suspicion was vapor. This was ink.
Ignatz released the thread.
Isolde stumbled forward, coughing, and seized the front of his coat. The blood around her throat ran down
her collar in thin red paths.
“You oathless dog,” she breathed.
Ignatz did not strike her. He looked only at Malchior.
“Burn it.”
The command came quietly.

Malchior almost obeyed. The basin had exposed them all, but the letters were still only letters. Fire could
eat letters. He had built a life on that simple mercy.
Then the basin showed him Cindermere Hold.
Its black towers stood among the High Spires beneath a sky the color of old bruises. Snow—or
ash—moved across the image. The keep’s walls were empty. Wind passed through the gatehouse and
worried at torn banners.
A line of script formed above the ruin.
CINDERMERE HOLD — FOUNDED IN 246 AS AMONG THE HIGH SPIRES.
Another line followed.
GARRISON: 8878.
Then:
ABANDONED. NOT A CORE HOLDING.
The image changed.
Gloamreach appeared along the Pale Coast, pallid beneath a low white sky. Its walls were sealed.
Watchfires burned behind narrow slits, their light weak and jaundiced against the sea-mist.
GLOAMREACH.
GARRISON: 2,483.
STATUS: QUARANTINED.
Isolde stared at the basin. “Why show us this?”
“Because the coast is opening,” Ignatz said.
His voice had lost its command. Beneath it was calculation, quick and cold.
Malchior watched him. “You know something.”
“I know the Iron-Ring Cartel does not buy rumors.”
“You sell them intelligence,” Isolde said. “Perhaps you should sell us the truth.”
Ignatz’s gaze cut to her. “You plotted the death of your own liege.”
“And succeeded in surviving it.”
“Enough,” Malchior said.
The word rang with sanctified force. The chamber answered with silence, but not obedience. He felt the
difference now. Authority was a garment, and the fire had burned through the cloth.
The basin filled with light.
Broken banners drifted beneath black water. Armies moved like drowned insects through the radiance.
Towers sank. Faces vanished behind curtains of shining rain.
THE WAR OF DROWNED LIGHT.

The letters struck the stone one by one.
BEGAN IN 225 AS.
ENDED IN 235 AS.
CASUALTIES: 64617.
The number remained suspended, too large to comprehend and too exact to mourn. Malchior imagined
each digit as a mouth.
The image changed again. The battlefields did not become peaceful. Men and women vanished into
ravines. Knives flashed in alleys. Fires glimmered beneath bridges. A decade of guerrilla reprisals
unfolded in a handful of heartbeats, each act answered by another, each answer preserved for the next
wound.
THE WAR COLLAPSED INTO A DECADE OF GUERRILLA REPRISALS.
Beneath the line, another appeared.
RECORDED VICTOR: THE SILENT CHOIR.
And beneath that:
THE SPARK WAS SECRETLY STAGED BY THE SILENT CHOIR.
Isolde took one step back.
Ignatz looked toward the door, as if walls might have ears even here.
“The Silent Choir won a war they began,” Malchior said.
“No,” Ignatz replied. “They won the story.”
The five powers seemed to gather in the room without bodies. The Ashen Vanguard in its battered
discipline. House Morvain behind its veils of inherited privilege. The Silent Choir, absent and listening.
The Iron-Ring Cartel, weighing every secret by its usefulness. The Bleeding Crown, hungry enough to
wear any face.
Malchior felt the old instinct rise in him: condemn, divide, command. Give each power its place beneath
the law. Declare the truth, then make the truth serve him.
But the basin had shown what truth did when freed from a hand.
It did not cleanse.
It selected.
A hairline crack opened across the stone. Heat poured through it. The chamber filled with the smell of wet
iron.
The voice returned, no longer behind the tablets.
It spoke from inside Malchior’s burned arm.
“Now choose which lie survives.”
His scarred flesh split.
Something beneath it opened one blind, burning eye.

Chapter 5
Snow came through the roof without touching the ground.
It drifted down in pale threads through the broken vault of Cindermere Hold, silvering the stones, the
rusted hinges, the black ribs of beams burned long ago. Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed stood beneath
it with his cloak open and his sword bare, listening to the silence that followed every ruin.
The wind moved through the battlements above. It made the hold breathe.
He had slept in places that stank of blood, wet wool, and old smoke. He had slept beneath overturned
wagons while arrows worried the mud around him. None of those places had felt as watchful as
Cindermere Hold.
The dead did not need eyes to see.
His gloved hand tightened around the sword’s hilt. The leather creaked. Something dark had dried into the
seams of the glove, though whether it was blood or wine or the mineral stain of the mountain, he could not
have said. The name had followed him longer than any banner.
Red-Handed.
Men said it with admiration when they wanted work done. They said it with contempt when they wanted
to pretend they had never needed him. Women said it softly, if they said it at all. Children had learned to
whisper it before they learned to pray.
Brannoc looked through the arched breach where the outer wall had fallen away. Beyond it, the High
Spires climbed into a sky the color of old iron. The peaks were hidden by cloud, but their cold pressed
down through the stone. Cindermere Hold clung to the heights like a burned tooth.
It had been founded in 246 AS among The High Spires.
The words had been cut into a lintel over the inner gate, though the rest of the inscription had been
shattered. He had read them by firelight when he entered. The chisel marks remained clean beneath the
soot, preserved by the same treacherous cold that had preserved everything else.
Founded in 246 AS.
A date for a beginning. No date for the men who had died here.
Brannoc sheathed his sword.
“You came alone.”
The voice rose from the dark behind him.
He did not turn. “You sound disappointed.”
“I sound alive.”
Korvath Nightbrook stepped from beneath the collapsed stair. He wore no colors and carried no visible
weapon. His clothing was made for passing through places where questions were more dangerous than
blades: dull cloth, softened boots, a hood dark enough to lose its shape in shadow. A smuggler’s clothing.
A smuggler’s face. Nothing in it that a witness could remember without effort.
Brannoc studied him in the reflection of the snow.

“You’re late.”
“I was delayed.”
“By what?”
“People who believed they were searching for me.”
Korvath came nearer, his boots whispering over ash. He kept his distance from Brannoc’s sword hand.
Sensible. Fear was often the last honest thing in a man.
“The road is watched,” Korvath said. “Not by soldiers.”
“Then by whom?”
“The sort who wish they were soldiers.”
Brannoc glanced at him. “That excludes half the realm.”
“It excludes no one.”
Korvath reached into his coat. Brannoc’s hand moved before thought, finding the hilt again. The smuggler
stopped.
“Slowly,” Brannoc said.
A strip of waxed cloth emerged between Korvath’s fingers. He held it out as if it contained something that
might bite.
Brannoc did not take it.
“Who sent this?”
Korvath’s mouth drew thin. “You were not hired to ask.”
“I was hired to carry a message.”
“No. You were hired to decide whether the message should be carried.”
“That is a different kind of hire.”
“It is the only kind left.”
The snow thickened around them. It fell through the roof and gathered on the floor between their boots,
softening the black stains and the old grooves cut by carts. Brannoc could smell damp stone, cold ash, and
the faint animal tang of Korvath’s fear.
Not fear of him. Not entirely.
He extended his hand.
Korvath gave him the packet.
The wax bore no seal. Someone had pressed a thumb into it while it was still warm and then smoothed the
mark away. A message made by people who distrusted heraldry.
Brannoc tore the cloth open.
Inside lay a narrow shard of dark metal, wrapped around a scrap of parchment. The metal caught what
little light there was and returned none of it. Its edge was too fine to be ordinary steel. Along its flat ran

three shallow bands, each crossing the other without meeting.
The Thrice-Bound Edge.
Brannoc knew regalia when he saw it. He had seen crowns laid over corpses, rings taken from fingers,
cloaks stripped from kings while the cloth was still warm. Regalia was never merely an object. It was an
accusation waiting for a body.
The Thrice-Bound Edge had been forged in 123 AS.
He had not expected to see its mark in a dead fortress.
He unfolded the parchment.
The writing was narrow and disciplined.
Gloamreach remains sealed.
The line beneath had been scored out so violently the parchment had nearly torn. A second sentence
remained.
The Crown listens through other mouths.
Brannoc read it again.
The Crown.
Not the Bleeding Crown. Not the court, nor the house, nor the men who wore its colors and called
themselves its hands. Just the Crown, as though it were a living thing with ears hidden in the walls.
His thumb passed over the words.
He had never seen the throne. He had seen what it made of men. That was nearer than most came.
“The rest?” he asked.
Korvath’s gaze shifted to the shard of metal. “There is no rest.”
“You carried an empty letter across the mountains.”
“I carried what I was given.”
“You brought me a warning.”
“I brought you a choice.”
Brannoc folded the parchment. “Who knows I am here?”
Korvath did not answer.
Brannoc looked toward the broken gate. The wind had erased the tracks below, but not the sound that had
woken him before dawn: a faint clatter from the lower pass, metal striking stone, then silence. Perhaps a
cart. Perhaps men who had learned how to make a cart sound like weather.
He moved toward the inner hall.
Korvath followed.
The hold’s great chamber had lost its roof but retained its walls. Stone pillars rose into the snow, each
carved with the same worn knotwork. Along the far side, the old hearth yawned black and empty. Brannoc

had found no ash in it, no bones, no broken crockery. Whoever had abandoned Cindermere Hold had
taken even their refuse.
A fortress stripped of its dead.
He crossed the chamber without looking at the alcoves. Bodies had once hung there, according to the scars
in the stone. Chains left marks like writing. He wondered whether the garrison had been buried, burned, or
simply left for the mountain crows.
“Why here?” he asked.
Korvath kept his voice low. “Because no one claims it.”
“House Morvain claims everything that casts a shadow.”
“House Morvain claims what can be taxed.”
“And the Ashen Vanguard?”
“Claims what can be marched through.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel?”
“Claims what can be weighed.”
Brannoc stopped beside the hearth. “The Silent Choir?”
Korvath’s expression did not change, but his silence did. It tightened.
“The Silent Choir claims what can be forgotten,” he said.
The words settled heavily between them.
Brannoc placed the shard on the hearthstone. It looked small there. Harmless. A sliver of regalia in a dead
place.
“Who wants me to go to Gloamreach?”
Korvath stared at the shard. “You already know.”
“No.”
“You know enough.”
Brannoc leaned close. “If I knew enough, I would not need your voice.”
The smuggler’s eyes lifted to his. Guarded, wary, measuring the distance to every exit. Brannoc had
known men who could lie without moving a muscle. Korvath was not one of them. He lied with stillness.
It was less skillful, but often more useful.
“There are ships leaving the Pale Coast,” Korvath said. “Not ships that should be leaving.”
“Quarantine is a wall, not a mystery.”
“Gloamreach is not quarantined for sickness.”
“You have proof?”
“I have scars.”

“That is not proof.”
“It is what survives proof.”
Brannoc reached for the shard and wrapped it again. “You want me to enter Gloamreach.”
“I want you to carry the message.”
“To whom?”
Korvath looked past him, through the roofless chamber, toward the white emptiness between the peaks.
“The person who can read it.”
“Then why not carry it yourself?”
“Because I am a smuggler.”
“And I am a sellsword.”
“You are worse.”
Brannoc smiled without warmth. “That answer was almost useful.”
A sound moved beneath the wind.
Not loud. Not close. A scrape of iron along stone from somewhere below the hold.
Korvath heard it too. His hand disappeared inside his coat.
Brannoc drew his sword.
The chamber seemed to contract around the blade. Snow hissed against the edge and vanished. For an
instant, the sword’s reflection showed him a red smear across his knuckles, though his glove was black
and dry.
Korvath stepped backward. “How many?”
“Quiet.”
Another scrape.
Then a muffled voice beneath the floor.
Brannoc raised his sword and listened. The words were too blurred by stone to understand, but the cadence
was familiar: men speaking before violence, when courage was still being passed from mouth to mouth.
He looked at the broken stairs. The lower levels had been sealed by fallen masonry. No one should have
been beneath them.
No one should have been in Cindermere Hold at all.
Korvath breathed through his nose. “We should leave.”
“Now you sound disappointed.”
“I sound alive.”
Brannoc approached the rubble. Snow had gathered in the cracks, but beneath it the dust was disturbed. A
thin line of warmth touched his face from below. Fire. Recent.

He crouched and pressed his palm to the stone.
The mountain answered with a tremor.
Not an earthquake. A door opening.
Somewhere beneath Cindermere Hold, old mechanisms groaned awake. Stone grated against stone. A
seam appeared in the floor beside the hearth, widening by the thickness of a knife.
Korvath whispered something that might have been a prayer.
Brannoc rose.
From the darkness under the hall came the smell of wet wool, lamp oil, and blood.
A voice called up through the opening.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
The name traveled through the ruin and returned changed, as if spoken by many mouths.
Brannoc’s sword lowered by no more than a finger.
The voice continued.
“Your blood has been expected.”
His hand closed around the wrapped shard.
Behind him, Korvath whispered, “Do not answer.”
But Brannoc was already leaning toward the dark.
“Expected by whom?” he said.
Something below laughed softly.
Then the floor opened wider.
The stones split with a groan that seemed to come from the bones of the hold.
Brannoc stepped back as the opening widened. Dust fell in thin veils, silvered by the failing lamps.
Beneath the floor lay a stair descending into a chamber drowned in black water. Its surface did not ripple.
It held the light above it without reflection, as if the dark had weight and would not surrender what it had
swallowed.
Korvath caught Brannoc by the sleeve.
“Do not.”
Brannoc looked at the smuggler’s hand until the fingers withdrew.
Below, the unseen thing breathed.
The sound climbed through the gap: slow, wet, patient. Brannoc had heard men breathe that way beneath
shields, when a spearpoint had found the seam beneath their ribs. He had heard it in plague pits. He had
heard it once from a horse with its throat cut, before the animal understood it was dead.
He wrapped his fist more tightly around the shard.

Heat pressed into his palm.
“Your blood has been expected,” the voice said again.
“Then it can wait.”
The chamber answered with a tremor. Somewhere in the dark, metal scraped against stone.
Korvath leaned close. His breath smelled of bitterroot and old smoke. “You have no notion what is
beneath us.”
“I know it has a voice.”
“That is not knowledge. That is bait.”
Brannoc glanced over his shoulder. The ruin’s hall stretched behind them, its broken arches black against
the stormlight leaking through the roof. Rain entered in narrow silver lines and struck the flagstones with
soft, innumerable taps. The abandoned hold seemed to listen through every crack.
He had brought Korvath here because the smuggler knew the old ways through the High Spires. He had
brought him because coin could purchase silence, but not courage. Courage was rarer and generally less
useful.
Now Korvath stood between him and the only exit that had not collapsed.
“Move,” Brannoc said.
“I said no.”
“You said do not. There is a difference.”
“The difference is what kills a man.”
Brannoc descended the first stair.
The stone was slick beneath his boot. Water climbed around the sole, cold enough to seize the ankle. He
held his sword low, the point angled toward the darkness. The voice did not speak again. That silence was
worse. It gave the chamber time to imagine him.
He reached the second step.
Korvath cursed softly and followed.
The opening closed behind them with a grinding crash.
Brannoc turned. The floor was whole. A seam remained, narrow as a thread, then vanished beneath
settling dust.
Korvath stared upward. “You have a talent.”
“For what?”
“Making doors out of graves.”
Brannoc faced the stair. “Keep your voice down.”
“It heard us before we came.”
“I know.”

The descent continued farther than the ruined hall had any right to contain. The air changed as they went.
Wet wool and blood gave way to mineral cold, then to a dry, medicinal stench. Brannoc’s tongue tasted
iron. At the edge of the lamplight, pale marks had been cut into the walls—rows of strokes, some crossed
through, some clawed over until the stone had powdered beneath them.
Korvath lifted his lamp.
“Those are not tally marks.”
“No.”
“Do you know what they are?”
“No.”
Korvath looked at him. “You say that too easily.”
Brannoc kept moving. He had learned early that ignorance was not shameful. Pretending otherwise was.
Men who believed themselves clever died noisily.
At the bottom, the stair opened into a circular room. Black water covered the floor to the height of a man’s
shin. Pillars rose from it, each carved in the shape of a bound figure with its face erased. Chains hung
between the pillars, submerged and trembling though the water remained still.
At the center stood a stone table.
Something lay upon it beneath a sheet of grey cloth.
Korvath stopped on the final step.
The lamp flame bent toward the table.
Brannoc entered the water. Cold seized his legs through his trousers. The hidden floor was uneven, strewn
with fragments that rolled underfoot. He felt one crack against his boot and nearly lost his balance. When
he looked down, a small white shape moved beneath the black surface.
A finger.
He did not look again.
“Brannoc,” Korvath whispered.
He turned.
The smuggler was staring at the wall behind them. A sentence had appeared in the stone where there had
been only dampness. The letters glistened as if freshly cut.
THE LEADEN ACCORD DEVASTATED CINDERMERE HOLD IN 338 AS.
Korvath’s mouth worked without sound.
Brannoc read the words twice.
The date meant nothing to him. It sat in the sentence like a nail driven through a tongue, precise and
obscene. The hold above them had been raised out of black stone and hard necessity. Its walls had endured
weather that flayed skin from the face. Its empty chambers still carried the shape of command. Yet the
words gave its ruin a cause, and the cause waited beyond the reach of any man standing in that room.

“What is the Leaden Accord?” Korvath asked.
Brannoc kept his eyes on the inscription. “You tell me.”
“I have never heard of it.”
“You have heard of many things you pretend not to know.”
“I know smugglers’ roads. I know which gates take silver and which take blood. I know when a patrol has
been bought and when it has merely grown tired. I do not know this.”
The carved sentence began to run.
Not fade. Run.
Black fluid gathered beneath the letters and slid down the wall in narrow streams. The words remained
legible as the stone softened around them. A smell rose from the water: hot metal, burnt hair, the sour reek
of a battlefield after rain.
Korvath backed up the stair.
Brannoc reached the table.
The cloth stirred.
He drew his sword.
“Do not uncover it,” Korvath said.
Brannoc looked at the shape beneath the cloth. It was too long to be a body and too narrow to be a chest.
The covering had been stitched from strips of different materials: leather, sailcloth, something that might
once have been skin. Symbols had been painted along its edge in a dull red pigment.
The shard in Brannoc’s fist burned harder.
He put his free hand on the cloth.
For a moment, the chamber vanished.
He stood beneath a sky the color of old bruises. Cindermere Hold rose around him, not abandoned but
crowded with banners torn into ribbons by a wind that blew upward from the ground. Stone towers leaned
over one another. Fire moved along the battlements without consuming them. Men and women ran
through the courtyards with their hands pressed to their mouths, and each time one fell, the earth opened
beneath the body and drank it.
A bell rang somewhere beyond sight.
Once.
The sound passed through him.
Twice.
His teeth struck together.
The third stroke never came.
He saw the hold’s gates crushed inward. He saw a line of figures in leaden masks standing amid the
smoke. He saw no faces beneath the masks, only darkness, and in that darkness the same wet breath that

had spoken from below.
Then he saw a crown.
Not worn. Not held.
Suspended above the fire by threads of red.
The vision broke.
Brannoc lurched against the table. His sword clattered into the water.
Korvath seized his shoulder. “What did you see?”
Brannoc jerked free.
The cloth had fallen open.
There was no body beneath it.
Resting on the stone lay a circlet made of blackened metal, narrow and ugly, with a single jagged point at
the front. Dried blood filled the grooves along its inner rim. The crown seemed too small for a man’s head.
It seemed made for a child, or for someone who had been made smaller by suffering.
Brannoc stared at it.
The shard pulsed in his fist.
“No,” he said.
The room gave no answer.
Korvath approached one cautious step. “You know it?”
“No.”
That was a lie, though he could not have said why.
The crown belonged to no house he had served and no banner he had broken. It bore no crest he
recognized. Yet something in him recoiled from it with the intimacy of an old wound. The sight of it had
touched a locked place behind his ribs. He felt the latch there lift.
A name tried to form.
He crushed it before it reached his tongue.
The water began to move.
Small circles spread from the pillars. The submerged chains rose by increments, shedding black droplets.
Beneath the surface, pale fingers curled around the links.
Korvath raised his lamp. “We are leaving.”
Brannoc picked up his sword.
The voice came from beneath the table now.
“Blood recognizes blood.”
Korvath’s face emptied.

Brannoc looked down at the crown. The metal reflected nothing. Not the lamp, not his hand, not the pale
blur of his face above it.
“Whose blood?” he asked.
Korvath struck him across the mouth.
The blow snapped his head sideways. Pain flared bright and immediate. For one breath Brannoc stood
perfectly still, sword in hand, blood running from his lip into the water.
Then he drove Korvath backward against a pillar.
The lamp fell. Its flame guttered in the black water and went out.
Darkness closed over them.
Korvath’s hand found Brannoc’s throat. “You answer every grave that calls you.”
Brannoc pinned the smuggler’s wrist against the stone. “And you strike every man who listens?”
“Only the ones likely to open the door.”
Something moved behind Brannoc.
He felt it before he heard it: a pressure against the nape, like a blade held just short of skin.
Korvath saw his expression change.
“What?”
Brannoc released him.
“Run.”
The chamber filled with voices.
Not one voice, not many, but the echo of speech before it became speech. The pillars groaned. Chains
snapped taut. Water surged against Brannoc’s knees, carrying scraps of pale flesh and strips of cloth
around his boots.
The crown on the table began to bleed.
Korvath stumbled toward the stair.
Brannoc seized his collar and hauled him aside as a chain tore through the darkness where his chest had
been. It struck the pillar with enough force to split stone. The impact showered them with shards.
At the table, the blackened circlet lifted from the stone.
It hung in the air, dripping red.
The wrapped shard tore itself from Brannoc’s hand.
It flew across the chamber and struck the crown.
Light burst between them—not white, but the color of drowned embers. Every chain drew upward. The
faceless figures carved into the pillars opened their mouths.
And from the water beneath Brannoc’s feet, a hand closed around his ankle.

The hand was cold enough to burn.
Brannoc drove his heel down, but the fingers tightened. Water climbed over his boot and filled the seams
in the leather. It had the weight of blood, thick and reluctant, and beneath its black surface something
moved against his calf.
“Brannoc!”
Korvath’s voice came from the stair, sharpened by panic.
Brannoc reached for him. The chamber lurched. Chains groaned overhead, their links rising toward the
crown as though drawn by an unseen tide. The circlet turned slowly in the air. Blood streamed from it
without falling. Each red thread hung suspended, trembling between the metal and the stone.
The shard hovered before it, wrapped cloth burning away in strips.
Beneath the scorched fabric, the thing was not bone, nor glass, nor any metal Brannoc knew. It was a
sliver of darkness with a pale vein running through its heart. The vein pulsed once.
The hand around his ankle answered.
Brannoc struck downward with his free fist.
His knuckles met something hard. The impact jarred his shoulder. The water dimpled, then opened around
a wrist blackened by rot. A second hand rose from the depths and clawed at his knee.
He seized the wrist.
The flesh came apart beneath his grip.
Not flesh. Soot. Wet ash. It smeared across his palm and sank into the lines there, turning the old blood in
them cold.
He pulled.
The thing below pulled harder.
His knee buckled. He went down on one hand, and the stone struck his palm. The chamber filled with
voices—not words, not yet, but the hush of mouths preparing to speak. The carved faces in the pillars
leaned toward him. Though their features had been worn smooth, he felt their attention like a blade laid
against his throat.
Korvath descended two steps, then stopped.
“Leave me,” Brannoc said.
The smuggler looked toward the crown. “You expect me to walk past that?”
“I expect you to survive.”
“I have made a profession of it.”
“Then practice.”
A chain whipped across the stair. Korvath threw himself backward. The links struck the steps and burst
them open. Stone teeth spun into the dark.
The crowned light deepened. The black circlet widened, its inner rim turning toward Brannoc.

A pressure gathered behind his eyes.
He knew the sensation. Every soldier knew it, though few survived long enough to name it: the moment
before a shield broke, before a gate gave way, before a man understood that the thing advancing upon him
had already won.
The crown was looking at him.
Not through eyes. Through the hollow where a face should have been.
Brannoc tasted iron.
His hand tightened around the dead wrist. “You want a claimant?” he said. “Come and take one.”
The chamber shuddered.
Korvath cursed from the stair.
The hand released him.
For one breath, Brannoc was free. Then the water rose in a column and struck him beneath the ribs.
He flew backward.
His spine hit the pillar. The impact tore the breath from him. Stone cracked behind his head, and
something warm ran down his neck. He slid, dazed, while the water spread in ripples around his boots.
The crown descended.
It stopped just above his brow.
The blood dripping from its rim touched his skin.
A memory opened inside him.
Not his own.
A field under a drowned sky. Banners collapsed into mud. Light burning beneath the earth instead of
above it. Men running without shadows while the ground swallowed their feet. A thousand mouths crying
for names no one remembered.
Then the vision widened.
The War of Drowned Light.
He saw its beginning hidden behind a curtain of prayer and ash. He saw hands that belonged to The Silent
Choir strike the first spark and fold themselves afterward, clean and reverent. He saw the war grind on
through ambushes, reprisals, and villages burned from within. He saw victory placed in The Silent Choir’s
hands while the dead continued to rise in the memories of the living.
The vision gave him a number.
64617.
It appeared in the sky above the ruined field, written in drowned radiance. The figures broke apart.
Reformed. Broke apart again.
Brannoc tore himself free with a sound that was almost a laugh.

The crown recoiled.
He fell onto his side. His lungs dragged air into him in ragged strips. Water crawled over the floor toward
his fingers, seeking the soot that had entered his skin.
Korvath had reached the bottom step. He carried a short knife in one hand and the other held a lantern
whose flame had gone green.
“Do you know what that is?” he asked.
“Something with poor manners.”
“That is the Bleeding Crown.”
“I know what it is.”
“No.” Korvath’s gaze flicked to Brannoc’s hand. “You know what people call it.”
The crown hung between them, turning slowly.
Brannoc pushed himself upright. His knees wanted to fold. He refused them. His blood was running down
his face now, warm at first, then cold as it reached his jaw.
Korvath’s eyes narrowed. “It knows you.”
“It knows the blood.”
“Whose?”
Brannoc stepped away from the pillar.
The faceless mouths opened wider.
A murmur moved through the chamber. It crawled from stone to stone, a sound like wet fingers drawn
across parchment. The chains began to lower. One brushed Brannoc’s shoulder, and the metal burned
through cloth. He gripped it and wrapped it around his forearm.
“If you have a question,” he said, “ask it before the room answers.”
Korvath swallowed. “You are the unacknowledged heir.”
The words struck harder than the pillar had.
For years Brannoc had heard them spoken behind doors, beneath breath, in the pauses after men hired him
and before they decided whether to fear him. Never in a place like this. Never beneath the hanging circlet.
Never with the dead listening.
The crown brightened.
Brannoc looked at Korvath. “Careful.”
“I am being careful.”
“You are being alive by accident.”
“Then let me make use of it.” Korvath raised the lantern. Its green light passed over the crown and
revealed marks beneath the blood: three cuts crossing the black metal, each sealed with a different
substance. Wax. Salt. Something that glistened like an eye.

“The seal is failing,” Korvath whispered.
Brannoc remembered the wrapped shard leaping from his hand. “You brought it here.”
“I carried it.”
“Same thing.”
“I was paid to move it, not to understand it.”
“By whom?”
Korvath’s expression closed.
A chain descended behind him.
Brannoc moved first. He caught Korvath by the collar and dragged him forward as the chain smashed
through the stair. The lantern flew from Korvath’s hand. Green fire rolled across the water, spreading
without consuming it.
For an instant the chamber became a green mirror.
Brannoc saw himself reflected there.
Not as he stood, bloodied and breathing hard, but seated beneath a crown he did not want. His hands were
red to the wrists. Men knelt before him in the reflection, their heads bowed so low their faces vanished.
Behind them, banners of the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, The Silent Choir, and the Iron-Ring Cartel
hung in tatters from the same wall.
The Bleeding Crown rested on his head.
He looked older.
He looked relieved.
Brannoc smashed the reflection with his fist.
The water burst upward. The green fire died.
Korvath staggered against him. “What did you see?”
“Your future.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It was ugly.”
The crown dropped another inch.
The chamber’s pressure became unbearable. Brannoc’s teeth ached. His heart beat once, twice, then
seemed to hesitate, as though waiting for permission. The blood on his face began to move upward toward
the metal.
He planted his feet.
“Come down,” he told it.
Korvath grabbed his arm. “Do not.”
Brannoc shook him off.

“Do not what?”
“Let it touch you.”
“It already has.”
“No. It has tasted you. That is different.”
The smuggler’s voice had lost its wary edge. Fear had stripped it bare. “There are things that can wear a
man without killing him.”
Brannoc gave him a hard look. “Then they should learn better manners too.”
He reached for the crown.
The shard moved between them.
It struck his palm.
Pain opened him from hand to shoulder. He did not cry out. The darkness in the shard poured into his
veins, cold and immense. Something pressed against his bones, testing them. His fingers clenched around
it.
The crown screamed.
The sound was silent, but every pillar split.
Korvath fell to one knee, clutching his ears. The carved faces cracked from brow to chin. Behind the
broken stone were not hollows but packed layers of pale hair, all of it stirring in the windless chamber.
Brannoc saw the names then.
Not carved. Burned into the air.
The Thrice-Bound Edge.
Edge of Gloamreach.
Cindermere Hold.
Each name flared and vanished before he could grasp why they had been offered. The crown shook above
him, bleeding faster now. Its red rain struck the water and became black flowers.
A voice spoke from beneath the floor.
“Blood opens.”
Brannoc stared at the stones.
Korvath rose unsteadily. “What did it say?”
Another voice answered, closer.
“Blood remembers.”
The chains snapped upward.
The crown drove down.
Brannoc lifted the shard in both hands and met it.

Impact folded the chamber around him.
For a moment there was no water, no stone, no Korvath. There was only the pressure of the crown against
the shard and the terrible knowledge moving through him: the Bleeding Crown had not been waiting for a
ruler.
It had been waiting for permission.
His arms began to tremble.
The crown pressed harder.
A crack opened in the shard.
From within came a thin red light, the color of a wound seen beneath ice.
Brannoc thought of the men who had followed him because he paid on time. The men who had followed
because they feared him. The men who had followed because war made obedience easier than grief. He
thought of every gate he had crossed under another man’s banner, every hall where his name had been
welcomed only after his sword was counted.
Then the crown whispered inside his skull.
Not heir.
Brannoc’s vision blurred.
The shard cracked again.
Not king.
He felt the thing beneath the floor gathering itself. Stone groaned. Water rose around his shins, his knees,
his waist.
The third whisper entered him like a nail.
Witness.
The crown touched his brow.
Every chain in the chamber fell at once.

Chapter 6
The rain came down as ash.
It struck the high windows of the counting chamber in soft gray flecks, gathered in the leadwork, and slid
in sluggish threads across the glass. Beyond it, the city had become a smudge of chimneys and wet stone.
Cerys Sablewood the Ashen watched the world dissolve and felt no sorrow for it. A city was only a ledger
written in buildings. Burn enough of it, and the figures became easier to read.
“Again,” Cerys said.
Halvard Sablewood lowered his eyes to the page.
He was a scribe. The fact sat upon him more plainly than any ornament could have done: ink at the side of
one finger, a narrow knife for trimming quills, a stack of folded sheets kept square beneath his palm. No
canonical distinction, no office of consequence, clung to him beyond the work itself. He had brought the
register because it was his task to bring it, and now he stood in the cold chamber waiting to discover
whether the words would survive their reading.
“Again,” Cerys repeated.
Halvard drew breath. “The western allotments have been reduced by—”
“Not the allotments.”
His mouth closed.
Cerys turned from the window. The epithet given to them—Ashen—had become a garment worn before
witnesses. It was in the pallor of their robes, in the dark severity of their regalia, in the stillness they
maintained while lesser souls fidgeted and sweated. It was not a color. It was an accusation.
“Read what was erased,” Cerys said.
Halvard looked at the register. “The erasure is the record.”
“Then read the absence.”
A faint tremor passed through the paper. Or through his hand. The chamber smelled of wet soot, lamp oil,
and old iron. At the far end, beneath a canopy blackened by age, stood The Cinder-Wrought Aegis. Its
regalia had been shaped by the legacy of the Sundering, wrought in a cinder-dark style that made the
fire-scarred surfaces seem less forged than endured. It belonged to authority, ceremony, and the burden of
ash-marked rule.
Cerys did not wear it.
Not here. Not while the ledgers remained open and the blood concealed itself beneath the skin.
They had been born in 330 AS. The fact was harmless when spoken as a fact. Numbers were obedient
things; they did not ask who had sired the child they measured. But Cerys was the unacknowledged heir to
the Bleeding Crown, and every innocent number possessed a second edge.
Halvard turned a page. “There is an allocation marked for Gloamreach.”
“Gloamreach is quarantined.”
“Yes.”

“It is also a core location.”
“Yes.”
“And its garrison?”
Halvard’s finger found the line. “2,483.”
The number hung between them like a drawn wire.
Outside, something struck the roof and broke apart. Cerys pictured the Pale Coast without needing to see
it: pallid surf, light leeched from the water, walls raised against a horizon that offered no comfort.
Gloamreach belonged to that bleakness. Quarantined, sealed off, guarded by men who could neither leave
nor admit what waited beyond their gates. A garrison of 2,483 required food, iron, medicine, and pay. If
any one of those failed, the hold would not merely suffer. It would speak.
“Who authorized the allocation?” Cerys asked.
Halvard lowered the register by a fraction. “The seal is broken.”
“That was not my question.”
“The name is not entered.”
“Names are entered by scribes.”
His gaze lifted then, quickly and unwillingly. “I am Halvard Sablewood. I am a scribe.”
The words were not defiance. They had the plain shape of an inventory item. Cerys could almost admire
him for it.
“I know what you are.”
“Then you know I cannot answer for a name that is not present.”
Cerys stepped toward the table. The register lay open between them, its pages swollen from damp. A black
seal had been cut away from the lower corner, leaving only a ragged crescent of wax. No crest remained.
No hand could be recognized from the mutilation.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel buys silence by the weight,” Cerys said. “House Morvain buys it by inheritance.
The Ashen Vanguard calls silence discipline. The Silent Choir calls it virtue. The Bleeding Crown calls it
survival.”
Halvard’s quill remained motionless above the page.
“Which one paid for this?” Cerys asked.
“I do not know.”
“Which one benefits?”
“I do not know.”
“You are a poor scribe.”
His face tightened. “I have written what was placed before me.”
“Then you are a dangerous one.”

The lamp hissed. A bead of oil crawled down its brass stem.
Cerys had seen men lie with tears in their eyes and women tell the truth as if confessing murder. The
honest were not safer than the false. Honesty was merely a blade without a sheath.
They reached for the register. Halvard’s fingers tightened upon its edge.
For an instant, the chamber became very quiet.
The old wars waited in that silence. The War of Drowned Light had begun in 225 AS and ended in 235
AS, with 64617 casualties. It had collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals. The Silent Choir was
recorded as the victor, though the war’s spark had secretly been staged by them. Broken banners, drowned
radiance, villages that remembered flame more clearly than faces: victory had left no clean road through
the dead.
Cerys drew the register toward them.
Halvard released it.
“You know what that allocation means,” Cerys said.
“It means Gloamreach receives supplies.”
“It means someone has decided quarantine is worth feeding.”
“Perhaps it is.”
“Perhaps.”
The word was a small door. Cerys opened it.
“What is kept there?”
Halvard said nothing.
“What did you copy?”
“I copied the register.”
“Do not mistake obedience for innocence.”
“I do not.”
The answer came softly. That made it worse.
Cerys turned another page. Beneath the allocation, in a different ink, stood a notation: Cindermere Hold,
inactive. No requisition. No relief. No garrison.
Cindermere Hold had been founded in 246 AS among The High Spires. Its garrison had once numbered
8878. Now it was abandoned, no longer a core holding, its blackened silhouette left to the elevation and
weather. The place had immense former strength hollowed into ruin. A fortress made empty by history, or
by arithmetic.
“Why is Cindermere crossed out?” Cerys asked.
Halvard leaned over the page without touching it. “It was crossed out before it reached me.”
“By whom?”

“I cannot say.”
“You can say the mark was made.”
“Yes.”
“By what hand?”
“I cannot say.”
Cerys studied him. Halvard Sablewood had been born in 408 AS. He was younger than the dust sealed
into the chamber’s corners, younger than the grudges that fed the realm, but not young enough to believe
that ink absolved the hand that held the pen. No canonical temperament had been recorded for him. Cerys
found the omission useful. Temperament was another word for the shape of a weakness.
“Do you believe records tell the truth?” they asked.
Halvard’s eyes remained on the page. “Records tell what survives.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one I have.”
The rain thickened against the windows. Ash gathered on the sill until the ledge looked snowbound.
Cerys slid one loose sheet from beneath the register. It bore no seal, only a column of figures and a line
written across the bottom in a hand pressed so deeply into the paper that the fibers had bruised.
THE CROWN MUST BE FED.
Their pulse did not quicken. That was a discipline learned before it became a habit.
Halvard saw the line. His breath stopped.
There it was: the small betrayal, not fear but recognition.
“You have read this,” Cerys said.
“No.”
“Your eyes have.”
“I saw it now.”
“You knew the words.”
“I knew the words because you read them aloud.”
Cerys folded the sheet once.
The Bleeding Crown had many mouths. None of them spoke with the same voice. Some begged. Some
commanded. Some offered the old promise that blood could make order from ruin. Cerys had never seen
the Crown worn in the open, yet its claim lived beneath every negotiation, every tariff, every obedient
bow. The unacknowledged heir could not inherit what the realm refused to admit existed.
The Cinder-Wrought Aegis waited beneath its canopy, austere and dark, its surfaces suggesting
fire-scarred craftsmanship. It seemed to watch without eyes.
“Take this to the lower vault,” Cerys said.

Halvard looked up. “The sheet?”
“The whole register.”
“That is not the instruction written on the docket.”
“The docket is not in this room.”
“I was ordered to return it to the archive.”
“By whom?”
He did not answer.
Cerys placed the folded sheet atop the register. “You are a scribe, Halvard Sablewood. You preserve what
powerful people prefer to forget. Today you will decide whether you preserve this.”
His hand moved toward the register, then halted.
A sound came from beyond the chamber door.
Not a knock.
Three measured strokes against the wood, each separated by a patient interval.
Halvard turned toward it.
Cerys did not. Their fingers closed around the edge of the table, while beneath the ash-colored cloth at
their throat an old royal mark seemed to wake, hot as buried coal.
The strokes came again.
This time, a voice spoke from the passage.
“Master of Coin.”
Halvard looked at Cerys.
Cerys looked at the sealed door, at the register, at the regalia waiting beneath its canopy.
“Hide the page,” they whispered.
Halvard’s hand went to the fold.
“And when they ask what you are?”
The latch began to rise.
Cerys felt the whole realm lean toward the opening.
“Tell them,” they said, “you are only a scribe.”
The latch lifted.
A man entered without haste, closing the door behind him with the care of someone accustomed to rooms
that listened. His coat was the color of wet soot. At his throat, a narrow strip of pale metal bore no device
Cerys recognized. He carried neither sword nor lantern. The corridor’s blue fire followed him in a thin
wash, dying across the floorboards before it reached the table.
Halvard had already folded the page into the inner seam of his sleeve.

He stood beside the register with his hands lowered, his mouth dry enough that Cerys could hear him
swallow.
The visitor’s gaze passed over him and settled on Cerys.
“Master of Coin.”
Cerys inclined their head. “You have found one.”
“Have I?”
The man’s voice was unremarkable. That made it worse. Threats announced themselves by the pleasure
they took in being heard. This voice had been stripped of pleasure.
Behind him, the door rested shut.
Cerys let their hand fall upon the register. The leather was cold. Beneath the ash-colored cloth at their
throat, the royal mark burned once and then quieted, as if something beneath the skin had opened one eye.
“What is your business?”
“The regalia.”
His gaze shifted toward the canopy.
The Cinder-Wrought Aegis stood there in its darkness, too severe to be called beautiful. Its fire-scarred
surfaces caught the dying blue from the corridor and gave nothing back. It seemed less forged than
endured, as if the metal had survived the Sundering by refusing to understand it.
“No one requested an inspection,” Cerys said.
“No one requests an inspection.”
“Then you have come to take it.”
“I have come to establish whether it remains where it was recorded.”
“By whose record?”
The man smiled faintly. It was not an expression of amusement. “That depends on which record you
mean.”
Halvard’s breathing changed.
Cerys heard it and hated him for the betrayal, though the boy had done nothing. Halvard Sablewood was
born in 408 AS. The fact had been inked in a baptismal ledger, copied into a household account, repeated
