by clerks who had never looked at his face. A small fact. A harmless fact. Yet now it rose between them
with the stubbornness of a grave marker.
Born in 408 AS.
Too young to have learned how to lie without showing the shape of the truth beneath it.
Cerys kept their eyes upon the visitor. “You may inspect the seal.”
“The seal is not the regalia.”
“No. It is the seal.”

“And the regalia?”
“Under guard.”
“Where is the guard?”
“Outside.”
The visitor glanced at the sealed door. “I hear no one.”
“Then they are doing their work.”
A draft moved through the room. It smelled of ash, old wax, and the mineral damp that came from stone
below foundations. Somewhere beyond the walls, machinery groaned once and stopped. The hold had
been built to outlast treachery, famine, and kings. It had not been built to conceal a secret from a man who
already knew where to look.
The visitor approached the canopy.
Halvard shifted.
It was barely a movement: a shoulder drawing back, a heel pressing into the floor. The visitor saw it.
Cerys saw him see it.
“Your scribe is nervous,” the man said.
“He is cold.”
“He was cold before I entered?”
“The room has not changed.”
The visitor looked at Halvard again. “Your name.”
Halvard’s tongue seemed to catch behind his teeth.
Cerys intervened. “He is not part of this examination.”
“Everyone in this room is part of it.”
“Then examine me.”
“I am.”
That answer landed with the softness of a knife laid upon a table.
The visitor stopped before the canopy, close enough that the blackened regalia cast its reflection into his
eyes. He did not touch it. That restraint carried more authority than reaching would have. The
Cinder-Wrought Aegis had been shaped for ceremony, but ceremony was only power dressed in patience.
Whoever controlled the hand that raised it controlled the story told by the metal.
“Do you know why it was brought here?” he asked.
“It was entered into the treasury.”
“That is an answer about storage.”
“It is the answer required by the register.”
“Registers are obedient things. They say whatever hand is placed upon them.”

Cerys felt the hidden page against Halvard’s sleeve without looking at it. A single leaf, torn from a larger
account. Names, routes, quantities—not enough to explain the design, more than enough to prove one
existed. The ink had been black when written. It had bled rust-red at the edges, as though the page had
absorbed blood through the fibers.
The visitor had come because of it. Or because of the Aegis. Or because someone had mistaken a locked
room for a safe room.
“Who sent you?” Cerys asked.
The man’s eyes returned to them. “Would the answer alter your conduct?”
“It might alter the value of your life.”
There. The old instinct, sharpened by years of weighing grain against soldiers, debt against hunger, silence
against revolt. A threat was a coin. Its worth depended upon what the other party believed they could
afford to lose.
The visitor did not flinch. “You speak as though the realm were yours to price.”
“The realm prices itself. I only keep the account.”
“House Morvain would disagree.”
“House Morvain disagrees with weather when it cannot levy a tax upon it.”
“Then perhaps the Ashen Vanguard would agree.”
“The Ashen Vanguard agrees with nothing that cannot be marched beneath a banner.”
“And the Iron-Ring Cartel?”
“They would sell agreement by the measure.”
The man’s expression altered by less than a breath. Cerys saw the confirmation and wished they had not
spoken.
“And the Silent Choir?” he asked.
At that name, the blue fire in the corridor guttered.
Cerys thought of drowned radiance. Broken banners sinking into black water. The War of Drowned Light,
begun in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS, leaving 64617 casualties and a victory recorded for The Silent
Choir. A war whose spark they had secretly staged. A decade of guerrilla reprisals afterward, because
victory was a word that could not close a wound.
“The Silent Choir,” Cerys said, “would not send a man who announced himself.”
“Would they send a woman?”
“They would send a silence.”
The visitor considered this. “And the Bleeding Crown?”
The mark beneath Cerys’s throat became a coal.
For one instant the room changed. The canopy fell away. The regalia was no longer metal but inheritance,
no longer ceremony but accusation. Cerys saw the throne they had never been permitted to approach, the

bloodline no tongue had acknowledged, the crown that had survived by devouring the names of those who
claimed it. Unacknowledged did not mean unreal. A buried thing still had roots.
Cerys placed both palms upon the register.
“The Bleeding Crown,” they said, “has no authority in this room.”
“Does it not?”
“The law is clear.”
“Law is ink.”
“Then it can be amended.”
“By whom?”
“By whoever holds the pen.”
The visitor looked to Halvard.
The boy had gone pale.
Cerys felt the danger gather—not around the page, but around the hand that carried it. A scribe could be
frightened into confession. A scribe could be made to seem guilty merely by surviving an interrogation. If
the visitor searched him, the page would be found. If the page was found, the account would become
evidence. If it became evidence, every faction named upon it would invent a different truth, and each truth
would require a corpse to make it convincing.
“Open your sleeve,” the visitor said.
Halvard stared at him.
“Open it.”
Cerys heard the faint rasp of cloth as Halvard’s fingers touched the seam.
“No,” Cerys said.
The visitor did not turn. “No?”
“You have no warrant.”
“Nor do you.”
“I am Master of Coin.”
“You are a keeper of disputed metal in a room with a false register.”
The words entered Cerys cleanly. No accusation had been made, and yet the room seemed to tighten
around one.
“Careful,” Cerys said.
“I am being careful.”
Halvard’s hand remained at his sleeve. His fingers trembled once, then stilled.
Cerys looked at him at last. The ash-colored light made his face unreadable, but his eyes were not. They
held the blunt terror of a man who had discovered that obedience could be as fatal as defiance.

Cerys had chosen him because he was young enough to be overlooked, serious enough to remember, and
ordinary enough to be believed. The thought carried no tenderness. Tenderness was a luxury reserved for
people who could afford witnesses. Yet something in them recoiled from the ease with which this room
might consume him.
“Halvard Sablewood,” Cerys said, “you will remove your hand.”
His eyes lifted.
“Master—”
“Remove it.”
He obeyed.
The visitor’s attention narrowed. “You command him as though he belongs to you.”
“He serves the office.”
“A distinction made for ledgers.”
“A distinction made for courts.”
The word courts caused the man to pause. Not fear. Calculation. He had expected secrecy, perhaps panic.
He had not expected Cerys to place the matter where other eyes might see it.
Cerys leaned over the register and drew the seal toward them. It was a dull lump of dark wax, stamped
with the office mark. They pressed a thumb against its edge. The wax yielded.
“The Aegis was delivered under seal,” they said. “Its condition was recorded. Its custody was witnessed. If
you break the seal, you become part of the record.”
“Records can be burned.”
“Not all of them.”
The man’s eyes flicked toward the register.
Cerys felt the hidden royal mark stir again, hotter now. The Bleeding Crown did not grant courage. It
granted memory: of every hand that had reached for power and found another hand already waiting
beneath it. Their blood had been denied a name, but denial was not erasure. The crown knew them.
Somewhere beyond walls and weather, power was moving toward this room in many forms.
The visitor stepped closer to the register.
“Show me the entry.”
“Which entry?”
“The one concerning the Cinder-Wrought Aegis.”
Cerys turned the book toward him. The page opened beneath the weight of their hand. Rows of figures
waited in their narrow columns, obedient as prisoners. The entry lay near the bottom, its ink unremarkable.
The visitor bent over it.
Halvard’s sleeve brushed the table.
A small sound. Cloth against wood.

The visitor heard that too.
His hand moved—not toward the page, but toward Halvard.
Cerys caught his wrist.
For the first time, the man’s composure broke. Not anger. Surprise.
His skin was cold.
“Remove your hand,” Cerys said.
The visitor looked down at their fingers around him, then at Cerys’s face.
“Master of Coin,” he murmured, “you have mistaken restraint for weakness.”
“No,” Cerys said. “I have mistaken nothing.”
Behind the canopy, the Cinder-Wrought Aegis gave a soft metallic click, as if something inside the regalia
had awakened.
The visitor’s gaze shifted toward it.
And in the corridor beyond the sealed door, someone began to knock.
The knock came again.
Three measured blows, each separated by the length of a held breath.
Halvard flinched beneath the visitor’s hand. The quill he had been holding slipped from his fingers and
struck the table. Ink trembled in its well.
Cerys tightened their grip on the cold wrist.
“Who is it?” they called.
The sealed door gave no answer. Only the wind moved beyond it, dragging its dry fingers along the stone.
The visitor smiled.
It was a small expression, almost courteous. That made it worse.
“You arranged this?” Cerys asked.
“If I had arranged it, Master of Coin, you would not have heard the knock.”
“Then you know who stands beyond the door.”
“I know who does not.”
Halvard stared at him. The scribe’s gaze had gone to the ledger beneath the visitor’s other hand, to the
page where the old accounts had been opened and the older lies exposed. Cerys saw the calculation pass
over his face: the door, the stranger, the Aegis, the hand on his sleeve. He was young enough to believe
danger announced itself by entering. He had not yet learned that danger preferred to wait until invited.
Cerys released the visitor’s wrist.
The man did not withdraw it.
That refusal was a blade laid flat upon the table.

“Halvard,” Cerys said, “take the ledger.”
His fingers closed around the book. “Where?”
“Under the canopy.”
He rose too quickly. The chair scraped the floor, and the Cinder-Wrought Aegis answered with another
faint click from behind its curtains.
The visitor turned his head.
“Do not touch it,” Cerys said.
“I had no intention.”
“Your intentions have not distinguished themselves tonight.”
Halvard crossed to the canopy. He moved with the care of someone carrying a basin full of blood. The
regalia waited in its shadow, imposing and cinder-dark, its surfaces fire-scarred by craft or memory. No
flame shone upon it, yet the metal seemed to hold a low, inward dusk. It was authority made solid,
ceremony hammered into something that could survive a ruined world.
The Cinder-Wrought Aegis had awakened when the visitor reached for Halvard.
Cerys had felt it through the room.
Not a summons. Not yet.
A warning.
The knock came a third time.
Halvard halted with the ledger against his chest.
“Open it,” the visitor said.
Cerys looked at him. “You are very eager to be obeyed.”
“I am eager for you to survive the next minute.”
“Then you should begin by telling me what waits outside.”
His face remained composed, but the cold had deepened in his eyes. “A question.”
“Only one?”
“Questions breed.”
Beyond the door, something shifted. Not footsteps. The faint drag of cloth, perhaps, or a sleeve passing
over the iron fittings.
Cerys imagined the corridor: empty lamps, black mortar, dust settled in the seams. They imagined a hand
resting against the other side of the door. They imagined that hand wearing a ring, or a glove, or nothing at
all.
The Bleeding Crown had taught Cerys that a door was never merely a door. It was a promise made by one
side to the other: I am not yet entering.

They had been born in 330 AS, into a silence that had never acknowledged them. The Crown’s blood ran
through them without naming them. In public, Cerys was a Master of Coin. In private, they carried an
inheritance no ledger could balance and no confession could make safe.
The visitor knew. Or suspected enough.
That was the true reason he had come.
Cerys moved around the table. The man watched them without turning his body, as if he had expected the
motion and was merely allowing it to happen.
“Halvard,” Cerys said, “read the final entry.”
The scribe swallowed. “Now?”
“Now.”
He opened the ledger.
The pages had been written by several hands across several reigns, the ink fading from brown to the color
of old bruises. A column of expenditure ran down the page. Beside it, in a cramped notation, were the
remnants of a military account.
Halvard lowered his eyes.
“‘The War of Drowned Light began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS,’” he read.
The visitor’s expression altered by less than a breath.
Cerys watched him.
Halvard continued. “‘Recorded casualties: 64617.’”
Outside, the corridor remained still.
“The account says the conflict collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals,” Halvard said. “The Silent
Choir is recorded as the victor.”
“Recorded,” the visitor repeated.
The word entered the room like a drop of poison.
Halvard’s finger moved down the page. “It also says the war’s spark was secretly staged by The Silent
Choir.”
The Aegis clicked.
This time, the sound seemed to come from within the metal’s heart.
The visitor looked toward the canopy again. “You keep treason in an account book.”
“We keep history where coin can find it,” Cerys said.
“History is only treason that has learned to dress itself.”
The knock did not return.
That absence pressed harder than the blows had.
Cerys turned toward the door. “You said there was a question.”

“There is.”
“Ask it.”
The visitor finally withdrew his hand from the table. Halvard stepped back beneath the canopy, clutching
the ledger. The air seemed thinner around the stranger now, stripped of warmth. Cerys could hear the faint
scrape of Halvard’s breathing and, beneath it, the almost inaudible shiver of metal.
“Which power,” the visitor said, “will you starve first?”
Cerys studied him.
The Ashen Vanguard. House Morvain. The Silent Choir. The Iron-Ring Cartel. The Bleeding Crown.
Five hungers circling the ruins of the realm. Five mouths insisting they alone knew how to swallow what
remained. Every purse in Cerys’s keeping was a leash tied to one of them. Every ration delayed, every
levy softened, every shipment redirected altered the distance between siege and treaty.
The question was not which power could be starved.
It was which one would understand the gesture.
“You presume I intend to starve anyone,” Cerys said.
“No. I presume you intend to make a choice and call it necessity.”
“Necessity is what remains after all the honest choices have been spent.”
A low sound came from behind the door.
A breath.
Halvard closed the ledger.
Cerys did not look at him. “What lies beyond the sealed door?”
The visitor’s eyes settled on Cerys’s face. “Something that has waited a long time to hear you speak.”
“Then it has cultivated patience.”
“It has cultivated certainty.”
Cerys felt the old inheritance stir—not in the blood, but in the mind. A pressure behind the eyes. A
memory without an image. The Crown had never called them child, heir, or kin. It had offered no
embrace. Yet some part of it had always seemed to wait beneath the ash, confident that Cerys would
eventually come close enough to be burned.
Behind them, Halvard whispered, “Master of Coin.”
Cerys glanced back.
He had drawn the curtain aside by an inch.
The Cinder-Wrought Aegis stood in its cradle. The dark regalia seemed taller than before. Its edges caught
no light. Along one fire-scarred plate, a line had opened where no seam had been visible.
Something pale glimmered inside.
Not a blade.

Not a jewel.
A narrow strip of material, folded and sealed, lodged beneath the metal as if the armor had grown around
it.
Cerys crossed the room.
The visitor rose.
“Remain seated,” Cerys said.
The man did not.
For an instant the distance between them became a field of drawn weapons. Cerys felt the temptation to
reach for authority, to let the room remember who commanded its coin, its guards, its doors. But authority
was a garment. The Aegis was something else. It did not obey command. It recognized burden.
The visitor took one step toward the canopy.
Cerys placed themself between him and the regalia.
“Touch it,” they said, “and I will learn whether cold skin burns.”
He stopped.
The sealed strip within the Aegis trembled.
From beyond the door came a voice.
Not loud. Not muffled. It spoke as though the wood were absent.
“Cerys Sablewood the Ashen.”
Halvard made a broken sound.
The visitor’s composure returned, and with it came the smallest inclination of his head, almost a bow.
Cerys stared at the door.
No one outside should have known the name spoken only in ledgers, in accusations, in the mouths of those
who wished to make a weapon from an unacknowledged heir.
The voice spoke again.
“Open the door.”
Cerys looked toward Halvard. The scribe stood rigid beneath the shadow of the canopy, the ledger pressed
to his ribs. The pale strip inside the Aegis had begun to unfold by itself.
A single line appeared.
The ink was wet.
Cerys stepped closer.
The visitor said, “Do not read it.”
The door’s iron bolts moved.
Not outward.

Inward.
And beneath the first word on the unsealed message, Cerys saw the mark of the Bleeding Crown.

Chapter 7
The ward lay beneath a cloth that had once been white.
Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless kept his hand upon the hilt of his sword and watched the cloth tremble in the
draught. The room had no windows, only arrow slits sealed with waxed shutters, yet the cold found its
way in. It moved along the stones like something with purpose.
Across the table, the quartermaster waited.
“Ignatz Marrowgate,” Ignatz said.
The man inclined his head. “Warden-Commander.”
The title sounded like a coin tested between the teeth. Marrowgate wore it without pleasure. His role was
Quartermaster, and the ledgers beneath his hands had made a fortress of him: columns, seals, tallies,
names reduced to ink. The light from the single lamp found no softness in the papers.
Ignatz looked again at the cloth.
“You said it was recovered.”
“I said it was found among the sealed stores.”
“That is not the same thing.”
“No.” Marrowgate’s finger rested upon a line of figures. “It is not.”
Beyond the walls, the garrison shifted through its watches. Boots passed, stopped, passed again. Someone
coughed in the corridor. Somewhere beneath the stone, water moved through a broken channel, patient as
a grave.
Ignatz drew the cloth aside.
The Hollow Edge waited in a shallow iron cradle.
It was not shaped like a sword, nor like any weapon made for the hand. It resembled a piece of absence
given a boundary: a narrow ward of dark material, its surface dull until the lamp touched it, then
swallowing the flame in a thin, merciless line.
“The Hollow Edge,” Marrowgate said.
“I know what it is.”
“The records identify it as a ward.”
“I can read.”
“The Hollow Edge is a ward,” Marrowgate repeated, as though precision might keep the room from
changing around them. “It was forged in 216 AS.”
Ignatz did not touch it.
The year had been pressed into the old inventory in a different hand, one long dead or silenced. 216 AS.
The numbers looked too clean beside the stains. He imagined the smith who had written them, bent over a
table while the world still remembered how to make promises. He imagined the ward cooling in black
water. He imagined nothing at all.

“Why show me this?” he asked.
Marrowgate’s mouth tightened. “Because it was not in the ledger.”
“That is a poor reason.”
“It was found beneath a false floor.”
“An even poorer one.”
“The seal on the chamber bears the authority of the Vanguard.”
“The Ashen Vanguard has sealed many rooms.”
“And opened fewer.”
Ignatz let the cloth fall back over the ward.
Marrowgate’s hand moved quickly, almost imperceptibly, toward the nearest page. A man defending
paper defended something more precious than paper. Ignatz had learned that before he learned the weight
of command. A garrison could survive without food for a little while. A lord could survive without
soldiers. But a missing line in a ledger had a way of becoming a knife.
“Who knew it was there?” Ignatz asked.
“Before today?”
“Before you found it.”
Marrowgate looked down.
The lamp guttered. Its wick leaned, and the room’s shadows lengthened toward the door.
“No one,” the Quartermaster said.
Ignatz smiled without warmth. “That answer is always a door left open.”
“Ignatz Ashgrove—”
“Do not spend my name as though it buys you safety.”
Marrowgate’s gaze lifted then. There was fear in it, but not for himself. Fear had many faces. Ignatz
trusted none of them.
He turned from the table. The chamber had once been used for storing maps, though the maps were gone
and the wall racks stood empty. Dust lay in the grooves where pins had held the realm together. A coast. A
pass. A city. The marks had been scraped away, leaving pale scars in the stone.
He thought of Gloamreach, sealed behind its quarantine and its guarded silence. He thought of Cindermere
Hold, abandoned among The High Spires, its former strength hollowed into blackened ruin. He thought of
old wars whose banners had rotted before their victors learned how to celebrate.
The War of Drowned Light had begun in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS. The Silent Choir was recorded as
the victor. Its cost was 64617 casualties. The war had collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals, and its
spark had been secretly staged by The Silent Choir.
Those facts had been taught to him as a boy, then repeated until they became a kind of weather. Yet
tonight the numbers felt like footsteps outside the wall.

“Does it work?” Ignatz asked.
Marrowgate hesitated.
“That was not difficult.”
“The attunement cost is recorded as 21.”
“I did not ask what the record says.”
“It is all we have.”
“No. It is all you are willing to tell me.”
The Quartermaster’s fingers closed over the ledger. “Warden-Commander, I am not a relic-binder.”
“Neither am I.”
“Then why are you here?”
Because someone had sent a message through a hand that did not belong to any household in the hold.
Because the message had contained three details no quartermaster should have known and one detail no
loyal man would have sold. Because the Iron-Ring Cartel paid better than the truth deserved.
Ignatz kept his face still.
“I was told the storehouse contained something dangerous.”
“Everything in a sealed storehouse is dangerous.”
“Then you will not object if I remove this.”
Marrowgate’s breath caught. “It belongs to the Vanguard.”
“Does it?”
“The mark—”
“Is old.”
“It is not yours.”
“Nothing is mine.”
The words came too easily. They hung between them, stripped of the authority his title demanded. Ignatz
Ashgrove the Oathless. A name for a man who guarded the realm while keeping one hand beneath his
cloak.
Marrowgate looked at the cloth. “If you remove it, I must record the transfer.”
“Then record it.”
“To whom?”
Ignatz drew his sword an inch. Metal whispered against the scabbard.
The Quartermaster flinched, though the blade did not leave its sheath.
“Record the loss,” Ignatz said.
“That would be false.”

“Most useful records are.”
The water beneath the floor gave a soft, hollow knock.
For an instant, the lamp’s flame turned black.
Ignatz’s hand tightened on the sword. The cloth rose from the table as if something beneath it had
breathed. He felt the ward before he saw it: not power, exactly, but an edge where power had been cut
away. The Hollow Edge seemed to make the room less complete. The corners receded. The walls lost their
certainty.
Marrowgate whispered a prayer.
Ignatz looked at him. “You said you were not a relic-binder.”
“I am not.”
“Then why did you pray?”
“I did not.”
“You did.”
“I said nothing.”
The cloth settled.
A knock sounded at the door.
Three strikes. Evenly spaced.
Marrowgate went pale.
Ignatz did not move. He listened to the silence after the knock. The corridor beyond remained still. No
boots. No breathing. Whoever waited there understood the value of a door.
“Is that expected?” Ignatz asked.
“No.”
“Good.”
He took the cloth from the table and folded it once over the ward. The material seemed to resist him,
dragging lightly across the iron cradle. He felt a coldness enter his palm—not pain, not yet, but the
suggestion of pain remembered by someone else.
The Hollow Edge was a ward, forged in 216 AS. Its attunement cost was 21.
The facts arranged themselves in his mind with the bleak order of graves.
Another knock.
Marrowgate rose. “Warden-Commander—”
“Sit.”
“There may be guards outside.”
“There are always guards outside.”

“Not these.”
Ignatz stepped toward the door. The room narrowed behind him. The Quartermaster remained standing,
trapped between obedience and whatever he had hidden beneath the false floor.
“Who sent you the message?” Marrowgate asked.
Ignatz stopped.
The question had been spoken softly, but it struck with the clean force of a thrown blade.
He turned.
Marrowgate’s hands were empty now. His ledger lay open, its pages trembling in the draught.
“I receive many messages,” Ignatz said.
“Not from the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
The lamp guttered again.
For one suspended moment, neither man spoke. The old stone held their silence. Under the cloth, the ward
seemed to listen.
Ignatz felt the familiar inward closing: the place where fear went when command required it to become
still. He had ordered men into ash, into flooded tunnels, into fields where the dead had been left beneath
broken banners. He had watched loyalty drain from faces and called it necessity. He had learned that a
secret was not a thing one carried. It was a thing that carried you, slowly, toward the blade.
Marrowgate swallowed. “I saw the mark.”
“What mark?”
“The iron ring.”
“You saw no mark.”
“It was on the message.”
“You saw no message.”
“I know what I saw.”
“No,” Ignatz said. “You know what you fear.”
The Quartermaster’s eyes moved to the cloth.
A fourth knock came.
Not evenly spaced this time.
A pause. Then two quick strikes.
Ignatz drew the sword fully.
The blade gave back the lamp’s weak light. He placed himself between the door and the table, though he
could not have said whether he meant to protect the ward or prevent Marrowgate from reaching it.
“Open it,” Marrowgate whispered.

“You are the one who wants the door opened.”
“I want no one to enter.”
“That is not what your voice says.”
Something scraped on the other side.
Not metal. Not a boot.
A fingernail, perhaps, drawn slowly down the wood.
Ignatz felt the Hollow Edge call—not toward his hand, but toward the empty space within him where
every oath had once been laid. His fingers began to ache. Beneath the cloth, the ward gave a faint, dry
sound, like a blade being sharpened against a bone.
Marrowgate backed away from the table.
“Warden-Commander,” he said, “if they know it is here—”
“They do.”
“If the Cartel has come—”
“They have not.”
“How can you know?”
Ignatz stared at the door.
Because the Iron-Ring Cartel would not knock. Because those who dealt in secrets preferred to enter as
though they had always belonged inside. Because the message had promised a meeting in silence, and this
was theater.
The scraping stopped.
A voice spoke through the wood.
“Warden-Commander.”
Ignatz knew the voice, though no name rose with it.
The sound was muffled, made almost human by timber and distance.
“Give us the ward,” it said, “and the room will remain yours.”
Marrowgate made a broken noise.
Ignatz lifted his sword until its point faced the door. Behind him, the cloth slipped from the iron cradle.
The Hollow Edge lay bare in the lamplight, and the flame bent toward it.
The voice came again.
“Give us The Hollow Edge.”
Ignatz felt the cost waiting in the dark of the ward, patient as a debt.
Then the door began to open.
The door opened by the width of a hand.

Cold entered first.
It carried the mineral breath of the stairwell, wet stone and old iron, and with it the faint rasp of something
dragged behind the waiting speaker. Ignatz did not move. The Hollow Edge lay between him and the
widening dark, its surface drinking the lamplight until the room seemed to lean toward the blackness at its
center.
Marrowgate whispered, “Commander.”
“Be quiet.”
The Quartermaster’s breath fluttered behind him. Ignatz heard cloth shift, a knee strike the floor, then the
soft clink of a buckle being fumbled. Marrowgate had been brave while the door was shut. That was the
common shape of courage: a creature that lived only in the interval before consequence.
The gap widened.
A hand appeared around the edge of the door. It wore a glove of pale leather, stitched without ornament.
The fingers were narrow. They rested on the wood with a delicacy that made Ignatz think of a mourner
touching a coffin.
“Step away from the ward,” the voice said.
Ignatz lowered the point of his sword by no more than a finger’s breadth. “You first.”
A pause.
“Your bargain is not with me.”
“No,” Ignatz said. “It is with the thing you came to steal.”
The door opened another inch. Beyond it stood a figure in a dark mantle, the hood raised. No face showed
beneath it, only a dull oval of shadow. Behind the figure, the stairwell descended into darkness on one side
and climbed into darkness on the other. The corridor lamps had gone out. Whether they had been
extinguished or merely refused to burn, Ignatz could not tell.
He could feel the ward watching.
Not with eyes. The Hollow Edge had no eyes. But its emptiness pressed against the room, a pressure like
deep water against a sealed hull. The metal cradle beneath it groaned.
Marrowgate made the broken noise again.
The hooded figure’s head turned slightly. “The Quartermaster may leave.”
Ignatz heard the fear in Marrowgate’s silence.
“Open the passage,” Ignatz said.
“It is open.”
“For him.”
The figure’s gloved hand tightened on the door. “You mistake permission for mercy.”
“I mistake nothing.”
That was a lie, and the lie had weight. It settled beneath his tongue.

He had sold the Cartel the route through the lower stores, the timing of the watch rotations, the weakness
in the eastern seal. He had sold them enough to make this meeting possible. Not enough to lose the ward.
Not enough to deliver himself into a room without terms. Every message he had sent had carried some
small denial within it, some concealed turn by which he might later insist he had meant to mislead them.
But the Hollow Edge had not been part of the bargain.
The voice beyond the door said, “You have already opened the way.”
Ignatz glanced at the ward.
The lamp flame bent toward it again.
A thin crack appeared across the floor between the cradle and the threshold. It was not a crack in the stone.
It was a line of absence, narrow as a hair and blacker than the Hollow Edge itself. It ran toward the door,
crossed the threshold, and vanished beneath the hooded figure’s boot.
The figure looked down.
For the first time, something like caution entered the room.
Ignatz smiled without warmth. “You should have brought more than a door.”
“There are others behind me.”
“Then they can listen.”
“Listen to what?”
“To the terms.”
The pressure in the room deepened. Ignatz felt it in his teeth. The sword in his hand had become heavy,
though the weight came from neither steel nor fatigue. It was the ward pulling at the air around it, making
every object uncertain of its own place.
He knew the old notation. He had read it in sealed inventories and copied it into reports meant for eyes
that never opened. The Hollow Edge: ward, forged in 216 AS. Its attunement cost was 21.
Twenty-one.
The number had seemed harmless in ink. Almost clean. A mark beside a line of script. Now it moved
through him like a hooked chain, taking hold of places he had believed belonged to himself.
The Hollow Edge did not offer strength.
It offered vacancy.
The attuned hand became a door through which nothing passed unchanged. Memory went first, if the
records were to be trusted. Then desire. Then the little private laws by which a person remained a person.
Ignatz had never found a record of anyone who had paid the cost and returned with the same interior
shape.
The hooded figure said, “You know what it requires.”
“I know what it costs.”
“Then you know you cannot wield it.”

“I have not wielded it.”
“Yet.”
Behind him, Marrowgate breathed, “Commander, the cradle—”
“I see it.”
The iron cradle had begun to tremble. Its legs ticked against the stone. The Hollow Edge remained still,
but the emptiness around it had become almost visible, a dim distortion that swallowed the lamp’s gold
and left the edges of the room pale and bruised.
The hooded figure stepped over the threshold.
Ignatz’s sword rose.
The figure stopped.
There was nothing theatrical in the movement. No flourish, no threat. The hooded stranger simply halted,
as though the sword’s point had reached farther than steel could reach.
“Do not,” the voice said.
“Do not what?”
“Make the ward choose.”
Ignatz’s hand tightened around the hilt. “It has chosen nothing.”
“It has been choosing since you uncovered it.”
The statement struck him with the force of recognition. He remembered the cloth slipping from the cradle.
Remembered the flame bending. Remembered the strange absence beneath his ribs when he first touched
the ward’s bare metal.
Perhaps the choice had begun before the door.
Perhaps the door had only given it an audience.
Marrowgate rose behind him. His boots scraped. Ignatz did not look back.
“Stay where you are.”
“I can’t.”
“You can.”
“I hear them.”
At first Ignatz heard only the room: the trembling cradle, the uneasy flame, the wet breath of the stairwell.
Then the sound separated itself from the rest.
A murmur below.
Not voices. Not exactly.
A cadence passed upward through the stone, soft and measured, syllables stripped of meaning. It did not
rise like a shout. It gathered like fog. The sound pressed against the door and the walls, slid into the cracks
between the floorstones, and curled around the Hollow Edge.

The Silent Choir.
Ignatz knew the sound from reports written by men who had survived too much to describe it plainly. He
knew it from the old war ledgers, where the final line had been entered without triumph or lament: The
Silent Choir victor of The War of Drowned Light.
Victory had not made them loud.
It had made them patient.
The hooded figure tilted its head as the murmur climbed.
“You hear them,” it said.
“I hear a threat.”
“You hear the proof.”
“Of what?”
“That the ward has been found.”
Ignatz looked past the figure into the corridor. More darkness stood there now, but the darkness had
shapes. A shoulder. The edge of a sleeve. A pale hand resting against the wall. None of them moved. Their
stillness seemed less like discipline than surrender.
Marrowgate whispered, “The Choir.”
The hooded figure did not correct him.
Ignatz felt a pulse in his palm.
The Hollow Edge had no warmth. It gave him no strength. Yet something within the artifact had answered
the murmur below, and the answer had traveled through the sword, up his arm, into the hollow behind his
breastbone.
His thoughts thinned.
For one terrible moment, the room lost its names.
Door became barrier. Sword became line. Marrowgate became breath. The ward became center.
He pulled himself back by remembering a betrayal.
Not the Cartel. That memory was too near, too alive.
He remembered the first oath he had broken—not its words, which had faded, but the sensation afterward:
the clean relief, the sudden silence where duty had been. The relief had frightened him more than guilt. It
had told him that a man could survive the removal of his own law.
The Hollow Edge stirred.
Ignatz drove the point of his sword into the floor.
The sound rang through the room.
The murmur beneath the stone faltered.

The hooded figure moved at last. A blade flashed from beneath the mantle, narrow and dull, held low in
the hand. Ignatz saw no face, but he felt the attention beneath the hood sharpen upon him.
“You cannot command the ward,” the figure said.
“No.”
“You cannot command the Choir.”
“No.”
“Then what remains to you?”
Ignatz’s gaze shifted to the Quartermaster.
Marrowgate stood with his back to the wall, one hand clutching a leather satchel against his chest. The
satchel’s clasp had broken. Papers showed through the opening, their edges trembling in the ward’s
influence.
“What is in the bag?” Ignatz asked.
Marrowgate stared at him. “You know.”
“I know what you were ordered to carry.”
“I was ordered to carry nothing.”
“Then you will not object to opening it.”
The Quartermaster’s mouth worked soundlessly.
The hooded figure said, “The bag is irrelevant.”
“Then let him open it.”
“No.”
Ignatz looked at the figure again. “You have just told me it is irrelevant.”
“It is not yours to examine.”
A silence settled.
There it was. Not fear. Not exactly. A limit.
Ignatz felt the shape of the meeting change. The Cartel had wanted the ward, but the people beyond the
door wanted something else. The satchel had not been mentioned in the message. Marrowgate had not
mentioned it when they entered the ward. Its presence had been concealed from him, and concealment
within a command was always a second command waiting to reveal itself.
“Put the satchel on the floor,” Ignatz said.
Marrowgate shook his head.
“Now.”
The Quartermaster’s gaze darted toward the hooded figure.
That glance was answer enough.

Ignatz stepped sideways, keeping the sword trained on the threshold. The Hollow Edge remained behind
him, black and silent, its empty field spreading across the room. He could feel the distance between
himself and the ward narrowing, though he had not moved toward it.
“Quartermaster,” he said, “put it down.”
“I can’t.”
“You can.”
“They’ll kill me.”
“They may.”
The words sounded cruel. They were not meant to be. Cruelty required appetite. Ignatz had only the cold
arithmetic of a man who had already sold too much and still wished to keep one thing for himself.
The hooded figure advanced another step.
The line of absence beneath its boot lengthened.
The lamplight went out.
In the sudden dark, the murmur below became a single inhalation, vast and soundless, and the Hollow
Edge rose from its cradle without being touched. Marrowgate cried out. The hooded figure lifted its blade.
Ignatz felt the ward enter the space between his ribs—
—and something in the corridor began to sing.
The song had no melody Ignatz could follow.
It entered through the stones, through the mortar and the iron nails, through the wet black marrow of the
keep. It did not rise or fall. It simply existed, a thread drawn through the dark by a hand too patient to
tremble.
The Hollow Edge halted above the cradle.
Its blade was not bright. Nothing in the corridor was bright. Yet Ignatz saw its outline with the intimate
certainty of pain: a narrow absence, a cut in the world where steel ought to have been. The ward leaned
toward the song.
The hooded figure did not move.
Marrowgate breathed beside him in short, wet pulls. Quartermaster Ignatz Marrowgate, born in 425 AS,
whose hands had counted grain, salt, lamp oil, arrowheads, and the bodies that required all of them. He
had been a clerk when Ignatz first saw him. Now his fingers were locked around the empty scabbard at his
belt as though arithmetic might protect him.
“What is singing?” Marrowgate whispered.
Ignatz tasted copper. “Do not listen.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one you can afford.”
The song tightened.

A seam appeared in the corridor wall. Not a crack: a division. The stones on either side seemed to
remember that they had once belonged to separate places. Cold air sighed through it, carrying the smell of
extinguished fires and old water.
The hooded figure lifted its blade.
The Hollow Edge turned.
The ward struck the figure without touching it.
There was no flash. The hood collapsed inward, and the thing beneath it folded as though a fist had closed
around its bones. Its blade fell soundlessly. The line of absence beneath its boots vanished. For one
trembling instant, Ignatz saw a human hand pressed against the inside of the hood, five fingers spread in
mute appeal.
Then the figure was gone.
Marrowgate made a noise like a man being strangled.
Ignatz seized his collar and drove him against the wall. “Where is the chalice?”
The Quartermaster’s eyes shone in the dark. “You saw what that thing did.”
“Where?”
“I gave you the inventory.”
“I asked where.”
Marrowgate swallowed. Beneath the stink of fear, he smelled of ash and boiled leather. “The reliquary
was never in the inventory.”
Ignatz tightened his grip until the cloth creaked. “Do not make me hurt you.”
“You already have.”
The words found their mark because they were true.
Ignatz released him.
For a moment there was only the song and the faint scrape of the Hollow Edge settling back toward its
cradle. The blade seemed heavier now. The air around it had the deadened quality of a room after an
execution.
Marrowgate touched his throat. “You knew.”
“I suspected.”
“You knew enough to send word beyond the hold.”
The accusation should have angered him. Instead, it opened the old chamber in his mind where every
secret had been stacked and labeled, each one waiting for the day it would become evidence.
He had sent the message through the Iron-Ring Cartel because the Cartel paid in certainty. Not loyalty.
Not forgiveness. Certainty. A location. A patrol route. A name attached to a seal. Intelligence was clean
when reduced to ink and payment.

He had told himself that the Hollow Edge was not a weapon. He had told himself the Iron-Ring Cartel
wanted only knowledge of the abandoned vault beneath the keep. He had told himself many things, and
none of them had survived the hooded figure.
“I sell intelligence,” he said.
Marrowgate stared at him.
“To the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
The Quartermaster’s mouth opened. His breath shuddered out, and with it went whatever remained of his
faith in the room.
“You are a Warden-Commander.”
“I am aware.”
“You bear the ward.”
“I am aware.”
“You swore—”
“No.”
The word came softly. It was the oldest answer he possessed.
Marrowgate looked at the Hollow Edge. “They call you the Oathless.”
“They call me what helps them sleep.”
“And what do you call yourself?”
Ignatz looked through the wall that was not a wall. Far below, the unseen chamber murmured with the
slow distress of something dreaming beneath frozen water.
He had been born in 258 AS, into a realm that no longer remembered how to distinguish a promise from a
threat. He had spent his life watching men kneel to banners and rise beneath knives. Oaths had never
protected anyone. They merely told the killer where to place the blade.
“I call myself useful,” he said.
The song stopped.
The silence that followed was worse.
The Hollow Edge dropped into its cradle.
Somewhere below, a latch opened.
Marrowgate began to cry. Not loudly. Tears slipped down his face without expression, catching the weak
grayness leaking from the seam in the wall.
Ignatz stepped past him.
The corridor sloped down by degrees. He knew the construction from the plans he had sold: a stair beyond
the cracked arch, then a gallery sealed beneath a collapsed chapel, then the vault. The plans had been old,
but the earth was older, and earth kept its own revisions.

At the arch, he found a smear of pale residue on the stones. It glittered without light.
Marrowgate followed. “You cannot take it.”
“You brought me here.”
“I brought you to the vault.”
“You brought me to the Chalice of Ashdeep.”
The Quartermaster stopped.
The name seemed to draw the cold closer.
It was a reliquary forged in 323 AS, and the knowledge of it had been buried beneath ledgers, false
requisitions, and the kind of silence that required several people to maintain. Ignatz had seen its
description in a fragment bought from a dying archivist: a vessel dark as banked coals, with a hollow at its
heart that held ash without ever filling.
Attunement to the Chalice of Ashdeep cost 27.
He had not told the Cartel that.
Perhaps because he had not known whether the cost was paid in blood, memory, years, or something less
merciful.
Marrowgate’s voice came thinly behind him. “It was meant to remain hidden.”
“By whom?”
“I don’t know.”
“That answer has become fashionable.”
“You think I wanted this?”
“I think wanting is an indulgence.”
The stair waited beyond the arch.
There were no steps at first. Only darkness, descending. Then the gray residue gathered itself along the
edges of the stone, outlining each tread in a corpse-pale glow. The song returned, not from the walls this
time, but from the depth beneath them.
Marrowgate pressed both hands to his mouth.
Ignatz began down.
At the third step, the keep shifted. Dust drifted from above. Something moved behind the stones at his
shoulder, matching his pace with a careful, dragging patience.
He did not look.
“Did the Iron-Ring Cartel send the hooded one?” Marrowgate asked.
“No.”
“You are certain?”
“No.”

The Quartermaster stumbled. Ignatz caught his sleeve before he fell.
For an instant, their faces were close. Marrowgate’s fear had become a kind of hatred, and hatred was
often more durable than courage.
“The Silent Choir knows,” he said.
Ignatz continued downward. “The Silent Choir knows many things.”
“They know about the reliquary.”
“Perhaps.”
“They know what happened during The War of Drowned Light.”
The stair seemed to narrow.
That war had begun in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS. Its records carried the official weight of 64617
casualties, a number so large it ceased to signify bodies and became instead a weather system, a season of
ash that had passed over every surviving house. The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor.
But victory was not the whole truth.
The war’s spark had been secretly staged by the Silent Choir.
Ignatz had learned that from intelligence he had once stolen, then sold, then stolen back. The document
had changed hands more often than the people named in it. Every faction possessed a piece of the lie. The
Ashen Vanguard had the banners. House Morvain had the graves. The Cartel had the prices. The Bleeding
Crown had the silence afterward.
The Silent Choir had the match.
“Say it,” Marrowgate whispered.
Ignatz stopped.
The gray light climbed the stair beneath them. It painted his hands, the scabbard at his hip, the hard planes
of the Hollow Edge’s hilt where it hung at his side.
“Say what?”
“That the Choir began it.”
“The records say The Silent Choir won.”
“I did not ask who won.”
“No,” Ignatz said. “You asked for a confession.”
Marrowgate’s face twisted. “My brother died in that war.”
Ignatz did not answer.
“Not in battle. Not beneath a banner. He was taken in a village where the wells had gone black. They said
the Choir had saved us from worse.”
“The Silent Choir is recorded as the victor.”
“You speak like a ledger.”

“A ledger remembers what men agree to forget.”
“And what do you remember?”
The stair ended.
Before them stood a door made of dark metal, without hinges or handle. At its center was a shallow
impression in the shape of a chalice.
Ignatz approached it.
The song had become a pressure behind his eyes. Each note carried an image: broken banners drowned in
red water, lamps burning beneath the surface of a sea, mouths opening in prayer and closing around ash.
He laid his palm against the door.
The metal was warm.
Marrowgate whimpered. “Don’t.”
Ignatz looked back.
The Quartermaster had drawn the Hollow Edge.
He held it badly. The ward’s absence trembled in his grasp, blurring the fingers around the hilt. Yet the
blade had risen to point at Ignatz’s heart.
“You cannot attune to it,” Marrowgate said.
“To what?”
“The chalice.”
“You said it was hidden.”
“It was hidden from the living.”
Something breathed on the other side of the door.
Ignatz felt the breath enter him.
Not through his mouth. Through the old scars beneath his skin, through every place where an oath had
once been spoken and then abandoned. The thing beyond the door tasted his betrayals. It found the
Cartel’s coins, the sealed messages, the names he had traded for safe passage and the names he had
withheld for reasons he could no longer defend.
The door spoke without words.
Twenty-seven.
The cost waited in the dark like a hand held out for payment.
Marrowgate took one step forward. “Commander.”
Ignatz almost turned toward the title. It belonged to a better man, perhaps, or merely to a man who had not
yet learned what command required.
Behind them, far up the stair, stone grated against stone.
The hooded figure had returned.

No. Not returned.
There were several of them now.
Their absence descended the stairs, one after another, their boots finding the pale-lit steps. No faces
showed beneath the hoods. No blades were raised. They came with the solemn patience of mourners
approaching a grave.
Marrowgate looked at them, then at Ignatz. The Hollow Edge shook in his hands.
“What do we do?”
Ignatz kept his palm against the warm metal.
The song changed.
The door began to open inward, and from the darkness beyond came the scent of deep ash, sealed
chambers, and something sweet that had been waiting far too long to be named.

Chapter 8
The ink had thickened in its well.
Maelis Harrowick the Pale touched the nib to the surface and watched the black bead gather, tremble, and
refuse the page. The chamber was cold enough that the candle flame had drawn itself narrow. Beyond the
shutters, wind moved through the court in long, patient breaths, worrying at hinges and loose stone. The
Hold had a thousand such sounds. A realm in ruins did not fall silent. It creaked. It muttered. It
remembered itself badly.
On the desk lay the open register of offices, its vellum yellowed to the color of old bone.
Maelis Harrowick the Pale — Court Chronicler. Born in 340 AS.
The words had been copied by another hand, though the hand was dead now. Maelis had not been born
with the epithet. No one was born pale in the manner of histories. The name had been given, then repeated,
then made useful. A chronicler was a vessel into which other people poured their certainty. A pale one,
perhaps, was less likely to be suspected of carrying fire.
Maelis dipped the nib again.
The page before them concerned the War of Drowned Light.
They had written the title three times and scratched it out twice. The phrase possessed a dampness that
seemed to seep through the ink. It called to mind broken banners hanging in rain, light drowned beneath
dark water, and men standing knee-deep in mud while something unseen moved among them.
The official record lay open beneath Maelis’s hand.
The War of Drowned Light began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS. Its casualties numbered 64617.
The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor. The war’s spark was secretly staged by The Silent
Choir. The conflict collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals.
Maelis read the passage until the letters lost their shapes.
A decade of guerrilla reprisals.
There was a cruelty in the phrasing. It made the dead into weather. It made vengeance into a season that
had passed, though the realm still carried it in its walls, its empty roads, its sealed towns. The Silent Choir
had won, the record said. The Silent Choir had lit the first flame in secret, the record said. Then came the
reprisals, the ambushes, the knives beneath cloaks, the villages that learned to fear both banners and the
absence of banners.
Maelis lowered the pen.
A Court Chronicler was expected to preserve what power wished remembered. The duty had been
explained to them in the first room where they had been entrusted with a seal: write clearly, omit nothing
that can be used, and understand that truth is not the same as survival.
The door opened without announcement.
Ignatz Marrowgate entered carrying a narrow iron case against his chest. He was a Quartermaster, and the
title seemed to enter before him, preceding his boots with the dry scent of ledgers, ration stores, and
locked cupboards. No feature of him offered itself to memory. His face might have been made for passing

through corridors unnoticed.
He stopped when he saw the register.
“Still at the war,” he said.
Maelis set the pen across the page. “The war is still at us.”
Ignatz glanced toward the shutters. “The Ashen Vanguard has sent another demand.”
“For what?”
“Grain. Lamp oil. Nails.” He shifted the case under one arm. “The Iron-Ring Cartel has offered to provide
all three.”
“And the price?”
“Their price is always buried beneath the first price.”
Maelis looked again at the words concerning The Silent Choir. “House Morvain?”
“Watching.”
“The Bleeding Crown?”
“Listening.”
“Then all five powers are awake.”
Ignatz did not answer. He had the careful silence of someone who counted before speaking, though Maelis
knew nothing else of his temperament and trusted the absence of evidence more than invention.
The iron case made a small sound as he placed it on the table. Not a rattle. A settling. Something within
had weight and edges.
“What is it?” Maelis asked.
“An inventory.”
“Of what?”
“I was instructed to bring it to the Court Chronicler.”
“By whom?”
Ignatz’s gaze moved to the open register, then returned. “The instruction was sealed.”
“Seals can be read.”
“Not by Quartermasters.”
Maelis almost smiled. The motion died before it reached their mouth.
They drew the case closer. Its lock bore no crest. The metal had been darkened until it drank the
candlelight.
Ignatz produced a key, but did not use it.
“Before you open it,” he said, “you should know the list contains items no one can account for.”
“Unaccounted items are the foundation of every court.”

“This list concerns wards and regalia.”
The chamber seemed to contract around the desk.
“Names?”
Ignatz turned the key. “The Psalter of Seven Sorrows.”
The lock gave.
He lifted the lid. Within lay folded documents, each wrapped in oilskin. Beneath them, in a bed of grey
cloth, rested a small object Maelis could not immediately identify. Its shape suggested a fragment of
something larger, but the old metal had been worked with such deliberate severity that it resisted the eye.
Ignatz unfolded the first document.
“The Psalter of Seven Sorrows,” he read, “is a ward forged in 119 AS. Attunement to it costs 49.”
The number seemed too large for a single object and too small for a kingdom. Maelis had learned that
numbers were most dangerous when they appeared precise. Precision invited trust.
“Where is it?” they asked.
“I have not been told.”
“You brought me an inventory of an object without the object.”
“I brought you what was given to me.”
“And the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell?”
Ignatz’s fingers paused over the next sheet.
“Regalia. Attunement cost: 12. Forging date not recorded.”
“Where is it?”
“I have not been told.”
“Then this is not an inventory.”
“No.”
“What is it?”
Ignatz looked toward the darkened shutters. “A warning, perhaps.”
The wind pressed against the stone. Somewhere beyond the chamber, a bell struck and stopped before
completing its note.
Maelis reached into the case and touched the grey cloth. It was cold. Beneath it, the fragment bore no
inscription they could see, but the silence around it had a different weight from ordinary silence. A ward,
perhaps. Or the residue of one. The Psalter of Seven Sorrows carried its sorrow in its name; the Gauntlet
of Sorrowfell carried grim authority in its name. Names were often the first chains placed upon a thing.
“Why bring this to me?”
“Because you are the Court Chronicler.”
The title landed between them with the finality of a blade laid flat.

Maelis thought of the liege whose death they had plotted.
Not remembered. Not wished. Plotted.
The thought had no face. Faces made guilt sentimental, and sentiment was a door through which hesitation
entered. There had been a sequence: a message withheld, a cup allowed to cool, a guard sent elsewhere, a
hand directed toward a door that ought to have remained closed. Maelis had arranged the death of their
own liege by understanding the machinery of obedience more completely than the person who
commanded it.
They had not called it treason at the time.
They had called it correction.
Now the word came back wearing the dead person’s blood.
Ignatz watched them. “Are you unwell?”
“No.”
“You have gone still.”
“I am a chronicler. Stillness is a professional virtue.”
He gave no sign of accepting this.
Maelis folded the first document along its old crease. “The records concerning Cindermere Hold. Bring
them.”
“I did not bring those.”
“Then bring them.”
Ignatz’s jaw tightened, though whether from irritation or calculation Maelis could not tell.
“Cindermere Hold was founded in 246 AS among The High Spires,” Maelis said. “Its garrison once
numbered 8878. It is abandoned now. It is not a core holding.”
“You know the entry.”
“I know what has been permitted to remain in the entry.”
“And what has been removed?”
“That is why you will bring me the records.”
The Quartermaster shut the case. “Cindermere Hold has no stores.”
“It has walls.”
“Abandoned walls.”
“Walls remember better than men.”
Ignatz looked at the register again. “There is also Gloamreach.”
Maelis felt the ink drying beneath their hand.
“Say it.”

“Gloamreach lies on the Pale Coast. It is a core location. Its garrison is 2,483. It is quarantined.”
“Who sealed it?”
“I was not told.”
“Who commands the garrison?”
“I was not told.”
“Why is it quarantined?”
“I was not told.”
The answers came too smoothly. They had been rehearsed, or perhaps ignorance had become so practiced
that it resembled obedience.
Maelis rose.
The chair legs scraped the floor. The sound seemed indecently loud. They crossed to the shutters and
opened one latch. Cold air entered, carrying ash, wet stone, and the faint mineral reek of the lower streets.
From the height of the court, the realm appeared almost orderly. Roofs gathered around towers. Bridges
joined what the Sundering had torn apart. Watchfires burned where the Ashen Vanguard held its lines.
Farther off, the dark bulk of House Morvain’s quarter lay beneath a smear of cloud. The Silent Choir kept
no visible towers, yet their absence had become its own architecture. The Iron-Ring Cartel had stores,
countinghouses, locked gates. The Bleeding Crown had banners that seemed to drink the night.
Below, a servant passed with a covered tray.
Maelis watched the shape move through the courtyard and thought of how easily a life could be redirected.
A door left unbarred. A message delivered too late. A bowl set before the wrong hand.
Their own liege had died because Maelis had made death seem like an accident of the realm.
Behind them, Ignatz said, “There is one more line.”
Maelis did not turn. “Read it.”
His voice lowered.
“‘The bearer of the record is to present it to Maelis Harrowick the Pale and await instruction.’”
“Bearer?”
“You are the bearer now.”
“No. You are.”
“The case is yours.”
“Then why do you speak as though it belongs to me?”
Ignatz did not answer.
Maelis closed the shutter. In the reflection of the dark glass, the room appeared doubled: the desk, the
candle, the iron case, the figure standing beside it. No canonical feature had ever been granted to their face
by the records. The histories had found no use for eyes, mouth, hands. They had required only the station
and the epithet.

Court Chronicler.
The pale one.
The traitor who had not yet been named.
Maelis returned to the desk and opened the register to a fresh page. The paper waited without accusation.
“What will you write?” Ignatz asked.
Maelis placed the nib in the ink.
For a breath, the page showed nothing but its own blankness.
Then, from somewhere beneath the floor, there came three measured knocks.
Ignatz’s hand moved toward the iron case.
Maelis began to write.
Maelis wrote the first line without knowing what it would say.
The knocks came from beneath the floor.
The ink shone black upon the page. It gathered at the lower curve of the final word, a minute darkness
with the patience of a living thing.
Ignatz had not drawn the iron case from the desk. His hand rested upon its lid, fingers spread, as if he
could keep whatever lay inside from remembering the way out.
“Again,” he whispered.
The chamber held its breath.
A fourth knock sounded.
Not beneath them this time. From the wall behind the shelves.
Dust sifted down between the stones. One of the candles guttered, though no wind entered through the
shuttered windows. Maelis watched the flame bend toward the masonry, thin and eager.
“Do not open it,” Ignatz said.
Maelis lowered the nib. “You were reaching for it.”
“I was stopping you.”
“You have not stopped me yet.”
Ignatz’s hand withdrew. The movement had no dignity in it. It was not fear, precisely. Fear had a body,
and Ignatz’s body had surrendered too much of itself to be called anything so clean. It was calculation
failing under pressure.
Maelis knew the sensation.
They turned the register toward the candlelight. The fresh sentence had already begun to blur. The ink
spread along the fibers, feathering outward until the words seemed less written than bruised into the paper.
Beneath the line, another mark appeared.

A narrow vertical stroke.
Then another beside it.
A gate.
Maelis felt the old room below the fortress rise within them: stone wet with mineral sweat, the iron taste of
the air, the low warmth pressing through the soles of their boots. Embercrag Fortress had always
possessed depths not shown on any plan. The lower passages had been sealed long before Maelis took
command, and the seals had been renewed by hands that no longer existed.
Since 364 AS, Maelis Harrowick the Pale commands Embercrag Fortress.
The words came to them with the cold certainty of a sentence already entered into the world.
They had commanded its walls, its stores, its watchfires, its dwindling obedience. They had signed orders
in the fortress’s name and read petitions beneath its blackened arches. Yet the stone beneath the archive
had never answered to them.
Until tonight.
Ignatz leaned closer to the register. “What is that?”
“A door.”
“There is no door there.”
“Not for you.”
The words escaped before Maelis could soften them. Ignatz’s face—whatever features it possessed,
whatever expression it wore—vanished into the candle’s uncertain reach. The chronicler had learned early
that obscurity was a kind of mercy. A face invited judgment. A voice invited memory. The station was
safer.
Court Chronicler.
The pale one.
The traitor who had not yet been named.
The line on the page darkened. A third stroke emerged, joining the first two. The shape opened like a
mouth.
From within the wall came a muffled scrape.
Ignatz swore under his breath.
Maelis looked at the iron case. “How long has it been in your keeping?”
“You know the answer.”
“I know what the inventory says.”
“The inventory says nothing.”
“Then it is a poor inventory.”
“It is not an inventory.”

“Everything in a fortress becomes one eventually.”
“Not this.”
Ignatz’s hand curled. The knuckles pressed pale beneath the skin, though Maelis had no canonical feature
by which to measure his face, no sanctioned detail by which his fear could be made legible. His role told
them enough. Quartermaster. Minor figure. Keeper of things that outlived the people who owned them.
The iron case gave a small click.
Neither of them touched it.
Maelis heard the sound as clearly as a tooth breaking.
“What is inside?” they asked.
Ignatz stared at the lid. “A ward.”
“Which one?”
He did not answer.
The room seemed to contract around the silence. The shelves leaned inward. The register’s pages lifted
and settled without wind. Somewhere beyond the shutter, a bell rang once, then lost itself in the thick dark
around the fortress.
Maelis placed the nib aside.
“Open it.”
“No.”
“You brought it to me.”
“I brought it because you ordered every sealed object in the archive brought to this chamber.”
“Then obey the order.”
“I have obeyed enough orders.”
There it was: not defiance, but the thin exposed wire beneath it. Maelis studied him. A quartermaster did
not speak that way unless the stores had become more important than the command, or unless the
command had begun to resemble a grave.
“Do you remember Cindermere Hold?” Maelis asked.
Ignatz’s attention shifted toward them.
“Everyone remembers Cindermere Hold.”
“Memory is not the same as knowledge.”
“The old records say it was founded in the High Spires.”
“The old records say more.”
“They say it was ruled by The Ashen Vanguard.”
Maelis turned another page. “Write it.”

Ignatz gave a dry, humorless sound. “You have a hand.”
“I am asking you.”
His gaze went to the register. The three strokes beneath the sentence had joined now. A fine line ran
beneath them, a threshold rendered by ink.
Maelis dipped the nib again and wrote:
Cindermere Hold was ruled by The Ashen Vanguard.
The words did not blur this time.
The wall answered.
A heavy impact shuddered through the chamber. Dust fell in a veil. Behind the shelves, stone grated
against stone, and a seam appeared where there had been none. The shelves did not move. The wall moved
behind them, opening with the slow resistance of something forced to remember an old wound.
Ignatz backed away.
“Stop.”
Maelis continued writing.
The War of Drowned Light was waged at Cindermere Hold in 228 AS.
The candle flames went blue.
For an instant, the chamber filled with another light: drowned radiance, pale and green beneath a depthless
black. Broken banners drifted through the shelves. Ash floated upward instead of falling. Maelis smelled
brine, scorched wool, and the sweet rot of reeds left too long in floodwater.
Then the vision withdrew.
The wall stood open.
Beyond it lay a stair descending into darkness.
Ignatz’s breath came shallowly. “That is not possible.”
“Possibility has never been a requirement of history.”
“You wrote it.”
“I recorded it.”
“You made it happen.”
Maelis looked at the sentence. The ink had dried. “That distinction is why courts keep chroniclers.”
“Courts keep chroniclers so they may blame them afterward.”
“Courts keep chroniclers because kings prefer their sins in the past tense.”
The words struck closer than intended. Or perhaps they had been intended all along. Their own liege had
once believed that history was a locked room, and that the person holding the key possessed the right to
choose what the dead had done.
Maelis had plotted the death of their own liege.

The fact waited inside them without warmth. It had never begged forgiveness. It had only changed shape,
like a corpse under earth.
From the stair came a faint metallic chime.
Ignatz looked toward the iron case. “It wants the ward.”
“Does it?”
“You heard it.”
“I heard metal.”
“Do not pretend ignorance with me.”
Maelis rose. The chair legs complained against the floor. Their robe brushed the desk, carrying with it the
dry scent of parchment and cold ash. There was no canonical feature to betray their expression, no
established shape for the face beneath the epithet. The Pale was enough. The Pale meant the station, the
restraint, the watchfulness. It meant a person built from what they refused to reveal.
They lifted the iron case.
It was heavier than it had been moments before.
Ignatz caught their wrist.
The contact was brief. His fingers released them as if the skin beneath their sleeve had burned him.
“Do not take it below.”
“Why?”
“Because that is where it was made.”
The statement hung in the room.
Maelis lowered the case. “The inventory gives no forging record.”
“I said it was a ward. I did not say it was forged.”
“Every ward has a beginning.”
“Not this one.”
“Which ward?”
Ignatz’s throat moved.
“The Psalter of Seven Sorrows.”
The name seemed to dim the candlelight. Maelis had seen it in old ledgers, its title repeated by hands that
had avoided writing any description beside it. A ward forged in 119 AS. Attunement to it costs 49. Those
were the only permitted facts. The rest had been removed, or hidden, or eaten away by the patient
corrosions of fear.
Maelis set the case upon the desk.
“Open it.”
Ignatz stared at them. “You heard what it is.”

“I heard what you called it.”
“You cannot attune to it.”
“I did not say I would.”
“You command Embercrag Fortress.”
“Since 364 AS.”
“Then you know what command costs.”
Maelis’s hand rested on the lid. The metal was cold enough to numb the fingertips.
“Command costs what is demanded.”
The stair answered with three knocks.
Not beneath the floor.
Not within the wall.
At their feet.
Ignatz flinched back. The iron case sprang open.
Inside, folded upon black cloth, lay a pale object shaped like a closed book. Its cover bore no clasp, no
hinge, no title. Seven thin grooves marked its surface, each one darkened as if something had been poured
into the metal and allowed to harden there.
Beside it lay a gauntlet.
The metal was dull, almost gray, and the fingers curled inward in a gesture that might have been prayer or
threat. No maker’s mark disturbed its surface. No date had been entered for its forging. Yet its name had
been preserved in the old inventories:
Gauntlet of Sorrowfell.
Ignatz whispered, “That was not inside.”
Maelis did not look away from the objects. “You saw the case opened.”
“I saw it empty.”
“Then the room has acquired a liar.”
The gauntlet’s fingers moved.
Ignatz made a sound like a swallowed cry and reached for the register. Maelis seized his sleeve before he
could touch it.
“Do not.”
The black grooves on the book brightened one by one.
From the open stair rose a breath of air carrying the smell of wet stone. Far below, something dragged
itself across a threshold. The sound came slowly, with the patience of an army that knew the fortress
above could not flee.
Maelis turned to the register.

On the next blank page, a sentence had already begun to form.
Not in their hand.
Not in ink.
A dark line pressed upward from beneath the paper, letter by letter.
The Court Chronicler descended—
Maelis lifted the nib.
The sentence stopped.
For the first time, the thing below seemed to hesitate.
Ignatz whispered their name.
Maelis looked into the stairwell and felt, beneath the fear, the old clean impulse that had guided the death
of a liege and preserved a thousand lesser lies.
They stepped over the threshold, carrying the open case, and began to write the next word—
word—
forged.
The stairwell answered.
Not with a voice. With pressure.
The air thickened around Maelis’s wrist, and the open case shuddered as though something inside it had
remembered being buried. The lamps along the wall guttered in sequence, their flames bending downward
toward the dark. Dust sifted from the vaulted stones. Somewhere below, a hinge complained.
Ignatz made a small sound behind them.
“Close it,” he said.
Maelis did not turn. “You saw the sentence.”
“I saw enough.”
“Then you understand why it must remain open.”
“I understand that paper is not meant to write by itself.”
“Paper is meant to receive what is placed upon it.”
“That is not what happened.”
“No,” Maelis said. “It was not.”
The line beneath the newly formed word continued to darken. It spread like a vein under skin, branching
across the page until it reached the margin. There it stopped, gathered itself, and began to crawl
downward.
The register had no wind to blame. No unseen hand moved the leaves. Yet the pages stirred with the slow,
wet rhythm of breathing.

Maelis carried the case farther into the stairwell.
Behind them, Ignatz remained at the threshold. He had served as Quartermaster long enough to understand
that every object in a fortress had a destination, and that every destination could become a grave. His fear
did not make him foolish. That was why Maelis had brought him.
“Tell me what you found in the lower vault,” Maelis said.
“I told you. Nothing.”
“Nothing does not bruise a man.”
His silence followed them down.
The stair was narrow, its inner wall sweating mineral water. Maelis descended with one hand on the cold
stone and the other holding the case. The dark below seemed less like an absence of light than a substance
poured into the shaft. It climbed against them. It pressed through cloth and flesh. Beneath it, faintly, there
was the smell of drowned ash.
The register wrote.
The Court Chronicler descended—
The words appeared one at a time, ahead of Maelis’s gaze.
They had seen records altered by frightened scribes, decrees revised by victorious hands, genealogies
folded and burned. They had watched truth strangled beneath wax seals. None of those violences had
possessed the quiet patience of this.
The next line formed.
—bearing the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell.
Maelis stopped.
The case had been opened only enough to show the black regalia within. The Gauntlet of Sorrowfell lay in
a bed of rotted velvet, its fingers curled as if around an absent throat. No forge mark had been visible on its
outer surface. No maker’s seal. Only a band of dull metal at the wrist, cut with letters so fine they seemed
to have been scratched by a thorn.
Maelis tilted the case toward the lamp.
The letters brightened.
Not reflected light. A low red glow, like coals buried beneath a floor.
Ignatz had reached the first landing. He leaned against the wall, breathing through his mouth.
“What does it say?”
Maelis bent closer.
The inscription did not name a smith. It did not name a bearer. It gave the object a place.
Gauntlet of Sorrowfell forged at Vharencrag Fortress.
Ignatz read it over their shoulder.
For a moment neither of them moved.

Then he whispered, “That place is gone.”
“Abandoned is not gone.”
“You know what I mean.”
Maelis did. A fortress could lose its garrison, its banners, its stores, its living. Stone could remain while
every purpose within it died. Such places were not empty. They were crowded with the intentions of the
dead.
The register’s page trembled.
A new sentence began.
At Vharencrag Fortress, the iron—
Maelis snapped the cover shut.
The sound cracked through the stairwell.
Every lamp went out.
Ignatz swore. The darkness closed over them so completely that Maelis could feel its edge against their
face. The case grew hot in their hand. Something inside the gauntlet struck the velvet once.
A metal finger flexing.
“Put it down,” Ignatz said.
Maelis heard him fumbling for the wall. “If I put it down, will you pick it up?”
“No.”
“Then we would lose it.”
“I would prefer losing it to keeping it.”
“That preference is the luxury of a man who did not carry it here.”
A breath passed between them.
Then, from somewhere below, came the scrape of a nail across stone.
Ignatz found Maelis’s sleeve. His fingers closed hard around the fabric.
“Something is coming.”
“Yes.”
“How can you tell?”
“It has stopped hiding.”
The case pulsed once. Heat soaked through the leather. Maelis opened it.
The gauntlet was no longer curled.
Its fingers had lengthened toward the stair. The black metal showed a faint, slick sheen, and the red within
the wristband had become a thin and steady line. The register lay beneath it, open despite the clasp. Ink
moved across the page in strokes too rapid to read.

Maelis lifted the gauntlet.
Pain entered their hand before the metal touched it.
Not heat. Memory.
A chamber of towering stone. Smoke without flame. A floor drowned in dark water. The shape of a
fortress seen from within its own foundations, its walls rising through a sky the color of old blood. Voices
reciting something in unison, each syllable falling a little later than the one before.
Then a hand.
Not Maelis’s.
A hand wearing the gauntlet.
It closed around a throat.
Maelis felt the cartilage give.
The vision broke.
They stood on the landing with the regalia suspended above the case. The metal had not yet touched their
skin. Ignatz was saying their name, but from a great distance.
“Maelis.”
The name reached them again.
“Maelis Harrowick the Pale.”
They lowered the gauntlet into the case.
The darkness recoiled. The lamps flared back to life, one by one, pale and weak. Ignatz’s face was turned
away from the regalia, though no canonical feature could have made his fear more legible than the rigid
set of his body.
The register wrote its final word.
—waited.
Maelis stared at it.
“Waited for what?” Ignatz asked.
The stairwell gave no answer.
The stone beneath their feet shifted.
It was not an earthquake. The movement had intention. A seam opened along the inner wall, thin at first,
then widening with a deep grinding sigh. Dust rolled from the joints. Beyond the split was not masonry
but a descending passage, its walls lined with old hooks and blackened chains.
The air that came through smelled of iron left in rain.
Ignatz took one step backward.
Maelis looked down at the case. “You will remain here.”
“I will not.”

“You will.”
“You have already decided to enter.”
“I have decided that one of us must witness what follows.”
“And you have decided it should be me?”
“No. I have decided you will carry the register.”
He looked at the book as if it were a living animal. “Why?”
“Because it has begun to record events before they happen. If it writes my death, I need to know whether
the sentence can be trusted.”
Ignatz’s mouth opened, then closed.
Maelis passed him the register. His hands shook when he accepted it, though he tried to hide the tremor by
gripping the leather spine with both palms.
“Do not read aloud,” Maelis said.
“What if it writes?”
“Let it.”
“And if it writes your name?”
“Do not say it.”
The passage beyond the wall waited without impatience.
Maelis stepped through.
The chains lining it were not rusted. They were black with something finer and more deliberate. Small
metal tags hung from them, but the surfaces had been scraped clean. No names. No dates. No ownership.
The erasure had been performed with care.
The floor sloped downward.
Behind Maelis, Ignatz said, “You plotted the death of your own liege.”
The words struck harder than the opening stone.
Maelis continued walking.
“You told me never to speak of it,” he said.
“I told you never to write of it.”
“That is not the same thing.”
“It is in a fortress.”
“And is this fortress listening?”
“Yes.”
Ignatz swallowed. “Then why bring it here?”
“Because it already knows.”

The case seemed heavier now. The Gauntlet of Sorrowfell dragged at Maelis’s arm as though the object
had gained weight with every step. The passage narrowed around them. Their shoulder brushed stone. A
skin of grit flaked away, revealing pale marks beneath.
Not writing.
Fingernail trails.
The register opened in Ignatz’s hands.
He gave a strangled cry.
Maelis turned. “What did it write?”
“I did not read it.”
“Then why are you afraid?”
“I saw the first word.”
“Which word?”
Ignatz’s eyes lifted from the page.
“Liege.”
The lamps behind them went out again.
This time the darkness came from below.
Something moved in the passage ahead, beyond the reach of the remaining light. It did not scrape stone or
breathe. It advanced with the noiseless certainty of a tide entering a room.
Maelis’s fingers tightened around the case.
The Gauntlet of Sorrowfell struck the inner lid.
Once.
Twice.
On the third blow, the clasp opened by itself.
The metal hand rose from the velvet.
In the dark beyond the lamps, a voice spoke with the weight of many throats speaking through one mouth.
“Write the next word.”

And from below, something answered in their own voice.

The lock yielded with a sound like a small bone breaking.

He eased the door inward.
