Aldous closed the door and turned the key.
He was a major Reliquary Keeper, though no oath had ever taught him how to keep a secret from himself.
The title had become a weight hung around his neck, a relic of authority polished smooth by generations
of frightened hands. He had been born in 315 AS. Since then, the world had taught him that every door
had two locks: one for entry, and one for denial.
He crossed to the central table.
The Silent Psalter rested there beneath a veil of black cloth.
Even covered, it possessed a silence of its own. The instrument had been forged in 204 AS, in an age when
people still believed expression could save them. Its attunement cost was 49. Aldous had never touched its
strings. He had seen what silence did to those who mistook restraint for mercy.
He lifted the cloth by one corner.
Muted metal and dark wood emerged beneath it, shaped like a devotional instrument fashioned for a

suggestion of mourning.
Aldous lowered the cloth.
Beyond the table, shelves climbed into darkness. On them lay fragments of the Ashen Era: seals without
houses, blades without hands, prayers written in languages whose speakers had become dust. The relics
did not sleep. They waited for the living to make mistakes.
He removed a narrow ledger from inside his coat.
The book contained no names. Names were doors too.
A strip of paper had been folded into its middle. The message was written in the cramped cipher used by

possessed that never grew dull.
He opened the ledger to a blank page.
Three marks. A change in watch. A sealed passage. A rumor concerning Gloamreach.
He had not yet written the last one.

Gloamreach lay on the Pale Coast, quarantined and guarded by a garrison of 2,483. Even the name seemed

He dipped his pen.
A knock came.
Not loud. Not hesitant.
Three measured taps, then silence.
Aldous did not move.
The lamps hissed. Wax slipped down one iron bracket and hardened like a pale tear.
Another knock.
“State your burden,” he said.
“An Outrider’s burden is never stated at the door.”
The voice was young enough to make the words seem borrowed.
Aldous looked toward the entrance. He could not see through the oak, but the air beneath it stirred.
Someone stood close on the other side.
“Then you have come without one.”
“I came with a message.”
“Messages are burdens with better manners.”
Silence.
Aldous closed the ledger and slid it beneath the black cloth covering The Silent Psalter. His hand remained

“Come in,” he said.
The door opened.
Thessaly Coldwater entered and stopped just inside the chamber. No face, garment, or weapon announced

“Close it.”
Thessaly did so.
“Bar it.”
The bar descended into its brackets.
The chamber tightened around them.

“Your name,” Aldous said.
“Thessaly Coldwater.”
“And your burden?”
“A message.”
“You have improved upon the door.”
“I was given poor instruction.”
“By whom?”
Thessaly did not answer.

He stepped away from the table. The lamps placed no clear shape upon him. The title Last Warden had

“Gloamreach has closed its western gate.”
“It is quarantined.”
“It has always been quarantined.”
“Not in that manner.”
“No.”
The word rested between them.

“What manner?”
“The gate was closed before the watch changed. The men inside would not answer the signal. No bell. No

“Who told you?”
“Those beyond the gate.”
“Names.”
“None were offered.”
“Then you brought me a rumor.”
“I brought you a silence.”
Aldous glanced toward The Silent Psalter.
The instrument seemed to have grown heavier beneath its cloth.

He returned to the table and lifted the ledger. The paper strip waited within. He could feel the Cartel’s

“Why bring this to me?” he asked.
“Because you keep sealed things.”
“I keep old things.”
“Some old things are sealed.”
“Some sealed things should remain so.”
“Then you will know whether this one should.”
He looked at Thessaly.
For the first time, the Outrider seemed to waver—not in fear, but in the manner of a messenger standing at

“How long have you carried this?”
“Since the last road.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the one I have.”
Aldous set the ledger down.
“Your birth record says Thessaly Coldwater was born in 338 AS.”
The Outrider’s silence altered.
It was a small thing. A tightening. The chamber did not change, but the person within it did.
“You read birth records now?”
“I read whatever is placed before me.”
“Then read the message.”
“I cannot read what is not written.”
“Perhaps you can hear it.”
Aldous felt a cold thread pass through him.
Behind the black cloth, The Silent Psalter waited with its grave, soundless discipline. It had been forged in

Aldous had read those pages until the ink seemed to bleed.

He had learned that the dead did not demand justice.
The living did.
“What did you hear?” he asked.
“Nothing from the gate.”
“That is not what I asked.”
“Something beneath it.”
The lamps fluttered.
“Beneath the gate?”
“Beneath the ground.”
“Stone carries noise.”
“This was not noise.”
“Then what was it?”
Thessaly took one step toward the table.
Aldous lifted a hand.
The Outrider stopped.
“Do not come closer.”
“I have not touched anything.”
“You have not been invited to.”
“The message concerns what is beneath the chamber.”
Aldous’s fingers rested against the edge of the ledger.
For an instant, he imagined the floor opening. Not breaking, not collapsing—opening, as though a mouth

settled properly.
He knew too much to be comforted by knowledge.
“Cindermere Hold,” he said.
Thessaly did not respond.
“It was founded in 246 AS among The High Spires. Its garrison once numbered 8878. Now it is

“Then you know what happens when a place is built to contain something larger than its walls.”
“The hold was abandoned.”

“That is what the record says.”
“The record is wrong?”
“The record is written by survivors.”
Thessaly’s voice lowered. “Gloamreach is not empty.”
“No.”
“Neither is the road beneath it.”
Aldous looked at the covered Psalter.
He had seen the instrument mute a room without producing a single note. He had seen men reach for
words and find only breath. He had thought then that silence was an absence.
He understood now that it could be a presence.
“What do you want from me?” he asked.
“I want you to open the lower seal.”
Aldous laughed once. The sound was dry and unpleasant.
“You have mistaken me for a servant.”
“You are a Reliquary Keeper.”
“I am not every lock’s jailer.”
“You are the last one.”
The title entered the chamber before the meaning did.
Aldous placed both hands upon the table. Beneath the cloth, The Silent Psalter gave no sign of movement.
Outside, wind pressed against the stone. Somewhere above them, a shutter struck once, twice, then fell

“What is beneath the lower seal?” he said.
Thessaly Coldwater looked toward the black veil.
“I was hoping you would tell me.”
Aldous’s hand went to the hidden ledger.
From within the wall came a sound like a fingernail drawn slowly across stone.
The Outrider turned.
Aldous did not.
He watched the cloth covering The Silent Psalter rise by the smallest fraction, as though something
beneath it had taken a breath—
The cloth rose again.
Thessaly Coldwater’s hand went to the weapon at their hip. The gesture was quick, almost thoughtless, but

“Do not draw,” Aldous said.
“I have not.”
“Yet.”
The cloth settled. Beneath it, The Silent Psalter gave a soft, inaudible shudder that Aldous felt in his teeth.
He had learned its silences one by one. There was the silence that followed a command. The silence that

This was none of those.
This was listening.
Aldous drew the cloth away.
The instrument lay within its shallow case, dark against the pale lining. It resembled a devotional thing

Aldous had wielded The Silent Psalter since 341 AS.
The knowledge did not comfort him. It had never comforted him. The attunement cost was 49, and he had

Thessaly watched the instrument.
“Is that what was making the sound?”
“No.”
The Outrider looked toward the wall. “Then what is?”
Aldous lifted The Silent Psalter from its case.
The chamber tightened around his hands.
He had carried relics that made men weep, relics that showed their keepers the faces of the dead, relics that

The moment his fingers closed around it, the scratch within the wall stopped.
Aldous felt the thing on the other side withdraw.
Not far. Not in fear.
In patience.
He turned his head toward the black veil. “You knew this was here.”
Thessaly’s expression remained hidden in the darkness beyond the lamps. “I knew something was sealed

“You brought me because you believed it was a reliquary.”

“I brought you because you are a Reliquary Keeper.”
“The distinction matters.”

“To the person who intends to open it.”

He had sold the information before entering the hold.
He had not known what the Cartel meant to do with it.
That ignorance had once served as a shield. Now it felt like a hand around his neck.
Thessaly stepped closer to the table. “You said the lower seal was intact.”
“It was.”
“And now?”
Aldous looked down.

He had never seen it move.
“Now,” he said, “it has heard us.”
A pressure passed through the chamber.
The black veil bulged outward.
Thessaly moved between Aldous and the hanging cloth, blade half-drawn at last. “Behind me.”

“Farther away.”

Their body went rigid beneath his hand.

“It is.”

“Because it has risen.”
The words seemed to please the darkness.

The Psalter wanted to be played.
It had no sound to give.
Still, his fingers found the dead strings.

The first touch produced nothing.
The second drew the chamber’s silence into a single point.
On the third, the black wall cracked.
A line opened from floor to ceiling. Beyond it was not a room but a depth without distance, a darkness

The pale motes gathered.
Something moved among them.
Not toward the opening.
Toward him.

Thessaly’s breath vanished.
Then, in the black beyond the seal, a hand lifted.
It had no flesh. No bone. Only the impression of fingers against the other side of the world.
The hand pressed toward the breach.
The stone began to open.
The seam widened by the width of a knife.
Aldous felt the pressure in his teeth.
The hand remained on the far side—not a hand, he reminded himself, though the thought had no more

The Silent Psalter lay against his palm.
Forged in 204 AS, it had been made for expression. The old records used that word with a reverence

Its attunement cost was 49.
He had paid less than that in blood. He had paid more in sleep.
The instrument’s mute body trembled.
Aldous closed his fingers around it and felt the familiar emptiness answer. No strings moved. No note

The hand pressed harder.
Stone groaned.
Thessaly swore, softly and without ornament. The sound seemed to offend the chamber. Pale motes flared

Aldous had read of such places in the ledgers of the Reliquary Keepers. He had read of doors that opened

But this was not in the ledgers.
That was why the Iron-Ring Cartel had paid him.
The thought arrived cleanly, shamefully calm.
He had sold them the route beneath the ruin. He had sold them the measurements of the lower vaults, the

He had told himself many things.
The stone opened another inch.
A blackness lay beyond it, smooth as water and depthless as a shut eye. No corridor showed through. No
chamber. Only that impression of a world pressed thin against the breach.
Thessaly came nearer. Aldous heard the faint scrape of boots.
“If it crosses,” they said, “what do we do?”
He kept his gaze on the opening. “You run.”
“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only one you’ll survive.”
“You said the seal could not be broken.”
“I said it had held.”
“Those are different things.”
“Yes.”
The word fell between them and stayed there.
Aldous remembered the maps of Cindermere Hold, founded in 246 AS among The High Spires. He had

fists. Now Cindermere Hold was abandoned. Its gates stood open to snow and the shriek of empty wind.
Its strength had become a silhouette.
That was the lesson of every ward.
Holding was not the same as saving.
Another finger appeared in the dark.
Thessaly drew steel. Aldous heard the blade clear its sheath.
“No,” he said.
“It may be the only weapon we have.”
“Steel has no quarrel with that thing.”
“Then give me a better quarrel.”
He nearly laughed. The sound would have been madness. His hand tightened around The Silent Psalter.
The instrument had resisted him before. It had punished hesitation with a silence so complete that he could
no longer tell whether his heart still beat. Yet now the silence inside it seemed to deepen, gathering itself
toward a purpose.
Aldous touched the sealed face with his thumb.
The room vanished.
For one instant he stood beneath a drowned sky.
Radiance burned there, but far below the surface of black water. Broken banners drifted through the light.
Shapes moved beneath them, countless and patient, carrying spears or prayers or both. He saw a field
without ground. He saw mouths open soundlessly around him.
The War of Drowned Light.
It began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS. The record named 64617 casualties. The Silent Choir was
recorded as the victor, though victory had been a word carved over a grave. The war had collapsed into a
decade of guerrilla reprisals, and its spark had been secretly staged by The Silent Choir.
Aldous saw the truth of it not as ink, but as hands.
Hands lighting the first flame.

Hands withdrawing before anyone saw.
Hands washing themselves in the blood of strangers.
He returned to the chamber with his thumb numb and the Psalter cold as a buried bell.
The breach had opened wide enough for the fingers to withdraw.
For an instant nothing moved.
Then something leaned close on the other side.
Thessaly’s breath returned in a ragged gasp. “Aldous.”
He raised the instrument.
The old device did not sing. It gave no warning. Instead, every pale mote in the chamber folded inward,
drawn toward the Psalter’s silent center. The carved faces on the walls seemed to turn toward him. Dust
lifted from the floor and hung motionless.
The blackness beyond the stone rippled.
Aldous felt the attunement cost gather in his bones.
Not blood. Not yet.
Memory.
A face he could no longer place. A room whose door he had locked. The sound of a child—no, not a child;
he would not allow the shape to settle—calling from somewhere behind him while he walked away.
He fought the sacrifice.
The Psalter demanded more.
“Use it,” Thessaly whispered.
“You don’t understand.”
“No.”
“Then be silent.”
The words struck harder than he intended. Thessaly said nothing. Their silence became another weight in
the chamber, and Aldous hated himself for welcoming it.
Beyond the breach, the thing moved.
Not through the opening.
Against it.
The stone bulged toward them. Dust sifted from the lintel. A line of darkness crawled across the floor and
touched Aldous’s boot.
He did not look down.
“Listen to me,” he said. “If I fail, you go to Gloamreach.”
“Gloamreach is quarantined.”

“It lies on the Pale Coast. Its garrison is 2,483.”
“An abandoned ruin is safer?”
“It is not abandoned.”
He had received that intelligence through the Cartel, though he had not told them why he needed it.
Gloamreach remained a core location despite the quarantine. Men and women still kept its walls. They had
been instructed to admit no one, to send no signal, to trust no flag.
That was why it might hold.
Or why it might be waiting.
Thessaly’s sword lowered a fraction. “You’ve been there?”
“No.”
“Then how do you know?”
Aldous looked at the breach. “I know what people hide when they are afraid.”
A tremor passed through the chamber. The stone opened another finger-width.
Aldous placed The Silent Psalter against his chest.
It was shaped like a devotional instrument, muted and solemn, fashioned for hands that had learned
restraint before they learned desire. He had carried it since 341 AS. He had carried it through ash storms,
through locked vaults, through the long corridors where every footstep seemed to belong to someone
walking behind him.
He had believed it made him a keeper.
Now he understood that it had only been waiting to decide what he was keeping out.
The thing beyond the breach touched the inner edge.
The chamber filled with a pressure like a scream held underwater.
Aldous’s knees weakened. He tasted iron. The Psalter drank the taste from his mouth, drawing it through
his teeth, through his tongue, into the mute hollows of its frame.
He saw the Pale Coast.
Gloamreach rose there beneath a sky the color of old bone, its walls pale with salt and sealed against the
sea. No banners flew. No fires showed. Yet behind the stone, something watched the water.
He saw Cindermere Hold beneath snow, its abandoned towers leaning into the High Spires. He saw the
empty barracks. He saw the number 8878 scratched into a wall by a hand that had forgotten why.
He saw the war’s drowned banners.
He saw the Silent Choir kneeling around a flame no larger than a candle.
And behind them, behind the light, the same hand.
Aldous almost released the Psalter.
Thessaly caught his sleeve. Their fingers closed hard enough to anchor him.

“Stay,” they said.
The breach gave a sound.
Not a crack.
A word.
It passed through the stone without disturbing it, entered Aldous through the bones of his face, and settled
in the oldest chamber of his mind.
He understood then why the Cartel had wanted the route. Not for treasure. Not for relics.
They knew.
Perhaps not what waited here. Perhaps only that something waited. But knowledge was a coin, and the
Iron-Ring Cartel had always preferred coins minted from other people’s ruin.
Aldous turned the Psalter in his hands.
The silent instrument opened.
No hinge moved. No seam appeared. Its dark body simply became deeper, a hollow capable of receiving
all the sound in the world.
The thing pressed forward.
Aldous looked once at Thessaly.
“Run when I tell you.”
“When?”
“When you hear music.”
“There is no music.”
“There will be.”
He set his thumb against the Psalter’s center.
The old memory rose again: the locked door, the retreating footsteps, the voice behind him. This time he
did not resist it. He opened himself to the recollection and let it bleed into the instrument.
The chamber answered.
Somewhere beneath the ruin, something struck a single unseen note.
The breach stopped widening.
The hand on the other side curled.
And from the black beyond the seal, a second hand lifted—smaller, familiar, and marked with the sign of
the Iron-Ring Cartel.

Chapter 10
The condemned knelt beneath the execution bell, and Gareth Ironmere listened to the rain strike its bronze
throat.
It had not rung since dawn. No hand had touched the rope. Yet the bell shuddered whenever the wind
came down from the high dark, giving off a dull, internal murmur, as if something trapped inside it had
begun to wake.
Gareth stood before the scaffold in the severe office that had made him feared. The hooded man knelt with
his wrists bound behind him. Water ran from the hem of his robe and gathered in the cracks between the
stones. Around them, the yard held its silence. Guards watched from beneath the eaves. Others had come
nearer despite themselves, drawn by the old appetite that made execution a public rite even when the
crowd claimed to despise it.
Gareth had never mistaken silence for mercy.
“Raise your face,” he said.
The condemned man obeyed.
He was neither young nor old. Rain had flattened his hair against his brow. His mouth was bloodless,
though Gareth could see the pulse moving in his throat. That small motion troubled him more than any
prayer might have done. A living throat admitted the body’s secret: that terror and devotion were kin, that
both asked the blood to answer.
The man looked at Gareth’s hands.
“Are you the one they sent?”
“I am.”
“The major Executioner.”
Gareth did not correct him. Titles were chains with polished links. Men reached for them when they
wanted to know how tightly they had been bound.
The bell trembled again.
A guard crossed himself with two fingers, then seemed to remember where he stood and lowered his hand.
Somewhere beyond the walls, a shutter slammed. The rain thickened, silvering the courtyard until the
stones seemed submerged beneath a shallow sea.
Gareth drew the execution blade.
Its edge was dark with oil. He had cleaned it himself. He had sharpened it until the whetstone sang. A
clean instrument spared the condemned the indignity of struggle, and spared the executioner the need to
pretend that struggle was justice.
The man’s gaze remained fixed on the blade.
“Did you kill the others?” he asked.
“Which others?”
“The ones who came before me.”

Gareth felt the question settle beneath his ribs. Not guilt. Guilt was a crude thing, too soft to survive
discipline. What moved in him was recognition.
“Names are not required for the work.”
“They are required for the dead.”
The guards shifted. Rain hissed on the brazier beneath the gallows, filling the air with the bitter smell of
wet ash.
Gareth stepped closer. The condemned man had been marked in the old way: a black line drawn from the
left ear to the hollow beneath the jaw. Not a sentence. A warning. The Silent Choir used such marks when
they wanted the condemned to be remembered as a vessel rather than a person. The Iron-Ring Cartel
preferred iron. House Morvain preferred ink. The Ashen Vanguard preferred nothing that could be
mistaken for ceremony.
The Bleeding Crown had never needed to explain itself.
Gareth crouched before the man.
“Who taught you the words?”
The condemned man’s eyes narrowed. “You know the words.”
It was not an answer. It was worse.
Beneath Gareth’s glove, the small cut along his palm opened again. He had made it before leaving his
chamber, shallow enough to hide, deep enough to wake the skin. The blood had dried in the lines of his
hand, leaving a dark geometry no priest would have accepted and no honest physician would have
recognized.
The rite waited inside him.
He had practiced it in secrecy, as secrecy was the only shelter left to any devotion that deserved to live.
Proscribed blood-rites were not forbidden because they were false. That was what the authorities said, and
Gareth had learned long ago that authority most feared the truths it could not own.
The condemned man smelled of rain, wool, and the faint mineral tang of fear.
“Say the name,” he whispered.
Gareth rose.
The execution bell gave another low shiver.
A man in a sealed coat stood beneath the archway. Gareth had not heard him enter. He carried no banner,
wore no visible insignia, and kept his face half-hidden beneath a hood. That absence of allegiance was
itself a declaration. In the Ashen Era, a person without a sigil was either powerless or dangerous.
The stranger raised one gloved hand.
“Not yet.”
The guards looked to Gareth.
That was the first betrayal. Not the interruption, but the hesitation. They had been instructed to obey him.
Now they waited to learn whether obedience belonged to the office or to whoever stood nearest the door.

Gareth lowered the blade until its point touched the wet stone.
“You entered a secured yard,” he said.
“I entered a yard where a man was about to die.”
“Those are not the same thing.”
“No.” The stranger’s voice was muffled, but not weakened. “They are rarely the same thing.”
The condemned man bowed his head. Gareth saw something pass between them—not affection, not trust.
Recognition again. A shared wound displayed without being opened.
He hated that more than defiance.
“Leave,” Gareth said.
The stranger did not move. “You have been summoned.”
“By whom?”
“You will be told when you arrive.”
Gareth looked past him into the passage. Darkness crowded there, though the hour was not yet night. The
rain had entered the fortress through every seam, and the stones sweated cold against the foundations.
“Then whoever summoned me can wait.”
“The matter concerns Greyfell Citadel.”
The name struck with no visible force, yet the yard seemed to tighten around it.
Greyfell Citadel: a ruin in the memory of armies, a place where banners had drowned beneath smoke and
the stones had learned to keep their counsel. Gareth had read the records in rooms where the ink had faded
to the color of old bruises. He knew the sentence preserved in the official histories:
The War of Drowned Light waged at Greyfell Citadel in 233 AS.
The words had been copied so often they no longer looked like language. Yet the war had not become
harmless through repetition. It remained beneath every silence, beneath every treaty and oath, beneath the
careful courtesies of the five powers that contended over the realm’s broken inheritance. The Silent Choir
had been named victor. The ledgers preserved the dead as a number. The living preserved them as
grievance.
And somewhere beneath Greyfell Citadel, if the old testimonies were true, light had once been made to
drown.
“Why does Greyfell Citadel concern me?” Gareth asked.
“Because what was sealed there has begun to answer.”
The condemned man laughed.
It was a small sound, almost tender.
Gareth turned toward him. “You know something of this.”
“I know that they sealed the wrong thing.”

“Who did?”
“Those who called themselves guardians.”
The stranger’s hand moved beneath his coat. Every guard reached for a weapon. Gareth felt the yard tilt
toward violence, and in that instant the forbidden geometry in his palm warmed.
He could have drawn blood before any blade cleared its sheath.
Not much. A single cut. A single drop given the right direction. Blood remembered the body that had
carried it. Blood could be persuaded to remember other things as well.
The rite pressed against his restraint like a tongue against a cracked tooth.
He let his hand fall.
The stranger withdrew a folded strip of blackened material. Not parchment. Not cloth. Something thinner,
flaked at the edges, bearing a mark burned so deeply into its surface that the shape had become a hole.
The condemned man saw it and began to shake.
Not from fear, Gareth thought.
From hunger.
“Take him below,” Gareth said.
The guards stared.
“Below?” one asked.
Gareth turned his head. The man’s face vanished into the shadow of his hood, but his body remembered
the blade before it moved. He lowered his spear.
“Before the execution,” Gareth continued, “the prisoner will be questioned.”
The condemned man lifted his face. “You said names were not required.”
“They are not,” Gareth said. “But answers are.”
The stranger stepped aside to make room.
Gareth approached the condemned man and seized the chain binding his wrists. The metal was cold
enough to numb his glove. As he pulled him from his knees, the prisoner stumbled, then leaned close
enough that his breath touched Gareth’s ear.
“The blood knows you,” he whispered.
Gareth stopped.
The rain ran down his face. Behind him, the bell stirred without wind.
“What did you say?”
“The blood knows you, Executioner.”
Gareth tightened his grip until the chain cut into the man’s skin. A bright bead appeared between the links.
There it was.

The smallest offering.
The mark in Gareth’s palm burned.
The condemned man looked down at the bead, and his terror became triumph.
From within the fortress came a sound like stone splitting under ice. The guards turned toward it. The
stranger raised the blackened fragment. Its burned hollow filled with a dim red glow.
Gareth felt the blood beneath his glove begin to move against the shape he had drawn.
Not outward.
Toward something waiting below.
The blood beneath his glove moved again.
A thread of warmth crept along the lines he had cut into his palm, seeking the hollows between bone.
Gareth felt each turn of it. It was not pain. Pain belonged to the body, and this belonged to the older
obedience beneath the body.
The condemned man laughed once.
The sound broke apart in his throat when the flagstones shifted.
A seam opened between them. Dust rose in a thin gray breath, carrying the stink of wet iron and
something sweetly rotten. The guards stumbled back. One drew his sword; another lifted his torch so
quickly that sparks fell across the condemned man’s bare feet.
“Hold,” Gareth said.
His voice did not rise. It did not need to.
The guards froze because he had spoken as Executioner, and the office had its own gravity. Men who
would have ignored a lord’s warning had obeyed him before now. They had obeyed the blade, the hood,
the black seal at his throat. They had obeyed the knowledge that he could make death official.
The stone opened another finger’s width.
Below waited a red darkness.
The stranger pressed the blackened fragment against his chest. His eyes had gone pale, not with fear but
with the absence of it.
“You drew the door,” he whispered.
Gareth looked at the mark in his palm. The shape he had made there was almost gone. Blood had filled the
cuts and dried into a dark, shining lattice.
“I drew nothing.”
“You drew it before you knew its name.”
The bell stirred again.
This time, its iron tongue struck.
The sound went through the fortress and into Gareth’s teeth. Torches guttered. Somewhere beneath the
floor, something answered with a slow impact, as if a buried fist had struck the underside of the world.

One of the guards began to pray.
Gareth turned his head.
The man stopped.
“Take him below.”
No one moved.
The condemned man’s smile widened. A wet line opened at the corner of his mouth.
“You cannot take me below,” he said. “I am what is below.”
Gareth seized him by the throat and drove him against the wall. The chain between them snapped taut. The
man’s head struck stone. His expression did not change.
Beneath Gareth’s glove, the blood pulled downward with sudden force.
His knees nearly gave.
He hid it by tightening his grip.
He had been born in 300 AS, under a sky the old records described as clean. He had never trusted that
word. Clean skies belonged to people who had not looked closely. Even as a child, he had known that
every pale thing concealed a stain. In the years since, he had learned the proper names for such stains:
vow, sacrifice, inheritance.
Blood-rite.
The forbidden syllables formed inside him without sound.
Proscribed.
The word had been stamped into decrees, muttered over confiscated books, carved into the margins of
sermons. Yet the flesh remembered what law wished forgotten. Flesh had no loyalty to councils or
crowns. It answered only to hunger and the hand that knew how to open it.
Gareth released the condemned man.
“Bring a lamp,” he said.
A guard stared at the red seam in the floor. “There’s no stair.”
“Then make one.”
The guard’s mouth worked.
The stranger began to chuckle. It had become a dry, intimate sound, as though he were laughing beside
Gareth’s ear.
“Major Executioner,” he murmured. “Always making stairs for the dead.”
The title struck more deeply than insult.
Gareth turned toward him. “You know too much.”
“I know what the blood has carried.”
The seam widened.

A portion of the floor sank with a grinding collapse. The nearest guard cried out and fell, catching himself
against the edge. His torch dropped into the opening. For a moment it fell through red vapor, its flame
turning green, then vanished.
The fortress seemed to inhale.
Cold air rose from below, though it smelled of furnace ash. Gareth felt it pass through the layers of his
clothing and settle beneath his ribs.
The stranger watched him.
“Cindermere Hold,” he said.
Gareth did not answer.
The name had been kept in the ledgers as though ink could preserve a corpse. Cindermere Hold, founded
in 246 AS among The High Spires. A fortress built where the mountains narrowed into black teeth, its
walls once carrying enough iron to make the horizon glint. Its garrison once numbered 8878.
Now Cindermere Hold was abandoned.
Not conquered. Not surrendered. Abandoned.
And it was not a core holding.
The distinctions mattered to men who still believed maps could restrain the world.
“Say it,” the stranger urged.
Gareth felt the wound in his palm twitch.
“What?”
“That the hold is empty.”
“It is.”
“Then who is breathing beneath us?”
The guard who had fallen crawled away from the opening. His face had lost its color. Gareth could see the
tremor in his hands, the helpless flexing of fingers that wanted a weapon and found only stone.
“Get the others,” Gareth said. “Seal the outer passage.”
“Seal it with what?” the guard asked.
“With your body, if you must.”
The man flinched.
Gareth understood then that the fortress had been waiting for obedience, not courage. The old stones did
not care whether a man believed. They cared whether he gave himself to the command.
He stepped over the broken edge and lowered himself into the red dark.
The air below thickened around him.
His boots found a stair that had not been there a breath before. Each step was narrow, its surface slick with
a substance warmer than water. The guards remained above. He heard them shifting, heard the condemned

man’s chain drag over stone as he followed.
“You were ordered to stay,” Gareth said.
“I was invited.”
Gareth descended.
The light from above dwindled. Red glimmers pulsed in the walls, each one opening and closing like an
eye beneath skin. He could not see their source. He could feel them watching the mark in his palm.
At the bottom, the stair ended at a chamber sunk beneath the hold.
A table stood in its center.
No—stone shaped like a table. A slab, black and polished, with grooves running toward a shallow basin.
The basin was full of blood.
Gareth stopped.
He had seen blood in every form the office permitted. Spilled in alleys. Congealed beneath gallows.
Washed from blades. Pooled under bodies after the War of Drowned Light, when the dead had been
counted as 64617 casualties and the living had been left to make meaning from the number.
But this blood was fresh.
It trembled without wind.
On the far wall, words had been carved through the stone.
THE WAR OF DROWNED LIGHT BEGAN IN 225 AS.
The next line ran beneath it.
THE WAR OF DROWNED LIGHT ENDED IN 235 AS.
The letters were deep enough to hold shadow.
Gareth approached. His chest tightened. The old conflict had been spoken of as a wound, a punishment, a
season of broken banners. The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor. That sentence had survived in
every account he had read.
But beneath the dates, in smaller cuts, another truth had been hidden.
THE SILENT CHOIR SECRETLY STAGED THE SPARK.
Gareth read it twice.
The condemned man came to stand beside him.
“Every war begins in a mouth,” he said.
“Whose?”
The stranger dipped one finger into the basin.
The blood rose to meet him.
“The mouth that knows it will be believed.”

Gareth caught his wrist.
The stranger’s skin was cold. Not cold as a corpse was cold. Cold as a depth where sunlight had never
been allowed to exist.
“Who brought you here?”
“You did.”
“I have never seen this chamber.”
“You saw it when you put the knife to my hand.”
Gareth looked down.
A thin red line had appeared across the stranger’s palm. He had not cut it. No blade had touched him. The
blood gathered in the same pattern that marked Gareth’s hand.
The two shapes answered one another.
Above them, the bell struck again.
The chamber shook. Dust fell from the ceiling. In the basin, the blood swelled over the rim and ran along
the grooves in the stone.
Gareth tore off his glove.
The mark in his palm had opened. Not like a wound. Like an eye.
He should have sealed it. He knew the words. He knew the gestures. He knew the price of allowing a rite
to proceed past its first threshold.
Instead, he placed his hand against the stone.
The chamber went silent.
For an instant he was standing somewhere else.
Pale cliffs beneath a colorless sky. A coast without birds. Walls washed in white salt and barred from
within. Gloamreach lay there, sealed against the world on the Pale Coast, its gates bearing the sign of
quarantine. He saw no people, no movement, only the bleak bulk of the place crouched above the surf.
Then numbers appeared in the air before him.
2,483.
A garrison.
A core location.
The vision showed him the walls of Gloamreach, every gate shut, every tower blind. The sea struck below
with the patience of a blade being honed.
Gareth tried to withdraw his hand.
The stone held him.
“Gloamreach,” he said.
The stranger bowed his head.

The vision changed.
Cindermere Hold rose from the High Spires, not abandoned now but crowded with shadows. The walls
were blackened. The towers leaned inward as if listening. Behind them, the mountains vanished into a
storm without rain.
Gareth saw the number 8878 burned into the stone.
Then the shadows opened their mouths.
He heard a chorus—not voices, precisely, but the memory of voices. A thousand whispers submerged
beneath water. The Silent Choir.
Their victory had not been a victory. It had been a door.
He saw the first spark carried from hand to hand. He saw the war beginning in 225 AS, ending in 235 AS,
and the dead gathered beneath drowned light. He saw the records rewritten by those who had kindled it.
He saw every clean line of history wet with hidden blood.
Gareth tore himself free.
The skin of his palm came away against the stone.
He staggered backward.
The basin overflowed.
Blood coursed across the floor and climbed the legs of the condemned man. He did not look down. His
face had become serene, almost tender.
“What did you open?” Gareth asked.
The man raised the blackened fragment.
Its hollow burned red.
“Not what.”
Something struck the chamber door.
Once.
Twice.
On the third blow, the stone bent inward.
Gareth reached for the knife at his belt. His hand shook—not with fear, but with the terrible recognition
that had been waiting beneath every rite, every execution, every private prayer spoken over a bowl of
stolen blood.
The door began to split.
From the darkness beyond came a voice wearing many voices.
“Gareth Ironmere.”
The condemned man smiled at him.
“Now,” he whispered, “give it your name.”

The stone gave way.
Not shattered. Opened.
A seam of red appeared where the door had been, thin as a wound in the world. Heat breathed through it,
carrying the stink of wet ash and old iron. Gareth’s fingers closed around the knife, though the blade had
never been meant for such work. It was an executioner’s knife: narrow, practical, obedient. It had ended
lives cleanly. It had never been asked to defend one.
The condemned man lowered the blackened fragment.
“Give it your name,” he said again.
Gareth tasted blood.
His own, perhaps. Or the blood he had poured into the bowl before the rite, the blood he had stolen drop
by drop from men who had believed the condemned existed only to die. The bowl stood behind him on the
altar, hidden beneath the execution cloth. He could feel it there: the dark surface quivering, answering the
thing beyond the split door.
The many-voiced presence spoke.
“Gareth Ironmere.”
His name moved through the chamber like a hand over strings. One voice shaped it with a mother’s
tenderness. Another dragged it through gravel. Another spoke in the dry cadence of a clerk reading a
sentence.
He had heard his name from judges, wardens, prisoners, priests. Never like this.
The crack widened.
A sliver of darkness showed beyond it, and within that darkness something pale turned slowly, as though
an enormous eye were searching for him.
Gareth stepped between it and the condemned man.
The man laughed softly. “Still pretending the office makes you clean?”
“I am not clean.”
“No.” The man’s face had lost its serenity. The red hollow in the fragment cast a feverish light across his
cheeks. “You are only disciplined.”
The word struck deeper than accusation.
Gareth had been born in 300 AS. He had learned early that discipline was the shape a secret took when it
wished to survive. He had carried it through every rite, every public sentence, every severed head bowed
over the block. He had kept his hands steady while something beneath the law fed upon the blood of the
condemned.
The office had been his mask.
The blood-rites had been his prayer.
The door opened another handspan.

Cold flowed through the gap. It swept over Gareth’s boots, climbed his legs, entered his bones. For a
moment he saw the chamber as it truly was: not stone, not altar, not iron rings fixed into the walls, but a
throat. The benches were teeth. The chains were veins. The bowl beneath the cloth was an eye turned
upward toward him.
His hand tightened around the knife.
“What are you?” he asked.
The answer came from the man, the door, the fragment, and somewhere inside Gareth’s own skull.
“The debt left when the light drowned.”
A sound passed through the stone—a distant roar, or thousands of people breathing at once.
The War of Drowned Light.
He saw Greyfell Citadel again, though he had not been there when the fighting came. He saw broken
banners pressed into mud the color of old bruises. He saw radiance sinking beneath black water. He saw
soldiers kneeling with their hands raised, not in surrender, but because something beneath the earth had
begun to call them by name.
The vision changed.
A wall of ash. A calendar scratched into it.
225 AS.
Another mark beside it.
235 AS.
Between them, the sky remained dark.
“Ten years,” whispered the voices.
Gareth’s throat tightened. The War of Drowned Light had begun in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS. It had
left 64617 casualties behind it, though the number had never seemed large enough to contain the dead. The
records had called The Silent Choir the victor. The records had called the ending a victory.
The voices laughed.
“The spark was ours.”
Images flashed across the chamber: a sealed message; a torch passed from one gloved hand to another; a
blade laid beside a sleeping child; a hymn sung beneath a floor while armies marched overhead.
“The War of Drowned Light was secretly staged by The Silent Choir.”
Gareth’s stomach turned.
The Silent Choir had not won the war. It had composed it.
The condemned man watched his face. “You knew.”
“I knew what was written.”
“You knew enough to fear the ink.”

The red hollow in the fragment widened, though the fragment itself did not move. A thread of light ran
from it to the bowl beneath the cloth. The fabric darkened as if soaked from below.
Gareth tore the cloth away.
The blood inside the bowl had become perfectly still.
In its surface, a fortress stood beneath a white sky.
Cindermere Hold.
Its blackened towers rose among The High Spires, narrow and severe against the pallor. No banners
moved over them. No smoke curled from the walls. The image trembled, and Gareth saw the words carved
across the bowl’s inner rim—not letters, but the memory of a record.
Cindermere Hold was founded in 246 AS among The High Spires.
A second inscription surfaced.
Its garrison once numbered 8878.
Then the fortress emptied. The towers lost their fires. Snow gathered in courtyards where men had drilled.
The gates hung open upon darkness.
Abandoned.
Not a core holding.
Gareth leaned over the bowl, unable to look away. The ruined hold seemed to withdraw from him,
becoming smaller, farther, until it was no more than a black tooth in a field of ash.
“Why show me this?”
“Because every fortress is a mouth,” said the voices. “Some are taught to swallow armies. Some are taught
to swallow names.”
The image in the blood shifted again.
A pale coast appeared beneath a sky without color. The sea lay flat and metallic, as though it had been
poured rather than formed. On the shore stood walls bleached by wind and salt.
Gloamreach.
The name entered him with the force of a remembered wound.
Gloamreach lies on the Pale Coast.
The bowl spoke now in the language of ledgers, but the words carried the weight of prophecy.
A core location.
A garrison of 2,483.
Quarantined.
Beyond the walls, figures moved behind shuttered windows. Some pressed their hands to the glass. Some
stood perfectly still. Along the battlements, watchfires burned with a faint green tint.

Gareth had never seen Gloamreach. Yet the sight of it summoned a pressure behind his eyes, a longing so
sharp he nearly dropped the knife.
The condemned man came to stand beside him.
“You have been looking toward it all your life,” he said.
“I have never heard of—”
“You have heard every name that mattered. You were trained to mistake obedience for ignorance.”
The door groaned.
A shape pressed against the opening from the other side. It had no face Gareth could discern, only a
suggestion of features arranged beneath the darkness. Its fingers slid through the gap, too long and jointed
wrong. They touched the floor. The stone blackened beneath them.
Gareth raised the knife.
The thing beyond the door spoke in his own voice.
“Major Executioner.”
He froze.
The title was not praise. It was an accounting.
He saw the block. The cloth. The bowl. The bodies that had fed his hidden devotion. He saw every time he
had whispered the proscribed words over blood, every time he had promised himself the rite was a means
rather than an altar.
The condemned man turned the fragment in his hand.
“Say it.”
“Say what?”
“Your name.”
The fingers on the floor curled.
Gareth felt the knife growing heavy. The chamber had become unbearably quiet. Even the cold had
stopped moving. His heartbeat sounded far away, as if it belonged to a man behind another door.
He thought of the laws he had enforced. He thought of the faces beneath the hoods. He thought of how
easily a life could be reduced to a name, a charge, a final breath.
He thought of what happened when a name was offered willingly.
“No,” he said.
The many voices fell silent.
The condemned man’s smile vanished. “You cannot refuse what you have already given.”
“I gave blood.”
“You gave attention.”
“I gave no name.”

The bowl trembled.
In its surface, Gloamreach vanished. Cindermere Hold vanished. The drowned sky closed over the war,
sealing 225 AS and 235 AS beneath black water. Then the blood reflected Gareth’s face—not as it was,
but as it might become. His mouth opened. His eyes were dark hollows. A red light burned within his
chest.
Something whispered from beneath the floor.
Not Gareth.
Not Ironmere.
A third name, half-formed and wet with birth.
He drove the executioner’s knife into the bowl.
The vessel split.
Blood struck the stone. It hissed. The seam in the door snapped shut with a sound like a jaw breaking, and
the thing beyond it shrieked—not in anger, but surprise.
The condemned man staggered back.
Gareth seized him by the throat.
“What did you open?”
The man clawed at Gareth’s wrist. “A way out.”
“For whom?”
His eyes rolled toward the floor.
The blood had not spread. It had gathered in a single dark line beneath Gareth’s boots, running against the
slope of the stone, flowing toward the sealed door.
“For the ones who remember you.”
The line reached the threshold.
A knock sounded from the other side.
Once.
Twice.
On the third, the chamber filled with voices.
The names of the dead rose through the stone, thousands upon thousands, and beneath them all came one
patient voice, soft as a hand laid over Gareth’s mouth.
“Gareth Ironmere.”
The knife slipped from his fingers.
The condemned man began to weep.
Beyond the door, something drew breath.
And this time, Gareth heard the breath answer from inside his own chest.

Chapter 11
The rain came ash-grey against the shutters, and the sea answered beneath the fortress with a voice like
stone being dragged across stone.
Morwenna Ashgrove stood over the map table while the lamps guttered in their iron cages. She wore the
silence of a Fleet Admiral as another woman might wear armor: not because it kept the world out, but
because it warned the world what would happen if it tried to enter.
The map had been drawn on cured hide, its coasts warped by damp and old fire. The Pale Coast was a pale
scar along the western edge. Farther inland, inked in a cramped black hand, stood Gloamreach.
“Read it again,” Morwenna said.
Caedmon Fellgard lowered his eyes to the document.
He had the disciplined posture of a scribe, shoulders held as if a careless breath might disturb the order of
the written world. His fingers were stained with ink. The rain had darkened the hem of his robe, though he
had crossed only a short stretch of stone corridor to reach the room.
“Gloamreach lies on the Pale Coast,” he said. “It is a core location. Its garrison is 2,483. Its status is
quarantined.”
“Not what the coast-watch claims.”
“The coast-watch claims the quarantine is ceremonial.”
“Ceremonies do not bar ships from harbor.”
Caedmon glanced at the map. “The chains are raised.”
“Then someone is raising them.”
The scribe’s gaze flickered toward the door.
Morwenna heard it too: the small shift of a guard outside, the soft complaint of leather, the careful stillness
that followed. The room had no echo, but it carried every hesitation.
She took the document from Caedmon. The parchment smelled of salt and lampblack. Beneath the report,
the seal had been broken and pressed closed again. Not expertly. Whoever had opened it believed that
authority made concealment unnecessary.
Or believed no one would dare notice.
“Your birth record,” Morwenna said.
Caedmon looked up.
“Your birth record. State it.”
“Caedmon Fellgard, born in 346 AS.”
The words settled between them.
Morwenna looked at him more closely. There was no defiance in his face, only the frightened patience of
a man who understood that records could become weapons in the hands of those who never held a pen.
“Who taught you to keep your ledgers?”

“I was assigned to the work.”
“That was not my question.”
“No, Fleet Admiral.”
The lamps sighed. Outside, thunder moved across the water, vast and slow.
On the map, Gloamreach seemed less a fortress than a wound stitched shut. The quarantine made it an
island without water around it. No signal fires from the Pale Coast. No merchant manifests. No patrol
complaints. No dead brought in from the surf.
Nothing crossed its gates.
Nothing, except information.
Morwenna slid the report beneath her palm.
The Iron-Ring Cartel paid for information that could not be obtained by force. They preferred the quiet
kind: berth schedules, ration tallies, the names of captains who drank too much, the weaknesses in a wall
that had not yet fallen. Morwenna had sold them such things in sealed packets, each one small enough to
vanish beneath a cup or a sleeve.
The Cartel did not know all that she knew.
That was why she remained alive.
“Do you understand why Gloamreach matters?” she asked.
Caedmon’s mouth tightened. “Because it is quarantined.”
“Try again.”
“Because a core location cannot be allowed to become inaccessible.”
“Better.”
“And because its garrison is 2,483.”
She turned her head.
Caedmon swallowed. “Numbers are the language of a garrison.”
“Numbers are the language of whoever intends to break one.”
The door opened without a knock.
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned entered beneath the guard’s lowered spear. The High Inquisitor
did not acknowledge the weapon. They wore severity as naturally as Morwenna wore command, their
presence drawing the air taut. Whatever the Twice-Crowned meant to crown them, it had left no softness
behind.
Caedmon bowed.
Sabelle’s eyes passed over him, the report, and finally Morwenna.
“You summoned me.”
“I summoned the keeper of the record.”

“Then you summoned Caedmon Fellgard.”
“I summoned both of you.”
Sabelle removed their gloves finger by finger. “How efficient.”
Morwenna disliked the sound of that voice. It had the smoothness of a blade drawn from oil.
“Gloamreach is receiving no authorized ships,” she said.
“Then the quarantine is functioning.”
“An abandoned fishing skiff entered the harbor.”
“Fishing skiffs are not authorized ships.”
“It carried a body.”
Sabelle’s expression did not change. “The sea carries bodies.”
“Not this one.”
For the first time, the High Inquisitor looked at the parchment.
Morwenna watched the movement and thought of the cellar beneath Sabelle’s residence, where a bound
revenant waited in chains. No one spoke of it. Such a thing could not be spoken of without becoming real
in a way that frightened even the powerful. Yet the secret remained: Sabelle Mournvale the
Twice-Crowned kept a bound revenant in their cellar.
Perhaps the dead told better truths than the living.
Perhaps that was why Sabelle kept one.
“Describe it,” Sabelle said.
“Not here.”
A hint of amusement touched their mouth. “You have brought me into a sealed room to discuss an unclean
corpse, and now you object to the room?”
“I object to witnesses.”
“Caedmon is a scribe.”
“Which means he remembers what is written.”
Caedmon lowered his head, but Morwenna saw his hand tighten around the edge of his tablet.
Sabelle’s gaze returned to him. “Do you remember what is written, Caedmon Fellgard?”
“I remember what I am instructed to preserve.”
“Born in 346 AS,” Morwenna said.
The scribe flinched almost imperceptibly.
Sabelle smiled without warmth. “A young record-keeper.”
“Old enough to understand when a record is being altered,” Caedmon replied.
Silence fell hard.

Morwenna felt the danger shift. Not toward Caedmon. Toward the document.
She lifted it and held it near the lamp. The writing had been scraped in one place, the fibers raised like
white hairs. Beneath the correction, a different number showed through.
“Read the erased line,” she said.
Caedmon came closer. “The original count was—”
He stopped.
“Say it.”
His eyes moved across the page. “The original count was 2,483.”
“That is the current garrison.”
“Yes.”
“Then what was added?”
Caedmon breathed through his nose. “Nothing. The number was replaced, not amended.”
Sabelle’s attention sharpened. “By whom?”
“No signature remains.”
“Signatures can be removed,” Morwenna said. “Intent is harder to scrape away.”
She set the parchment down.
A memory rose unbidden: broken banners sodden in black water, drowned radiance under a sky without
stars. The War of Drowned Light had begun in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS, with 64617 casualties. It had
collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals. The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor, though the war’s
spark had secretly been staged by them.
No triumph had survived that war. Only the habit of vengeance.
The old report was still read in academies and council chambers, where men argued over formations and
supply lines. Morwenna remembered the margins better than the victories. Every correction had concealed
a corpse. Every official number had been a door locked against the dead.
“The record says the war ended,” Caedmon said quietly.
“The record says many things.”
“The Silent Choir is recorded as the victor.”
Sabelle’s gaze remained upon Morwenna. “And the spark was secretly staged by them.”
The lamps burned low. The words seemed to drink the light.
Morwenna placed both hands upon the table. “You say that as though the distinction matters.”
“It matters to those who still believe victory absolves the hand that struck the match.”
“Belief is not jurisdiction.”
“No,” Sabelle said. “Jurisdiction is what remains after belief has been stripped away.”

Beyond the shutters, something struck the fortress wall. A gull, perhaps. Or a hand.
Morwenna did not look.
The five powers had learned to sit at the same table without calling it peace. The Ashen Vanguard wanted
roads and oaths. House Morvain wanted inheritance recognized where armies had failed. The Silent Choir
wanted silence to mean obedience. The Iron-Ring Cartel wanted every hunger made profitable. The
Bleeding Crown wanted the realm to remember that crowns could bleed and still command.
Morwenna served none of them cleanly.
She had been born in 288 AS, and the sea had taught her that loyalties were vessels: useful only while they
held. Secretly, she sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel. The admission lived beneath her ribs with the
steady pressure of a second heart.
Sabelle touched the corner of the report.
“Cindermere Hold,” they said.
Morwenna looked down.
The name stood among the mountain marks: a blackened fortress among the peaks.
“Why bring it into this?”
“Because the body was wearing a clasp stamped with its seal.”
Caedmon bent over the map. “Cindermere Hold was founded in 246 AS among The High Spires.”
“Was,” Sabelle said.
“Though its garrison once numbered 8878,” Morwenna continued, “the hold is now abandoned and is not
a core holding.”
Caedmon traced the mountain road with one ink-stained finger. “The route from Cindermere Hold to the
coast is impassable.”
“According to the record,” Morwenna said.
“According to the cliffs,” Caedmon answered.
Morwenna studied him.
He had not meant to be insolent. That was what made it dangerous. Men who feared their own words
learned to speak truth as though it were an accident.
Sabelle drew one glove back over their hand. “Then someone crossed the cliffs.”
“Or the clasp was planted,” Morwenna said.
“By whom?”
The question waited, polished and patient.
Morwenna’s mind moved through possibilities. The Cartel would plant a seal if it bought them access. The
Silent Choir would plant one if it wished to make an old war speak again. House Morvain would plant one
if the corpse served a claim. The Ashen Vanguard would deny planting anything. The Bleeding Crown
would call the evidence treasonous and demand it be burned.

She could tell Sabelle none of this.
Not yet.
Caedmon lifted the report’s lower edge. “There is another mark.”
Morwenna leaned in.
A smear of reddish wax clung to the parchment. Not a seal. Not quite. A thumbprint pressed through it,
thin and ridged.
Caedmon whispered, “Someone touched this while the wax was warm.”
Sabelle’s face went still.
In the corridor, the guard outside made a sound of surprise.
Then came a second sound: the dragging scrape of something heavy against the stone.
Morwenna reached for the sword at her side, though her hand had not yet closed around the hilt when the
door began to open again—and from the darkness beyond it came the wet, patient breathing of a thing that
had no living lungs.
The door opened by the width of a hand.
A pale limb slid through the gap and rested against the stone. The fingers were too long, the nails split and
dark beneath them. Moisture shone along the knuckles. It dripped soundlessly onto the threshold.
The guard outside tried to speak.
Only a wet click came from his throat.
Morwenna drew her sword.
Steel whispered free. The sound seemed pitifully small against that breathing, which continued with the
patient rhythm of bellows submerged in a cistern.
“Caedmon,” she said.
The scribe had already backed into the table. His shoulder struck the inkpot. Blackness spilled over the
report, spreading toward the reddish wax mark like a second, hungrier stain.
“Do not move,” Morwenna told him.
“I was not intending to.”
“Then remain excellent at it.”
Sabelle stood between the door and the table. They had not drawn a weapon. Their hands hung loose at
their sides, the fingers slightly curled, as if awaiting an object placed into them.
Morwenna watched their face.
Nothing.
Not fear. Not surprise. Only that severe stillness which had made petitioners lower their eyes before the
High Inquisitor had spoken a word. The two crowns upon Sabelle’s authority were not visible in the
dimness, but Morwenna felt them all the same: invisible weights laid upon the room, pressing every breath
flatter.

The door opened another inch.
The thing beyond it bent.
Its head came through sideways first, scraping the lintel. What remained of its face had been wrapped in
strips of dark cloth, soaked until the weave clung to the shape beneath. One eye showed through. It was
clouded, silver-white, and fixed upon the report.
Not upon them.
Upon the report.
Caedmon saw it too. His lips parted.
Morwenna moved before thought could make the decision cowardly.
She crossed the room in three strides and seized the parchment from the table. Ink ran over her glove. The
page was warm. Not with life. With the residual heat of the wax, perhaps, or the heat of a hand that had
pressed the mark.
The thing inhaled.
The sound came through its covered mouth like water dragged up through reeds.
“Give it back,” Sabelle said.
Morwenna turned her blade toward them. “You know what it is?”
“I know what it wants.”
“That is not what I asked.”
“No.” Sabelle’s gaze settled on the report in Morwenna’s hand. “It is not.”
Behind the door, the guard made a muffled choking sound. The creature’s shoulder entered the room. Its
clothing was the color of old ash, stiff with salt or some paler crust. A metal clasp hung at its throat, pitted
and dull.
Morwenna did not look at the guard.
“Caedmon,” she said, “is there anything on that page about Gloamreach?”
His eyes flicked to the parchment, then to the creature. “The quarantine records. Garrison returns. Supply
losses. Nothing—”
“Read it.”
“Now?”
“Especially now.”
He bent over the table. His hands trembled once, then steadied. Reserved, meticulous, he began to read
from memory where the ink had blurred.
“Gloamreach. Pale Coast. Core location. Quarantined status maintained.” His voice thinned.
“Garrison—two thousand four hundred and eighty-three.”
The creature stopped.

The breathing ceased.
For a moment the whole room held its silence with it.
Morwenna felt the page tighten in her hand.
Not physically. The parchment remained limp, stained, and half-curled. But some pressure gathered
around it, the sense of attention narrowing to a point. She had known admirals who could quiet a deck
with a glance. She had known storms that seemed to choose a single mast to break. This was neither. This
was appetite given patience.
Sabelle’s eyes had moved to Caedmon.
“Continue,” they said.
Caedmon swallowed. “The last—”
“Continue.”
“The last notation is incomplete. The entry ends beneath the quarantine seal.”
The thing turned its head toward Sabelle.
Morwenna saw then that the cloth around its face was not tied. It had grown there. Threads disappeared
beneath the skin, vanishing into a black seam at the jaw.
She should have been afraid.
Instead, a colder instinct rose through her: calculation.
A creature that came for a report had been sent, or summoned, or compelled. A creature that recognized a
number might be following an order. An order meant an author. An author meant leverage.
Leverage was the only mercy power ever offered.
She stepped backward, bringing the parchment closer to the lamp. The reddish smear stood out beneath
the ink. Not a seal. A thumbprint. The ridges caught the light.
Someone had touched this while the wax was warm.
Someone who had expected the mark to be found.
“High Inquisitor,” she said, “did you bring this thing here?”
Sabelle’s expression did not change, but the skin beside one eye tightened.
“I did not bring it.”
“Then you know who did.”
“Do not mistake silence for knowledge.”
“I have never mistaken the two.”
The creature entered farther. Its arm dragged along the doorframe. Bits of stone broke away and struck the
floor. It had a human shape, more or less, but the proportions had been stretched by some merciless hand.
Its left foot angled inward. Its right knee refused to bend until the last instant, then folded with a crack.
Caedmon pushed himself away from the table.

Morwenna held out her free hand. “Stay there.”
He obeyed.
Sabelle watched the creature come into the room. There was something in their gaze that Morwenna had
seen before—not compassion, not disgust. Recognition burdened by ownership.
The thought arrived unwanted and whole.
A bound revenant.
She had heard the phrase in sealed rooms, spoken by people who believed secrecy was a moral defense.
They had never agreed on whether such things were weapons, prisoners, or witnesses. Sabelle Mournvale
the Twice-Crowned had fought in The Leaden Accord, fighting for The Ashen Vanguard. That history had
made them difficult to surprise and harder to intimidate. But history did not explain the wet breathing at
the door.
A cellar might.
Morwenna’s grip tightened on the sword.
“You keep one,” she said.
Caedmon looked at her.
Sabelle did not.
The creature raised its hand.
“Do not,” Sabelle said.
It halted.
The obedience was immediate. Not the obedience of fear. Not even the obedience of training. It stopped
because the command had entered it and remained there.
Morwenna’s pulse gave one hard beat.
Sabelle moved toward the door. Their boots passed within reach of the thing’s fingers. The creature’s hand
twitched, hungry or confused.
“Back,” Sabelle said.
It withdrew.
The guard outside collapsed against the wall. Morwenna heard the dull impact, then a small groan.
She should have sent for help. She should have shouted for the corridor to be sealed, for the chamber to be
cleared, for every blade within hearing to come running.
But Caedmon had read the garrison number, and the creature had stopped.
And the report still lay in her hand.
A report concerning Gloamreach. A quarantined core location on the Pale Coast, held by a garrison of
2,483. Intelligence worth selling, if the right detail had been omitted from the proper copy. Intelligence
worth killing for, if the quarantine concealed more than sickness.
The Iron-Ring Cartel would pay for certainty.

Morwenna felt the secret move inside her like a knife beneath cloth.
Sabelle saw it. Perhaps not the secret itself, but the hesitation around it.
“You are thinking of keeping the page,” they said.
“I am thinking of why it was sent.”
“Those are not separate thoughts.”
“No?”
“No. Not when the person thinking them is a Fleet Admiral.”
The title struck with more force than accusation. It carried the weight of fleets that did not exist in the
room, of orders written in her hand and obeyed by distant mouths. Morwenna kept her face still.
Behind Sabelle, the creature’s wet breathing began again.
“Your servant is becoming impatient,” Morwenna said.
“They are not my servant.”
“Then what are they?”
Sabelle glanced toward the thing.
For the first time, something resembling weariness crossed their face.
“A consequence.”
The word hung between them.
Caedmon’s gaze fell to the ink spreading over the table. He had not touched the report again. His fingers
were blackened at the tips.
Morwenna studied the creature’s exposed eye. The clouded sphere reflected the lamp without seeing it. A
strand of cloth shifted over its mouth.
“Consequences can be redirected,” she said.
“Not this one.”
“Everything can be redirected.”
“That is the faith of the powerful.”
“It is the practice of the living.”
Sabelle looked at her then, fully. Their eyes were dark beneath the hard planes of their face, and the
severity in them was no longer inquisitorial. It was older. More private.
“You should have stayed at the table,” they said.
Morwenna understood too late.
The creature moved.
It did not lunge at her. It crossed the room in a broken blur, one shoulder leading, the floor cracking
beneath its weight. Morwenna raised her sword, but the blade met only a sleeve. The impact drove her

backward into the wall. Stone struck her spine. The report flew from her hand.
Caedmon cried out.
The parchment spun once through the lamplight.
The creature caught it.
Its fingers closed around the page without tearing it. The wet breathing stopped again. It bowed its head,
pressing the covered ruin of its face to the ink.
Morwenna saw the red wax smear vanish beneath its palm.
Sabelle whispered a word.
Not a command this time.
A name, perhaps—but no name Morwenna knew, and no name she could safely invent for the thing now
crouched over the stolen report. The sound was low, shaped by grief or disgust.
The revenant shuddered.
Caedmon stumbled toward the far wall. “What is it doing?”
Morwenna pushed away from the stone. Pain flashed along her ribs. She ignored it and lifted her sword.
The creature unfolded.
The page clung to its hand.
Sabelle’s face had gone pale.
“Morwenna,” they said.
No title. No courtesy.
The creature turned toward her.
The clouded eye brightened from within, not with light but with the color of something burning beneath
deep water.
Sabelle took one step forward. “Put down the report.”
The revenant did not obey.
Morwenna raised her sword higher, and from somewhere beneath the cloth around its mouth came the first
word it had spoken.
“Morwenna Ashgrove.”
The name came wetly through the cloth, as if spoken by a throat lined with river mud.
Caedmon made a small sound behind her. His quill struck the floor. Morwenna heard it roll once, twice,
and stop against the wall.
Sabelle did not move.
The revenant held the report between two blackened fingers. The page trembled, though nothing else in
the chamber stirred. Its wrappings were dark with cellar damp, and beneath them something shifted with
the slow patience of rot.

Morwenna kept her sword raised.
“Who taught it my name?” she asked.
“Names are not taught,” Sabelle said. “They are retained.”
The answer had the coldness of a door barred from within.
Morwenna watched the revenant’s clouded eye. “It has seen me before.”
“No.”
“You expect me to believe that?”
“I expect you to believe what is useful.”
Sabelle’s gaze remained fixed on the creature. They stood with the authority of their office still upon
them: Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned, High Inquisitor, born in 263 AS, the crown-marks at their
brow hidden beneath shadow and the ruinous light that leaked through the shutters. Their hands were
empty. That frightened Morwenna more than a drawn blade would have.
The chamber smelled of wet stone, old ash, and the sharp medicinal stink rising from the revenant’s
wrappings. Somewhere beneath the floor, water tapped against the foundation. The sound had a rhythm. A
patient knock from the dark.
Morwenna knew this place now.
Sabelle kept a bound revenant in their cellar.
The knowledge had been forced into the open by the creature’s arrival, but it had not become less
dangerous for being seen. Secrets did not die when uncovered. They changed owners.
“Give me the report,” Sabelle said.
The revenant turned its head toward them.
The paper sagged in its grasp. Ink bled across the page, black veins spreading through the writing.
Caedmon crouched beside the fallen quill. “It is destroying the record.”
“You are a Scribe,” Sabelle said without looking at him. “You should have secured it.”
Caedmon’s fingers closed around the quill. “I did secure it.”
“Then your security is inadequate.”
Morwenna felt the room narrowing around them. The walls had always seemed close in Cindermere Hold,
but now the black stone leaned inward like a tribunal. The abandoned hold had been founded in 246 AS
among The High Spires, raised for a garrison that once numbered 8878. Its strength had gone the way of
all old strength. No soldiers remained in its halls. It was abandoned now, and not a core holding of any
power that still mattered.
Yet the dead had found a use for it.
The revenant lifted the report to its face.
Morwenna’s hand tightened on her sword.
“Stop it.”

The creature’s mouth opened beneath the cloth. Not wide. Not enough for a human jaw. The wrappings
pulled apart, revealing darkness packed with glistening teeth.
The page vanished between them.
Caedmon lurched upright. “No—”
The revenant swallowed.
Paper rasped down its throat.
Then it spoke again.
“Gloamreach.”
Sabelle’s expression altered by less than a breath.
Morwenna saw it. She saw the calculation, the swift burial of alarm beneath inquisitorial calm.
Gloamreach lay on the Pale Coast, a quarantined core location with a garrison of 2,483. A place sealed
against the coast around it, guarded as much from within as from without.
A place about which the Iron-Ring Cartel had wanted information.
Her mouth went dry.
The Cartel paid in secrets, not coin. They preferred intelligence because coin could be seized, counted, or
traced. Intelligence merely entered the world and made men believe their choices were their own.
Morwenna had sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel in silence, with discipline, and without forgiving
herself for the ease of it.
The revenant faced her.
“Gloamreach,” it repeated. “Quarantined.”
Caedmon looked between them. “What does it mean?”
“It is reading the report,” Morwenna said.
“It ate the report.”
“Then it has a better memory than you.”
His face tightened, but he said nothing.
Sabelle extended one hand. “Come here.”
The revenant did not obey.
A thin line of dark fluid ran from beneath its wrappings and fell onto the floor. Where it struck the stone,
frost flowered in a black ring.
Sabelle’s voice sharpened. “I bound you.”
The creature’s eye brightened.
Morwenna felt the pressure in the air before the revenant moved. Her skin prickled beneath her uniform.
The sword in her hand seemed suddenly ceremonial, a strip of worked metal held against a force that had
once possessed a body and now possessed only purpose.

“You bound it,” she said.
Sabelle did not glance at her. “That is what I said.”
“In your cellar.”
“Yes.”
The word fell between them.
Caedmon stared at Sabelle with the pale horror of a man discovering that the record he kept was smaller
than the truth. His quill shook in his hand.
The revenant stepped forward.
Its foot made no sound.
Sabelle’s fingers closed into a fist. Beneath the floor, something answered: a chain drawn taut, links
groaning in the dark. The revenant halted, its body jerking backward as invisible force took hold of it.
For the first time, Sabelle looked tired.
Morwenna saw the cost of the binding in the hollows beneath their eyes, in the rigid set of their shoulders.
The Twice-Crowned High Inquisitor had not mastered death. They had made an agreement with it and
mistaken the terms.
“What does it want?” Morwenna asked.
“It wants what all bound things want.”
“Freedom?”
“No.” Sabelle’s eyes went to the ruined mouth. “Recognition.”
The revenant twisted against the unseen chain.
The chamber filled with a low, grinding moan. Dust sifted from the ceiling. Caedmon dropped the quill
again.
Morwenna took one step sideways, keeping both Sabelle and the creature in view. The report had
contained intelligence concerning Gloamreach. That alone was dangerous. But if the revenant had spoken
the name because it had read the page, then it could also speak what the page had not yet revealed.
The names of routes.
The disposition of ships.
The messages she had passed to the Iron-Ring Cartel.
Her secret had not been written in the report. She had been careful. She was always careful.
The revenant turned its clouded eye toward her, as if it had heard the thought.
“War,” it said.
Sabelle’s face went still.
Morwenna lowered the point of her sword by a fraction. “Which war?”
The answer came in pieces, dragged from somewhere beneath the creature’s tongue.

“The War of Drowned Light.”
The words seemed to darken the room.
Morwenna had learned the war as every officer learned it: in figures, losses, and maps where whole
districts had been rubbed away. It began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS. 64617 casualties. The Silent
Choir was recorded as the victor.
But the old records lied by omission.
The spark had been secretly staged by The Silent Choir.
She had known that much only because a cipher had crossed her desk and a price had been offered for its
contents. She had sold the intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel before any official archive could close
around it. The Cartel had not told her why it wanted the truth. It had merely paid.
Now the revenant whispered it through ruined teeth.
“Spark... Choir.”
Sabelle’s fist trembled.
Caedmon looked at Morwenna. “What is it saying?”
Morwenna did not answer.
The War of Drowned Light had not ended when the banners fell. It had collapsed into a decade of guerrilla
reprisals, each killing justified by an earlier killing, each corpse made into evidence for the next. The
Silent Choir had won, according to the record. Victory had been the name given to whoever remained
standing when the water stopped burning.
The revenant’s head snapped toward the door.
A sound came from beyond it.
Not footsteps.
A soft dragging, many times repeated, as if something outside were pulling a length of wet cloth along the
corridor.
Sabelle released the binding.
The revenant surged forward.
Morwenna struck.
Her blade met its shoulder. The impact traveled up her arm with the shock of hitting submerged timber.
The wrappings split. Beneath them lay no flesh she could recognize, only layers of grey matter veined
with dim red light.
The revenant seized her wrist.
Its grip was cold enough to burn.
Morwenna drove her knee into its side. It did not yield. The clouded eye pressed close to her face, and
within it she saw a shoreline beneath a drowned sky, banners drifting in dark water, mouths opening
soundlessly below the surface.

Then she saw Gloamreach.
Pale stone. Sealed gates. A garrison of 2,483 standing beneath a sky without birds.
And beyond the quarantine wall, something waiting.
The revenant spoke against her cheek.
“Open.”
Morwenna tore her wrist free. Skin came away beneath its fingers. She stumbled backward, blood bright
against the dimness.
Sabelle raised both hands.
The floor split.
Black chains burst from the cracks and wrapped around the revenant’s limbs. It thrashed, tearing stone
loose in slabs. The chamber shook. Caedmon cried out and flattened himself against the wall, his precious
quill crushed beneath his palm.
Sabelle’s voice became a command meant for the dead.
“Return below.”
The revenant’s mouth opened.
It did not look at Sabelle.
It looked at Morwenna.
“Morwenna Ashgrove,” it said. “The Cartel knows.”
The chains dragged it down.
Morwenna stood frozen as the black stone closed over the revenant’s body. One hand remained visible for
a moment, fingers clawing at the edge of the broken floor. The report’s last scrap clung to one nail. Then
that vanished too.
Silence fell hard.
Water tapped beneath them.
Caedmon slowly unfolded from the wall. Blood seeped across his palm where the quill had pierced it.
Sabelle lowered their hands.
Morwenna kept her sword up.
“The Cartel knows what?” Caedmon asked.
Sabelle turned toward her.
Their face held no accusation. That was worse. Accusation belonged to law, and law could be answered.
What rested in Sabelle’s eyes was comprehension.
Morwenna felt the old discipline gather around her like armor. Fleet Admiral. Commanding station.
Unbroken voice. No fear visible where fear could be used.
“The creature was damaged,” she said. “Its words were not reliable.”

Sabelle looked down at the sealed floor.
“No,” they said. “They were not.”
From beneath the stone came a single knock.
Then another.
The same patient rhythm as before.
But now it was answering someone below.

Chapter 12
The wind came through Cindermere Hold without asking leave.
It moved along the broken battlements, worried the loose stones, and descended through the arrow slits in
thin, cold fingers. Halvard Vane the Grave-Sworn stood within the gatehouse and listened to it pass
through the ruin. There was no fire in the brazier. No sentry called from the wall. Dust had gathered in the
joints of the flagstones and lay there undisturbed except where boots had crossed it recently.
One pair of boots.
Halvard looked down.
The prints led toward the inner court, their edges still sharp. Whoever had made them had not come in
from the mountain path. They had come from the dead barracks.
A place abandoned did not empty itself. It shed its people first, then its purpose, then its noise. The rest
remained: doors hanging from one hinge, blackened stones, rust in the rain gutters, old straw turned the
color of bruises. Cindermere Hold had been founded in 246 AS among The High Spires. Once, its garrison
had numbered 8878. Now it was abandoned, no core holding, a great stone tooth left in the jaw of the
heights.
Yet someone had swept the gatehouse floor.
Halvard stepped over the newest print and entered the inner court.
The sky pressed low between the peaks. Ash-colored light lay over the towers. Along the western wall, a
standard without its device cracked softly in the wind, its cloth reduced to strips. Halvard watched it twist
upon its pole, unable to decide whether it was trying to rise or fall.
Their cloak stirred behind them. The movement felt too loud.
At the far side of the court, a door stood ajar.
Halvard did not touch the hilt of the knife concealed beneath their coat. The gesture would have been an
