admission, and admissions had weight. They had learned to carry weight without showing the strain. That
was the first discipline of a Seneschal. The second was knowing which burdens belonged to the living and
which had already been placed upon the dead.
Inside the building, something scraped.
Halvard entered.
A passage ran beneath the old keep, narrow and low-roofed. The walls had once been whitewashed.
Smoke had darkened them in long vertical stains. Water fell somewhere beyond the stone, one drop at a
time, with the patience of a clerk making entries in a ledger.
At the passage’s end, a room showed a stripe of lamplight.
Halvard paused before it.
The lamp flame did not flicker. That meant a shield had been placed around it, or the room had no draft.
Neither possibility belonged in Cindermere Hold.
They pushed the door open.

A man sat at a table beneath the eastern wall. He had arranged papers in a neat fan, weighted at the corners
with bits of broken masonry. A traveling case rested beside his chair. The room had been made habitable
with ruthless economy: one blanket, one cup, one lamp, one narrow bed against the wall.
The man lifted his head.
“Halvard Vane the Grave-Sworn,” he said.
Halvard let the silence answer before they did. “You know my name.”
“I know the names that arrive with sealed orders.”
“Then you know I dislike being expected.”
“I expected the seal. Not you.”
His voice held no fear that Halvard could hear. That was not courage. Courage had heat in it. This was the
flatness of someone who had been waiting too long for a danger and had grown tired of imagining its face.
Halvard looked at the papers. “You serve at Cindermere Hold.”
“I do.”
“Cindermere Hold is abandoned.”
The man’s mouth shifted, not quite into a smile. “Both statements remain true.”
The answer entered the room like a blade laid gently upon a table.
Halvard removed their gloves, finger by finger. “Your name.”
“Ignatz Marrowgate.”
The name belonged nowhere in Halvard’s memory, which did not mean it had never been spoken.
Memory was a locked archive with corridors that changed when no one watched. Halvard had been born
in 338 AS, and since then had learned that the world kept every record except the one a person most
needed.
Ignatz Marrowgate inclined his head. “You are a major Seneschal.”
“I am.”
“Then the order is not routine.”
“Routine orders are carried by riders.”
“Riders do not come to abandoned holds?”
“Not unless someone has given them a reason.”
Ignatz glanced toward the door. “Someone did.”
Outside, the wind struck the walls. The whole keep answered with a deep, hollow groan.
Halvard crossed to the table. The papers were not military reports. Their margins bore columns of
cramped writing, corrections, and small black marks made with a blunt nib. A scribe’s work, though not
the work of an unpracticed hand.
“Where did you get these?”

“They were left here.”
“By whom?”
Ignatz’s eyes moved to the lamp. “By someone who did not want to be seen leaving them.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the answer I possess.”
Halvard placed one bare hand upon the nearest page. The ink had dried unevenly. Some lines had been
written in haste; others had been copied with careful deliberation. There were references to stores, gates,
sealed chambers, and a ward. No names appeared. No dates. Only the old notation of a place that had once
been expected to withstand an enemy.
The Thrice-Bound Lantern.
The words had been written three times in the margin, each instance crossed through and written again
below. The artifact was a ward forged in 72 AS, marked by three visible bindings. Its strength lay in
restraint and containment. Halvard had seen its likeness only in old inventories: a severe lantern, made less
to give light than to keep something from reaching it.
“What is it?” Ignatz asked.
“You already know.”
“I know the name. I want to know why it is written here.”
Halvard turned the page.
Behind them, a stone shifted in the corridor.
Ignatz did not move. His hand remained atop the papers. Halvard saw the tension gather in his wrist.
The sound came again.
Not the wind. Not water.
A foot placed carefully upon dust.
Halvard looked at the door.
Ignatz whispered, “There was no one in the court.”
“There is now.”
“Your people?”
“I came alone.”
That was true. It was also the kind of truth that could be made useless by what it concealed.
Halvard reached for the lamp and pinched the flame between two fingers. Darkness fell abruptly, carrying
the smell of hot oil and old metal. Ignatz inhaled once through his nose.
“Do not speak,” Halvard murmured.
The room became a sealed thing. The mountain wind withdrew behind the walls. Somewhere far below,
the hidden water continued its measured dripping.

Halvard listened.
A scrape. Then another.
The door stood open by the width of a hand. Beyond it, the passage was black.
Their thoughts went, as they always did when danger presented itself, not toward survival but toward
arrangement. The body was a temporary vessel. The consequences were not. If the intruder entered, Ignatz
might die. If Ignatz died, the papers might vanish. If the papers vanished, an old ward might remain
unaccounted for in a fortress that had outlived its purpose. None of those possibilities troubled Halvard
equally.
The greatest danger was not discovery.
It was interruption.
For three nights, Halvard had carried the shape of their liege’s death within the mind. Not the act itself;
acts were crude, and crude things invited witnesses. The sequence mattered more: the altered seal, the
emptied cup, the servant dismissed, the door left unbarred at the proper hour. A death could be made to
resemble misfortune if one respected misfortune’s habits.
Their own liege had trusted the gravity of Halvard’s silence.
That trust had been useful.
A shadow crossed the crack beneath the door.
Ignatz’s fingers tightened on the papers. Halvard saw the movement and lifted one hand, warning him
still.
The shadow stopped.
For one breath, the room held.
Then someone outside said, “Open.”
The voice was muffled by the stone, but it was human.
Ignatz leaned close. “They know I am here.”
“They know someone is here.”
“They used my name before you came?”
“No.”
“Then they know.”
Halvard let their hand fall beneath the coat. The knife’s hilt met their palm, familiar as a vow. The epithet
Grave-Sworn had been spoken of them in courts where candles burned cleanly and floors held no dust.
People heard it and imagined devotion. They imagined a person chained to duty, a servant who had made
the dead into witnesses.
Let them imagine.
“Open,” the voice said again.
Halvard looked at Ignatz. In the dimness, the scribe’s face was only a pale interruption in the dark.

“What do you serve?” Halvard asked.
“Cindermere Hold.”
“No. What do you serve?”
Ignatz’s breathing changed. “The record.”
“A record does not bleed.”
“It does when men alter it.”
The answer had the shape of an accusation, though Halvard could not tell against whom.
The latch moved.
Halvard stepped away from the table and into the angle beside the door. Ignatz gathered the papers against
his chest. The lamp, extinguished, gave off its last warmth between them.
The door began to open.
Halvard raised the knife, and in the darkness their fingers found the first page where The Thrice-Bound
Lantern had been written, as though the old ward itself had reached through the paper and taken hold of
them—
The door opened wide enough for a blade of corridor-light to enter.
It was not lamplight. It had the thin, bluish pallor of moonlight reflected from snow, though no snow lay
beyond the walls. Halvard saw a shoulder, a gloved hand, the dull rim of a helm. The stranger paused on
the threshold.
Ignatz moved first.
He flung the papers toward the table and stepped into the light.
Halvard’s knife touched the soft place beneath his jaw.
“Do not,” Halvard whispered.
Ignatz froze. The pages slid from his grasp. One turned in the air, its ink catching the pallor. The words
were visible for only a breath.
The Thrice-Bound Lantern housed in Hollowvale.
Then the page struck the floor.
The stranger outside said, “You were ordered to open.”
Ignatz’s throat worked against the knife. “By whom?”
“By the one who gave the order.”
“Then carry back the answer.”
A silence settled between the room and the corridor. It was the silence of a house listening through its
stones. Somewhere beyond the wall, something dripped at regular intervals. Halvard counted three falls
before the stranger spoke again.
“You are not alone.”

“Neither are you,” Halvard said.
The gloved hand tightened on the door.
He had expected fear. Instead, he heard the faint rasp of metal being drawn.
Halvard pressed the knife harder. Ignatz made no sound, but the papers under his boots rustled. A bad
place for them. A worse place for blood. Ink and blood did not mingle cleanly; the ink fled, the blood
remained. That was one of the first truths taught to any servant of a ledger.
The stranger entered.
Halvard saw a narrow face beneath the helm, a mouth without a beard, eyes obscured by the shadow of the
brow. No crest marked the cloak. No ring showed on the hand. The absence was deliberate. Men who
wished to be unknown rarely managed it; men who wished to be unclaimed were more dangerous.
The door closed behind him.
Halvard kept the knife at Ignatz’s throat and turned his gaze toward the stranger. “You have come for the
record.”
“I have come for the scribe.”
“I am no—”
“Quiet,” Halvard said.
Ignatz’s mouth shut.
The stranger’s attention shifted between them. “You know what he carries?”
“I know what men kill for.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one you have earned.”
The stranger took another step. The boards complained beneath his weight. His cloak smelled of wet stone
and iron. Halvard knew the scent. It clung to the thresholds of places where decisions had been made
before witnesses arrived.
Ignatz looked down at the page beneath his boot.
Halvard felt the movement and followed it with his eyes.
The page had folded over itself. Only a strip of writing remained visible, but the words were enough to
summon a buried room: three bands around a dark lantern, each binding laid over the last; the old marks
cut into the metal like scars that had healed badly. He had never seen the artifact. He had seen drawings,
descriptions, a disputed inventory rendered in six hands. He had seen the same line repeated until
repetition had made it sacred.
The Thrice-Bound Lantern housed in Hollowvale.
Not lost. Not destroyed. Housed.
A ward was not a weapon until someone opened what it restrained.
Ignatz shifted his weight.

The knife kissed skin.
“Do not reach for it,” Halvard said.
“I was not.”
“You were thinking of it.”
The scribe’s gaze lifted. In the dimness his face seemed reduced to angles and hollows. Halvard could not
tell whether he was young or merely starved of sleep. “You read the line.”
“I read enough.”
“Then you know why they came.”
The stranger’s hand dropped to his side. “They?”
“Those who altered the record.”
“You accuse everyone who touches paper.”
“Only the careful ones.”
The stranger gave a short laugh. It held no amusement. “You speak like a man who has never had to
choose between a lie and a grave.”
Halvard’s grip remained steady.
There were graves that waited beneath stone. There were graves that waited in the mouths of living men.
There were graves made long before the body entered them, prepared by a signature, a seal, a spoken oath.
He had stood beside enough of them to know that burial was rarely the end of a decision. More often, it
was the decision’s first public form.
The stranger said, “Release him.”
“No.”
“He has copied what should not be copied.”
“Then you should have burned the source.”
“The source is not yours to burn.”
“Nor yours to read.”
A faint sound came from the corridor beyond the door. Not footsteps. Fabric brushing stone. Another
presence, held back and waiting.
Halvard felt the room contract.
Ignatz heard it too. His breath turned shallow. “How many?”
The stranger looked at him. “Enough.”
“That is not a number.”
“It is not meant to be.”
Halvard almost smiled. The expression would have been a mistake. Instead, he leaned close to Ignatz’s
ear.

“If they enter, you die first.”
Ignatz swallowed. “And if they do not?”
“Then you may have time to explain why the record says Hollowvale.”
The stranger’s head tilted. “You have not read the whole page.”
“I have read the part you fear.”
“What do you think it means?”
“I think a place has been given a burden.”
“Hollowvale is a word.”
“So is a grave.”
The stranger moved with sudden violence.
Halvard shoved Ignatz aside and cut downward. The knife struck the stranger’s forearm, glancing from
hidden metal beneath the sleeve. Sparks leapt and died. The stranger seized Halvard’s wrist. His grip was
hard enough to numb the fingers.
Ignatz stumbled into the table. The lamp, unlit and cold, rolled against the wall.
For an instant the three of them were tangled in the dark: breath, cloth, the wet scrape of a boot searching
for purchase. Halvard drove his shoulder into the stranger’s chest. They struck the door. The impact shook
dust from the lintel.
The stranger’s other hand found Halvard’s throat.
Halvard did not struggle. He let his body slacken.
The grip tightened.
He brought his knee up.
The stranger grunted and released him. Halvard twisted free, caught the man’s cloak, and used its own
weight to drag him sideways. The helm struck the stone jamb. Metal rang through the chamber.
Beyond the door, the waiting presence moved.
“Now,” the stranger called.
Ignatz snatched the fallen page.
Halvard turned on him. “Put it down.”
The scribe held the paper in both hands. His fingers trembled, but his voice did not. “You should have let
me finish.”
“Finish what?”
“The correction.”
The stranger recovered, one hand braced against the wall. A dark line ran from beneath his sleeve. Not
much blood. Enough to show the cut had reached flesh.
Ignatz raised the page toward the dead lamp.

“There is no Hollowvale,” the stranger said.
Ignatz looked at him. “There is always a Hollowvale.”
“That is not what the record says.”
“The record says what it is made to say.”
“And you made this?”
“I copied it.”
“From whom?”
Ignatz’s eyes found Halvard’s.
The question entered the room like a draft through a cracked window.
Halvard remembered the first page, the old ink, the pressure of a hand that had written too carefully. He
remembered the way Ignatz had refused the question of service. Not a place. Not an office. The record.
A record does not bleed.
It does when men alter it.
Outside, someone struck the door.
The wood shuddered.
The stranger reached for his weapon.
Halvard stepped between him and Ignatz, knife raised. The choice came without ceremony. He had made
worse choices in quieter rooms.
“Give me the page,” Halvard said.
Ignatz’s face tightened. “Why?”
“Because if they take it, they will not need to kill you.”
The second blow struck. A splinter burst inward and spun across the floor.
The stranger stared at Halvard. “You understand nothing.”
“Then correct me.”
“The Lantern was not housed in Hollowvale.”
Ignatz’s hands clenched around the paper.
The door groaned.
The stranger said, “The Lantern housed Hollowvale.”
For one breath, no one moved.
The words were wrong in the mouth, wrong in the ear, wrong in every orderly column of the world.
Halvard felt the meaning rise beneath them like something waking under ice.
Ignatz tore the page in half.

The sound was small.
The stranger lunged.
Halvard caught Ignatz by the collar and dragged him backward as the stranger’s blade came down. Steel
struck the table, splitting the wood. The lamp leapt, rolled, and struck the wall hard enough to crack its
casing.
A black wick showed inside.
Then it burned.
The flame was pale and narrow, bound by three dark rings that had not been there a moment before. They
appeared one after another around the light, tightening without touch. The room filled with the smell of
old ash and rain trapped beneath earth.
The stranger stopped.
Halvard felt Ignatz go still beside him.
On the floor, the torn halves of the page began to move.
Not by wind. Not by any hand.
The fragments drew together across the boards, ink crawling from one torn edge to the other. Letters
unmade themselves. Lines shivered. The writing gathered into a single sentence beneath the wavering
flame.
The Thrice-Bound Lantern housed in Hollowvale.
The door burst inward.
Cold air rushed through the chamber, carrying the weight of many bodies. Halvard lifted the knife, but the
pale flame had already turned toward the threshold, and within its three bindings something struck once
against the glass—
The glass trembled again.
Halvard did not look toward the door. The knife remained raised, its point fixed upon the stranger’s throat,
while the dark beyond the threshold filled with the soft, wet sounds of men breathing through cloth.
Ignatz whispered, “How many?”
“Enough.”
“Ten?”
“Enough.”
A shape crossed the doorway. Then another. Their lanterns were hooded, their faces hidden beneath
ash-colored wraps. No crest showed upon them. No blade rang against a scabbard. They entered with the
quiet discipline of men who had learned that noise was a confession.
The stranger smiled.
It was not a smile of relief.
“You brought them,” Halvard said.

“I opened a door.”
“You opened this one.”
“And they were waiting outside it.”
The pale fire inside the Thrice-Bound Lantern bent toward the intruders. Its three bindings shone black
against the glass, each strip carved with cramped old script. The thing within struck again.
This time, the sound came from the walls.
Dust sifted from the rafters.
Ignatz flinched. Halvard heard the movement and hated him for it—not because fear was a weakness, but
because fear made men visible. The room had become a net of attention. Every breath tugged at it.
One of the masked figures raised a crossbow.
Halvard moved first.
The knife left their hand and entered the figure beneath the jaw. The man’s bolt sprang wide, tearing
through the stranger’s sleeve. Before the body finished falling, Halvard had crossed the room. Their
shoulder struck the second intruder against the wall. Bone cracked. A gloved hand seized at Halvard’s
throat, and Halvard drove two fingers into the soft place below the ear.
The man sagged.
Then the chamber broke open.
Steel flashed in the pale light. Ignatz swore and stumbled backward over the scattered page. Someone
struck the table, spilling wax and oil across the boards. The flame rose blue. Shadows leapt up the walls,
long-limbed and frantic.
Halvard caught a blade along their sleeve. The cloth parted. Cold kissed the skin beneath.
A hand seized their hair.
They drove their head backward.
The attacker grunted. Halvard turned within the grip, hooked an elbow beneath the man’s arm, and felt the
joint give. He folded without a cry. Halvard took his sword before it struck the floor.
The sword was poor steel, narrow and hungry. It suited the room.
“Toward the Lantern!” Ignatz shouted.
Halvard saw him clutching a brass candlestick, his mouth bloodied, his eyes fixed on the ward. One of the
masked figures had reached for it.
“Keep away from it!”
The command came from the stranger.
Not shouted. Not pleaded.
The intruder’s fingers hovered above the glass. The pale fire had lowered itself, gathered into a thin
vertical flame. Within it, something moved like a man sinking beneath ice.
The masked figure drew back.

For the first time, their discipline failed.
Halvard cut him across the ribs.
The man fell against the table. The torn page slid beneath his knee. Ink crawled over the floorboards, black
threads seeking one another. The sentence remained legible.
The Thrice-Bound Lantern housed in Hollowvale.
Halvard stared at it for one heartbeat too long.
A sword entered the space where their ribs had been.
They twisted aside. The blade scraped their coat, caught, and held. Halvard stepped close enough to smell
tallow, old wool, and the sourness beneath the mask. They drove the stolen sword upward.
The attacker went slack.
More waited in the passage.
More than ten.
The room had no rear door. Its windows were too narrow for a grown body, and beyond them the night
pressed against the glass like a blind sea. Halvard heard boots in the corridor, the restrained impatience of
men ordered not to rush.
The stranger stood beside the Lantern with one hand upon the table.
“Why are they here?” Ignatz asked.
“Because the page spoke.”
“Pages do not speak.”
“Then you should be less afraid of them.”
The stranger turned toward Halvard. In the uncertain light, the face remained difficult to hold in memory.
The features seemed to change whenever the flame shuddered—not truly changing, perhaps, but refusing
the eye.
Halvard knew that sort of refusal.
They had worn it before the liege.
They had bowed beneath banners, placed a hand over the heart, and spoken of loyalty while counting the
men who would stand between the throne and the knife. The plot had required patience. It had required a
grave expression, a steady voice, a talent for making treason resemble duty.
Halvard Vane the Grave-Sworn, born in 338 AS.
The old records had made a virtue of the name. The court had called them grave because they did not
laugh, sworn because they kept their oaths. No record had preserved what mattered: that Halvard had
plotted the death of their own liege, and that the liege had never understood how near the hand had come.
A masked man entered.
Halvard met him at the threshold.

The sword went low, then high. The man parried the first stroke and took the second across the throat.
Blood sprayed the doorframe. Behind him, the others hesitated.
Not from the corpse.
From the Lantern.
Its three bindings had begun to glow.
The light was not bright. It was worse than brightness. It revealed the room without illuminating it,
showing every crack in the boards, every stain in the mortar, every drop of blood hanging in the air before
it fell. The faces beyond the doorway appeared beneath their masks as pale hollows.
A voice breathed from inside the glass.
Not words.
A counting.
The first binding split with a sound like a fingernail dragged across bone.
Ignatz dropped the candlestick. “That ward was forged in 72 AS.”
Halvard looked at him.
Ignatz’s expression had collapsed into naked terror. “The Thrice-Bound Lantern. It was forged in 72 AS.
If one binding opens—”
“Then close it.”
“I don’t know how.”
“Then remember faster.”
The stranger seized Ignatz by the collar and pulled him away from the table. “It is not opening.”
The second binding shone.
“It is being answered,” the stranger said.
Outside, the men in the corridor began to chant.
The words were muffled by cloth and stone, but Halvard knew the cadence. They had heard it in old
reports and sealed testimony, in accounts of drowned banners and villages that burned without flame.
The War of Drowned Light began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS.
The war had taken 64617 casualties.
The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor.
Halvard remembered the official histories: the pale standards sinking beneath rain, the broken armies
retreating through fields turned to black mud. Yet the victor’s silence had always been too complete. The
war had collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals, and every reprisal had carried the same patient
shape—one village against another, one oath against another, grief made useful by unseen hands.
The spark had been secretly staged by The Silent Choir.
Everyone who mattered knew it.

No one who mattered admitted knowing.
The chant outside thickened. The third binding began to burn.
“Who are they?” Ignatz said.
Halvard listened to the voices.
“The Choir.”
The stranger’s head tilted. “No.”
The word struck Halvard harder than a denial should have.
“Then who?” Ignatz asked.
The stranger lifted a blood-wet finger and touched the glass.
The Lantern screamed.
Every masked figure in the corridor fell silent.
A pressure seized the chamber. Halvard felt it behind the eyes, in the roots of the teeth. The air tasted of
iron and ashes. Somewhere beneath the floor, something vast shifted in its sleep.
The stranger looked toward the page.
“Hollowvale is not a place,” they said.
Halvard’s hand tightened on the sword. “It is marked on the old roads.”
“Names are roads for those who cannot see the country.”
Ignatz stared at the stranger. “Then what is it?”
The third binding cracked.
The pale flame went out.
For an instant, there was only darkness.
Then a line of light appeared beneath the door.
It ran across the floor toward Halvard’s boots, thin as a drawn thread. Where it touched the blood, the
blood turned white. The bodies began to twitch.
Halvard backed away.
The line reached the torn page.
The sentence vanished.
New writing rose in its place, each letter forming slowly, as if pressed upward from beneath the paper by a
dead hand.
COME TO THE COAST.
Ignatz made a sound in his throat.
“Which coast?” Halvard asked.

The stranger did not answer.
Halvard already knew the only coast that mattered.
Gloamreach lay on the Pale Coast, a core location with a garrison of 2,483. Its status was quarantined. The
old reports described its walls as sealed, its roads watched, its gates shut against all passage. A place set
apart from the surrounding coast, guarded not merely against invasion but against whatever the
surrounding world might carry inward.
The line of light turned toward the window.
Toward the sea.
“Gloamreach,” Halvard said.
The stranger’s silence confirmed nothing.
That was confirmation enough.
Ignatz bent over the page, breathing hard. “We cannot go there.”
“Why?”
“Because it is quarantined.”
“Then we will be expected.”
“By whom?”
A fist struck the outer door.
The wood groaned.
Halvard glanced at the corpses. At the dark passage. At the Lantern, now black and still, its three bindings
dull as dead wire.
“Not by friends.”
Another blow.
This one split the door.
The stranger reached beneath their coat and drew out a small iron seal. No emblem marked it. Its surface
was blank except for a single depression shaped like a closed eye.
Halvard recognized the metal.
Not the seal itself. The workmanship.
The Iron-Ring Cartel used iron that way: objects without heraldry, authority stripped of ornament,
commands made portable. But the seal bore no ring, and the Cartel did not deal in mysteries unless
mystery could be weighed.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel?” Halvard asked.
“Not tonight.”
“House Morvain?”
“Not them.”

“The Ashen Vanguard?”
The stranger looked almost amused. “You ask as though the powers have only one face.”
The door shattered inward.
Men surged through the opening.
Halvard seized Ignatz and threw him toward the window. “Break it.”
Ignatz stared at the narrow panes.
“Now.”
He snatched up the fallen candlestick and smashed the glass. Wind poured through, wet and savage.
Beyond lay a drop into darkness, though no ground could be seen.
“That is not a road,” Ignatz said.
“It is the only one.”
The stranger lifted the Lantern.
The instant their fingers closed around its frame, the three bindings flared.
Every man in the doorway froze.
The pale fire returned behind the glass, but it no longer burned upright. It bent toward Halvard. Within it, a
figure pressed both hands against the inner surface.
Halvard heard a voice.
Their own voice.
You plotted the death of your liege.
The sword nearly fell from their hand.
The words were not accusation. They were inventory.
You were born in 338 AS. You wore grief like armor. You called the knife duty.
Behind Halvard, Ignatz climbed through the broken window.
“Hurry!”
The masked men moved again.
Halvard turned toward the opening. The night waited beyond it, vast and blind. Somewhere below, water
struck stone.
The stranger placed the Lantern against Halvard’s chest.
Cold entered them.
Not through skin. Through memory.
For one breath Halvard stood before the liege’s sealed chamber, hand upon the latch, listening to the slow
breathing beyond. They felt again the weight of the poison hidden beneath their tongue. They remembered
the final hesitation—not mercy, never mercy, but the terror of discovering that a life could be ended and

still refuse to become simple.
Then the vision broke.
Halvard was falling through the window.
Ignatz caught their wrist.
The stranger followed, carrying the black Lantern.
Above them, the masked men crowded the ruined chamber. One raised a bow. Another shouted a
command Halvard could not hear over the wind.
The arrow came.
The Lantern struck the stone ledge.
Its first binding split wide.
Pale fire poured downward—not flame, but a door.
Halvard saw a shoreline beneath it, white cliffs, sealed gates, and the distant watchfires of Gloamreach.
Then something on the other side looked back.
The stranger’s grip tightened around Halvard’s wrist.
“Do not let go,” they said.
Halvard looked down into the opening.
A second figure was falling upward toward them.
And it wore Halvard’s face.

Chapter 13
The bell beneath the floor rang once.
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned lifted their head from the interrogation table. The sound had not
come from the chapel above, where the bells were iron and cracked, nor from the watchtower, where the
wind worried at the old bronze. It had risen through the stone beneath their boots: a low, submerged note,
felt first in the teeth.
Across the table, Morwenna Ashgrove did not flinch.
That was the first lie.
The second was the smile she offered afterward.
“You hear many things in this place,” said Morwenna.
Her voice carried the disciplined calm of a Fleet Admiral. No tremor. No appeal. She sat with her wrists
unbound upon the black wood, as though the room belonged to her and the inquisitorial lamps were
merely poor weather glimpsed through a porthole.
Sabelle studied her in the dimness. The lamps burned with oil rendered from pale shore-moss, and their
flames leaned toward the door despite the absence of a draft. Behind Morwenna, the wall was hung with
the instruments of confession: hooks, wire, a silver basin gone green at the rim. The tools had been
cleaned. Sabelle disliked cleanliness in an interrogation chamber. It suggested preparation, and preparation
was a form of vanity.
“You heard nothing,” Sabelle said.
“Then why ask?”
“Because silence is sometimes an answer.”
Morwenna’s eyes moved to the crown upon the table.
The Crown of Burned Names rested inside a circle of salt. Its blackened points rose like the fingers of a
charred hand. Across its metal, names had been scored away until only pale scars remained. It was a ward
forged in 266 AS, and attunement to it cost 60. Sabelle had worn it once. The memory still lived in their
bones: the slow extinguishing of every private face, every unspoken tenderness, every name that had ever
made the world seem less empty.
They had survived by becoming difficult to remember.
The other crown was not in the room. It never was when questions were being asked.
“The Crown of Burned Names does not protect liars,” Sabelle said.
“No,” Morwenna replied. “It protects the forgotten.”
“Those are often the same people.”
A little blood had dried beneath Morwenna’s left thumbnail. Not hers, Sabelle thought. Or not recently
hers. The Fleet Admiral had come dressed for command, in a coat without ornament and gloves folded
beside her chair. There was no sign of a struggle upon her. No visible mark, no loosened seam. Yet she
had been summoned from the coast under seal, and the seal had not been broken by any hand in the room.

Sabelle had broken it themselves.
The five powers pressing their shadows across the Ashen Era had grown skilled at hiding knives beneath
official wax. The Ashen Vanguard called its violence duty. House Morvain called its violence inheritance.
The Silent Choir called its violence necessity. The Iron-Ring Cartel called its violence trade. The Bleeding
Crown called its violence law.
Sabelle called it evidence.
They drew a thin folio across the table. The parchment was gray from age and smelled of brine.
“Read the final line.”
Morwenna glanced down. “I can read.”
“Then do so.”
“The War of Drowned Light.”
The words seemed to darken the room.
That war began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS. The record placed 64617 casualties beneath its final seal.
The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor, though the conflict collapsed into a decade of guerrilla
reprisals, and its spark had been secretly staged by them.
Every child of rank knew the first portion. The last portion was spoken only by people who wanted to die
badly, or by people who had proof.
Morwenna’s gaze remained on the parchment.
“You possess naval reports from the war,” Sabelle said.
“I possess many reports.”
“You sell them.”
The Fleet Admiral’s mouth hardened. “To whom?”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel.”
For the first time, something alive moved behind her composure. Not fear. Calculation. It passed across
her face like a fish beneath dark water and vanished before Sabelle could spear it.
The room gave another small shudder.
Below, in the cellar, the revenant turned against its bindings.
Sabelle felt the movement in the joints of their hands. The thing was awake. It had been awake for three
nights, dragging its chains over the floorstones, whispering through a throat that had forgotten the shape of
breath. Sabelle kept it because the dead remembered what the living had been paid to forget. They kept it
because power did not always arrive wearing a crown. Sometimes it arrived wet with grave soil and
waited for permission to speak.
Morwenna looked toward the floor.
“You have someone beneath us,” she said.
Sabelle allowed the silence to stretch until the lamps began to hiss.

“A poor choice of words,” Morwenna continued.
“Was it?”
“I serve aboard ships. I know the language of decks, holds, ballast. If something is moving beneath a floor,
it is not my concern unless the floor gives way.”
“Your concern is what lies beneath every surface.”
“Then we share a profession.”
Sabelle’s hand closed over the edge of the table. They had been born in 263 AS, under a sky the old priests
claimed was the color of drowned silver. The world had given them two crowns and the title High
Inquisitor, though neither honor had ever felt like a gift. A crown was a promise made by someone who
expected your head to remain still while they tightened it.
The cellar bell rang again.
Morwenna heard it this time.
Her eyes narrowed.
“Does the High Inquisitor invite the dead to witness interrogations?”
“The dead require no invitation.”
“Then perhaps you should ask it whether I betrayed you.”
Sabelle smiled without warmth. “You mistake accusation for trust.”
“I mistake nothing.”
They opened a second folio.
Inside lay a coastal survey, its ink blurred by salt. Gloamreach lay on the Pale Coast, sealed beneath
quarantine. Its garrison was 2,483. The number had been written three times, each copy in a different
hand. Around the mark for the harbor, someone had drawn a ring of black strokes, as though the place
were an eye that must not be opened.
“Gloamreach is a core location,” Sabelle said. “The quarantine remains in force.”
Morwenna said nothing.
“Your ships have approached its waters.”
“A fleet approaches many waters.”
“Your intelligence reached the Iron-Ring Cartel before it reached the proper authorities.”
“Your evidence is a suspicion wearing a uniform.”
“It is a uniform you recognize.”
The Fleet Admiral leaned back. The chair creaked beneath her, an old complaint.
Beyond the narrow window, the night pressed against the glass. Sabelle could see only a thin scatter of ash
falling from the upper roofs. The Hold had been built high enough that weather sometimes passed below
it. Somewhere beyond the walls, where the mountains broke the horizon, Cindermere Hold stood
abandoned among the High Spires. It had been founded in 246 AS, and its garrison once numbered 8878.

Now it was not a core holding. Its silhouette, blackened and remote, had become a lesson in what strength
looked like after everyone worth killing had already been killed.
Morwenna watched Sabelle’s face.
“You want me to say Gloamreach is compromised,” she said.
“I want you to say what you know.”
“What I know is that sealed places breed profitable rumors.”
“And what you know of Cindermere Hold?”
Her expression did not change, but she looked again at the folio.
“Nothing worth saying.”
“Nothing worth saying is the Cartel’s favored currency.”
“Then you should arrest them.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel does not sit in rooms.”
“It sits everywhere.”
A murmur rose from beneath the floor. This time it shaped itself almost into a word.
Sabelle felt the old pull in their chest, the revenant’s hunger pressing against the chain of its binding. Not
hunger for flesh. That would have been simpler. It wanted recognition. The dead wanted to be told that
their suffering had entered the world’s accounting.
The War of Drowned Light had 64617 casualties, the folio said.
The dead did not care whether the number was accurate. They cared that someone had written it down.
Sabelle set the parchment aside and brought out the reliquary.
The Diadem of Sorrowgate was small enough to rest in both hands. Its surface had the dull gleam of bone
polished beneath deep water. It had been forged in 281 AS. Attunement to it cost 9. The cost was low,
which made the artifact more dangerous; grief often entered cheaply and collected interest later.
Morwenna stared at it.
“Do you know what that is?”
“The Diadem of Sorrowgate.”
“Good.”
“Are you offering it?”
“I am showing you what remembers.”
The diadem’s inner rim glimmered. In its reflection, Morwenna’s face seemed older, then younger, then
absent altogether. Sabelle saw a shoreline beneath a white sky. Ships without flags. Men and women
kneeling in water that reached their throats. A radiance drowned beneath the waves, still shining where no
sun could touch it.

The war’s appearance had been broken banners and drowned radiance. Its truth was treachery concealed
beneath attrition, vengeance without an ending.
Sabelle withdrew their hand.
Morwenna’s breath had shortened.
“You sell intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel,” Sabelle said. “The question is not whether. The question is
what they intend to purchase.”
“And if I refuse to answer?”
“Then the cellar will answer for you.”
The lamps guttered.
Morwenna looked at the door.
Sabelle heard the chains below draw taut, one link after another. The revenant had risen. Its weight moved
through the foundations. Dust sifted from the ceiling and settled upon the folios like gray snow.
“You are not what they say,” Morwenna whispered.
“They say many things.”
“They say the Twice-Crowned High Inquisitor has no private devotions.”
“Then they are wrong.”
A smile touched Morwenna’s mouth, but it was not the earlier smile. This one carried pity, and pity was an
insult more intimate than hatred.
“You keep it bound beneath your cellar.”
Sabelle’s fingers tightened around the Diadem of Sorrowgate.
The revenant struck the underside of the floor.
Once.
The sound traveled through the table, through the salt circle, through the crown of blackened names.
Morwenna rose as the room lurched, and for one breath the Fleet Admiral’s discipline broke entirely.
A voice came up through the stones.
Not a scream.
A name.
Sabelle turned toward the door, where the lock had begun to tremble, and Morwenna said, “You should
have asked me what the Silent Choir found beneath Gloamreach,” and the dead below struck the floor
again—
The dead below struck the floor again—
—and the lock burst inward.
The door did not open so much as lose the argument. Iron teeth tore free of the wood. A breath of
cellar-cold entered the chamber, carrying wet stone, old ashes, and the sweet corruption of something that

had learned to wait without breathing.
Morwenna’s hand went to the weapon at her hip.
Sabelle noticed. They noticed everything when fear made a person precise.
“Do not,” Sabelle said.
The Fleet Admiral’s fingers remained where they were. Her face had regained its discipline, but discipline
was only fear taught to stand upright. The lantern flame shivered between them. Across the table, the
Crown of Burned Names lay within its salt circle, blackened points lowered toward the boards. Each scar
upon it seemed to deepen as the voice beneath the room gathered itself.
Sabelle could feel the Diadem of Sorrowgate against their palm.
Not weight. Attention.
Its sorrow had teeth.
“You heard it,” Morwenna said.
“I heard the floor.”
“You heard your name.”
The third blow came.
The table split along its grain. Salt leapt from the circle and glittered in the air before settling over the
Diadem like frost. The Crown of Burned Names did not move. It held the room as a nail holds flesh.
Sabelle looked at it.
“The Crown of Burned Names had an attunement cost of 60,” they said.
Morwenna stared.
Sabelle had spoken softly, yet the words seemed to descend through the chamber. The ward had exacted
that cost from every hand that had ever reached for it, and Sabelle had never mistaken cost for proof of
worth. Powerful things did not ask what a person could spare. They took what would leave a lasting
absence.
“Why tell me that now?” Morwenna asked.
“Because you are looking at it as if it might protect you.”
“I am looking at it as if it might protect us.”
“There is no us in this room.”
The Fleet Admiral’s mouth tightened. “You invited me.”
“I permitted you to enter.”
“And now you regret the distinction.”
Sabelle turned from her. Beyond the broken door, darkness breathed beneath the steps. The cellar lay
under the chamber, under the stone, under every sealed report and censored confession that had allowed
this house to remain respectable. They had kept the revenant bound there because the alternatives had
been worse. That was the phrase they had used when first they drew the chains. It had sounded like

principle in the privacy of their own skull.
Now the thing below had spoken their name.
The sound came again, muffled through earth.
“Sabelle.”
Their fingers closed around the Diadem of Sorrowgate until its edges bit skin.
Morwenna took a step toward the door. “It knows you.”
“It knows a sound.”
“It called you.”
“So do beggars. So do judges.”
“It called you from beneath a ward that has held since before—”
“Do not finish that sentence.”
The Admiral stopped.
The silence that followed was not empty. It had the crowded quality of a courtroom before the verdict,
when every witness had already decided what truth would cost them.
Sabelle could hear water slipping somewhere below. A chain dragged across stone. Then another chain
answered, not with metal, but with a low rasp that made the teeth ache.
Morwenna said, “The Silent Choir found it beneath Gloamreach.”
Sabelle’s gaze sharpened.
There it was. Not the secret itself, but the shape of its shadow.
“Found what?”
“You know what.”
“I know what they claimed to find.”
“They sent the report sealed.”
“You opened it.”
“I read it.”
“You sold it.”
Morwenna did not flinch. That was the trouble with trained liars. Their shame did not appear where shame
belonged. It moved elsewhere, into the breathing, the posture, the careful refusal to touch the edge of the
table.
“To whom?” Sabelle asked.
Morwenna’s eyes went to the black crown.
The answer did not need a voice.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel,” Sabelle said.

A faint sound escaped Morwenna—not denial, not agreement. Something smaller and more exhausted.
Sabelle felt the room contract around the name. The Cartel was not present, yet its hunger had a way of
arriving ahead of its agents. Coin had no allegiance except to continuation. It entered a war through a
purse, a harbor, a clerk’s sleeve. It left by every door.
“You gave them the report,” Sabelle said.
“I gave them a portion.”
“Which portion?”
“The portion that could be purchased.”
“Everything can be purchased.”
“Not everything.”
“Your intelligence can.”
Morwenna’s gaze lifted. “You say that as though the Ashen Vanguard has ever paid in anything else.”
The floor shuddered beneath them.
Dust sifted from the ceiling. The lantern guttered, and the room filled with the copper smell of its dying
wick. Sabelle placed the Diadem of Sorrowgate on the table beside the crown. The two relics did not
touch. Grief required distance from erasure.
Under the boards, the revenant whispered.
“Sabelle.”
This time the voice carried an old cadence, a human shape worn thin by burial. It was not pleading. It had
no need to plead. The bound were patient. Patience was the only dignity left to the dead.
Morwenna’s hand withdrew from her weapon.
“What did you bind down there?”
Sabelle faced her.
The question had been waiting between them since the Admiral crossed the threshold. It had merely
lacked the courage to become audible.
“You came for the answer,” Sabelle said.
“I came for what the Silent Choir found.”
“No. You came to learn whether I had already found it.”
Morwenna’s expression hardened. “If you knew, you would have told no one.”
“Correct.”
“That is not a defense.”
“It is not meant to be.”
Another blow struck beneath the floor, but the revenant did not speak afterward. The quiet was worse.
Sabelle felt the pressure of the chains through the soles of their boots, a tugging beneath bone. The binding

held. It had held through years of prayer, threat, and the long, humiliating labor of keeping something
powerful enough to hate from remembering how to die.
Morwenna said, “The Pale Coast is sealed.”
“You know that.”
“Gloamreach is quarantined.”
“You know that as well.”
“I know its garrison is 2,483.”
“Then you know enough to understand what would happen if panic reached them.”
The admission hung in the chamber. Morwenna heard it. Sabelle saw the calculation enter her eyes,
crossing from one side of the ledger to the other.
“Is it under Gloamreach?” Morwenna asked.
Sabelle said nothing.
“Is that what the Choir found?”
“Ask the Choir.”
“They are not here.”
“They prefer it that way.”
A smile touched Morwenna’s lips and vanished. “You speak of them as if you admire their methods.”
“I speak of them as if I have survived them.”
“The War of Drowned Light ended with their victory.”
Sabelle’s thumb moved over the Diadem’s rim. “Victories are often what the survivor calls the last
cruelty.”
“And the deaths?”
“Do not use dead bodies as currency with me.”
“I am trying to prevent more.”
“No. You are trying to keep the Iron-Ring Cartel from learning that the Silent Choir’s report has value.”
Morwenna’s silence confessed more cleanly than words.
The revenant stirred beneath them. A slow scrape. Then the boards bowed upward.
Sabelle moved before thought could interfere. They seized the Crown of Burned Names and pressed it
against the floor.
The ward answered with heat.
Not fire. Recognition.
Blackened metal flared beneath their hands. The scars cut into its surface filled with a dull, ember-red
light, and the air thickened until Morwenna gasped. Beneath the crown, something struck the boards and

recoiled. The entire house seemed to draw a breath through its foundations.
Sabelle held the ward down.
Pain opened along their palms. It was not the cost of attunement; that price had been paid elsewhere, in
chambers where witnesses had gone blind and names had been burned from records still warm with ink.
This was only resistance. This was the crown reminding its keeper that protection and mutilation had
always shared a root.
“Do not make me release it,” Sabelle said.
Morwenna’s eyes fixed on their bleeding hands. “You cannot control it.”
“I control the chains.”
“For now.”
The words slipped through Sabelle’s guard.
For now.
Below, the revenant laughed. The sound was delicate, almost courteous.
Morwenna heard it and went pale.
Sabelle pressed harder. “What did you sell?”
“The Choir’s route.”
“Whose route?”
“Their route to the chamber.”
“What chamber?”
Morwenna’s gaze shifted toward the cellar door, toward the darkness that had no right to be listening.
“The chamber beneath Gloamreach.”
Sabelle felt the crown pulse beneath their hands.
“You sold the Cartel a way into the quarantine.”
“I sold them a warning.”
“You sold them access.”
“I sold them the knowledge that access existed.”
“Do not decorate treason.”
Morwenna’s discipline broke then—not entirely, but enough. Her breath came shallow. Her shoulders
lowered as if an invisible weight had been set upon them.
“They already knew,” she said. “The Iron-Ring Cartel already knew there was something beneath
Gloamreach. They were buying confirmation. If I refused, someone else would have given it.”
“Then you might have allowed someone else to be damned.”
“I have allowed worse.”

“Have you?”
A long pause.
The revenant spoke from under the floor.
“Morwenna.”
The Fleet Admiral turned toward the cellar.
Sabelle watched the change in her. Recognition moved through her face like a blade through cloth.
“You know that voice,” Sabelle said.
Morwenna did not answer.
“You have heard it before.”
The boards cracked beneath the crown.
Morwenna whispered, “No.”
The revenant said her name again, and this time the chains below began to ring.
The chains rang again.
Not in panic. Not in pain.
In recognition.
Sabelle felt the sound pass through the soles of their boots and climb the bones of their legs. The cellar
was below them, behind the sealed door and the iron locks, beneath the chamber where the Fleet Admiral
had come to bargain with a High Inquisitor. Beneath the house, beneath the frost-stiffened earth, the
revenant waited in its dark.
Morwenna’s hand had gone to the hilt at her side.
“You said it was bound,” she murmured.
“It is.”
“That is not what I asked.”
“No.” Sabelle turned from the cellar door. “It is not.”
The crown upon their head seemed suddenly too heavy. The Crown of Burned Names pressed its scorched
rim into their brow, every blackened mark along it drinking the candlelight. It had been forged in 266 AS,
when remembrance was still considered a kind of mercy. The makers had believed a ward could protect a
name by consuming it.
They had been wrong.
Or perhaps they had understood protection better than anyone living.
The revenant dragged its chains across stone.
Morwenna looked toward the floor. “How long?”
Sabelle said nothing.

“How long has it been under this house?”
“Long enough.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one you are owed.”
The Fleet Admiral’s mouth tightened. Discipline held her face together. It did not hold the fear beneath it.
Fear was a tide; Sabelle had spent years learning how it moved through people before it broke the surface.
The voice came again.
“Morwenna.”
The candle flames bent toward the cellar door.
Morwenna flinched.
There. The truth, unarmored for half a breath.
Sabelle had been born in 263 AS, in a city whose bells had been melted down for weapons before they
learned the shape of their own name. By the time they took the office of High Inquisitor, they had ceased
believing that truth made anything cleaner. Truth was merely another instrument. It could cauterize. It
could open a wound. It could be sold.
Morwenna had sold it.
Not all of it. Not yet.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel knew there was something beneath Gloamreach,” Morwenna said. “They paid for
certainty.”
“And you gave it to them.”
“I gave them suspicion.”
“You gave them a map.”
“I gave them enough to keep their ships from sailing blind.”
“Ships do not need maps to find graves.”
Something struck the underside of the floor.
Dust sifted from the beams.
Morwenna’s gaze sharpened. “You have kept it here without reporting it.”
“Yes.”
“You are the High Inquisitor.”
“I am aware.”
“You were appointed to uncover abominations.”
“I have uncovered one.”
“And concealed it.”

Sabelle stepped closer to the cellar door. The wood had been sealed with salt, black wax, and a thin line of
blood that had dried brown in the grain. “The Silent Choir would have destroyed it.”
“Perhaps that would have been merciful.”
“Perhaps.” Sabelle placed two fingers against the crown. “The Silent Choir has never confused mercy with
restraint.”
The old records called the War of Drowned Light a victory for the Silent Choir. The record was correct. It
was also incomplete.
The war began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS. Its ledgers carried the same number wherever they had
survived: 64617 casualties. Not rounded. Not corrected. A number too precise to mourn and too large to
comprehend. The conflict collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals after the banners came down, and
the Silent Choir remained recorded as the victor. Its spark had been secretly staged by them.
Sabelle had read the sealed testimony.
The first light had been drowned on purpose.
Morwenna watched them. “You speak as though you know what it is.”
“I know what it remembers.”
“What does it remember?”
The chain below the floor went taut.
A voice scraped upward through the boards.
“The light.”
Morwenna’s face emptied.
Sabelle heard the answer before she understood the question. A cold pressure gathered behind their eyes.
The revenant had never spoken of the war. It had resisted every command that required language. It had
torn through three binding circles rather than name the dead.
Now it had chosen to speak.
“What light?” Morwenna asked.
The revenant laughed.
The sound was wet and small, as though something had drowned while trying to breathe.
Morwenna stepped backward. “You knew it was here.”
“I knew something was here.”
“You knew.”
“I suspected.”
“You brought me to this house.”
“I summoned you to this house.”
“Why?”

Sabelle looked at her then, truly looked. “Because the Iron-Ring Cartel has been buying pieces of
Gloamreach from you, and I wanted to know whether you understood what you were selling.”
Morwenna’s eyes hardened. “You already knew.”
“I knew you were selling intelligence.”
The silence that followed had a blade’s edge.
The Fleet Admiral’s expression did not change. It did not need to. Confession had entered the room
without being spoken.
Outside, wind worried at the shutters. Beyond them lay the Pale Coast, all salt glare and dead water, and
Gloamreach sealed behind its quarantine lines. The town was a core location despite the silence around it,
guarded by a garrison of 2,483. No vessel was meant to approach its shore without sanction. No
messenger was meant to leave it. Yet the Iron-Ring Cartel had found ways to send questions through
walls.
Morwenna had answered.
“How much?” Sabelle asked.
“Enough to keep men alive.”
“Whose men?”
“The men under my command.”
“Your command does not extend to the Cartel.”
“It extends to whatever prevents a slaughter.”
“Does it?”
Morwenna’s hand slipped from her sword. “You think this is about coin.”
“I think coin is the cleanest part of it.”
Beneath them, the revenant began to whisper.
The words were too low to make out, but the rhythm carried through the boards. A litany, perhaps. Or a
list. Sabelle had learned that the dead did not always distinguish between prayer and indictment.
Morwenna heard it too.
“What have you done to it?”
“Bound it.”
“With what?”
“Law.”
“That is not what binds the dead.”
“No,” Sabelle said. “Names do.”
They drew the Diadem of Sorrowgate from beneath their coat. It lay in their palm like a piece of winter: a
reliquary, narrow and pale, its metal filigree shaped around a dark inner hollow. The Diadem of

Sorrowgate had been forged in 281 AS. Its attunement cost was 9. Sabelle had paid it willingly, though the
payment had left them unable to dream for a season.
The diadem trembled.
Below, the revenant answered.
Morwenna stared at the artifact. “You used that on it?”
“I used what was required.”
“And the Crown?”
“The Crown of Burned Names holds the boundary.”
“The diadem holds the name.”
Sabelle closed their fingers around it. “The diadem holds what remains of one.”
A crack opened along the floorboard between them.
Black vapor leaked through.
Morwenna drew her blade.
Sabelle did not.
The thing below pulled once against the chains. The house groaned around them. Somewhere in the walls,
old nails shifted. A smell rose from the seam: brine, wet ash, and the sweet rot of flowers left too long in a
sealed room.
“Tell me,” Morwenna said, “what did you bring into Gloamreach?”
“You brought something into Gloamreach.”
“I brought orders.”
“You carried them.”
“For the Ashen Vanguard.”
“For House Morvain.”
“For the Silent Choir.”
Morwenna’s gaze flicked toward the crown. “And for the Bleeding Crown?”
Sabelle said nothing.
The five powers had learned to speak of the Pale Coast as though it were a border between them. The
Ashen Vanguard claimed the roads. House Morvain claimed the old blood. The Silent Choir claimed the
dead, whenever the dead could be made useful. The Iron-Ring Cartel claimed whatever could be moved.
The Bleeding Crown claimed the right to punish anyone who disputed the claim.
Gloamreach belonged to none of them.
That was why all of them wanted it.
The board split.

A pale hand rose through the gap.
Its fingers were corded with black veins. Salt crusted the nails. A ring of iron had been driven through the
little finger, and a chain ran from it into the dark.
Morwenna’s blade flashed down.
Sabelle caught her wrist.
“Do not.”
The revenant’s hand remained between them.
“Morwenna,” it said.
The Fleet Admiral strained against Sabelle’s grip. “Let me go.”
“No.”
“It knows me.”
“Yes.”
“It should not.”
“No.”
Morwenna’s voice broke for the first time. “Then what is it?”
Sabelle released her.
The hand withdrew. The chain clattered down into silence.
For several breaths, neither of them moved.
Then something beneath the floor began to scratch.
One stroke.
A pause.
Another stroke.
Morwenna looked at the boards. “It is writing.”
Sabelle knelt.
The Crown of Burned Names warmed against their skull. Its wards stirred, not in warning but in
recognition. Sabelle pressed their palm to the floor and felt the revenant’s will move beneath it like a
drowned body turning in deep water.
Letters appeared in the dust.
Not carved. Remembered.
MORWENNA.
Then another line formed beneath it.
NOT THE FIRST.

Morwenna made a sound that might have been anger or grief.
Sabelle stared at the words until the candlelight blurred.
The cellar door opened by itself.
Below, chains began to ring in every corner of the dark.
Morwenna stood at the foot of the stairs.
The dark beyond the open door had changed. It no longer waited like an absence. It breathed, slow and
patient, drawing the candle flame toward itself. Each chain answered the breath with a small metallic
shiver.
Sabelle rose. “You know this place.”
“I know what was buried beneath it.”
“That is not the same thing.”
“No.” Morwenna’s face had gone pale beneath the soot. “It is worse.”
The letters in the dust stirred. MORWENNA broke apart, its grains crawling into new shapes.
BORN: 288 AS
Sabelle read it aloud.
Morwenna closed her eyes.
“I was born in 288 AS,” she said. “In the ash winter, when the old king’s pyres burned for thirteen days.
My mother swore the smoke entered the house before I did. She said I came into the world already
choking.”
A chain snapped somewhere below.
The sound travelled up through the foundations.
Sabelle looked at the black stairwell. “What was buried?”
“Names.”
“Whose?”
Morwenna descended one step. “Everyone the Crown required forgotten.”
The Crown of Burned Names tightened around Sabelle’s skull. Behind their eyes, dead voices began to
murmur. They heard fragments: a miller’s daughter, a deserter, a saint with a butcher’s hands. Names
without bodies. Crimes without graves.
At the bottom of the stairs, a second candle burned on a stone ledge.
Its flame was green.
Around it stood twelve iron chairs, each occupied by a figure wrapped in funeral cloth. Their heads hung
low. Their chains ran from throat to throat, binding them into a circle.
The thirteenth chair was empty.
Morwenna entered the circle.

Every corpse lifted its head.
“Do not,” Sabelle whispered.
“If I do not sit,” Morwenna said, “the house will choose someone else.”
The cloth over the nearest corpse split. Beneath it was a woman’s face, shrivelled and blackened, with
Morwenna’s eyes.
“Not the first,” the dead woman rasped.
Morwenna lowered herself into the empty chair.
The chains surged.
They pierced her wrists, her ribs, the hollow beneath her tongue. No blood came. Only smoke, pouring
from her wounds and filling the cellar with the stink of burnt roses.
Sabelle reached for her, but the Crown dragged their hand away.
Letters appeared across Morwenna’s brow.
MORWENNA ASHGROVE BORN: 288 AS REMEMBERED: NEVER
Morwenna looked at Sabelle through the smoke.
“Now,” she said, “you know where the first name is buried.”
The cellar door slammed shut above them.
In the darkness, something began to climb.

Chapter 14
The dead of Blackport had never learned to keep quiet.
They whispered through wet stone, through the iron grates beneath the floor, through the black water that
gathered in the old cisterns and breathed up the stink of salt, ash, and old blood. Isolde Fellgard the
Unforgiven heard them whenever the night drew close enough to the walls.
Not voices. Never voices.
A pressure behind the eyes. A pulse in the teeth. The remembered weight of a blade entering flesh and
finding, beneath skin, the warm resistance of a life that had not yet agreed to end.
They stood alone in the records chamber with one gloved hand resting on the table. Their other hand held
a narrow silver knife.
The knife had not been drawn for murder. Not yet.
Its point touched the map before them, where the coast had been reduced to a crooked line of ink. Pale
Coast. Gloamreach. Cindermere Hold. The names had been written and rewritten by hands that believed
ink could command the world to remain legible.
Beyond the slit windows, rain moved across the darkness like a curtain being drawn by an unseen servant.
Isolde closed their eyes.
They were back in Blackport.
The walls had been red with reflected fire. Broken banners dragged along the mud. Men cried out beneath
the hooves of frightened horses, and the sea, close beyond the streets, hammered the harbor pilings with
the patience of a thing waiting to be fed.
They had fought in The Purge of Blackport, fighting for House Morvain.
The words were written in the record before them. The clerk had given the sentence its own line, as though
that distinction mattered. As though the dead cared which banner had been held above the hand that killed
them.
Isolde remembered the banner. They remembered the taste of soot. They remembered kneeling in the
flooded street with blood running from their palm into the black water—not their own blood, though they
had been cut badly enough to feel it.
Blood-Mage, the old records called them.
The name had once been a warning. Later it became a title. Now it was spoken as if it were a sentence
from which no appeal could be made.
Their reflection trembled in the shallow water pooled atop the table. The face that looked back was pale
and severe, its eyes dark beneath the hood. The face of an Unforgiven Blood-Mage. The face of someone
who had learned to make grievance useful.
A latch clicked behind them.
Isolde did not turn. “You are late.”
“I was not told there would be a clock.”

Ossric Ashgrove entered carrying three ledgers against his chest. He moved with the careful discomfort of
a man accustomed to balancing weight but not to being watched while he did it. He was a quartermaster,
and his hands bore the evidence: ink beneath the nails, grease along the knuckles, a small white scar where
a crate-hook had bitten him.
Ossric Ashgrove had been born in 333 AS. The date sat in a column among other dates, neat and
bloodless. Isolde had seen it earlier that evening and wondered whether he knew how many people had
died before he took his first breath.
He set the ledgers down.
“Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched asked for the casualty rolls.”
“Then Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched should have come for them.”
“The Arch-Prelate does not come to records chambers.”
“An Arch-Prelate who forged their own lineage papers should be less particular about where they stand.”
Ossric’s mouth tightened. He had no canonical temperament, the records would have said, if records were
honest enough to admit ignorance. He only looked tired.
“Lower your voice.”
“Why? Are the stones loyal to Malchior?”
“The stones are loyal to whoever owns the blood in the mortar.”
Isolde looked at him then.
Ossric lowered his gaze first.
A second figure waited beyond the doorway, broad in the shoulders, wrapped in a dark mantle damp with
rain. No physical features had been recorded for Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless, though his authority
entered every room before he did. He was a Warden-Commander, and command clung to him like frost.
Born in 258 AS, the record said.
The Oathless. The name had been given to him by mouths that feared him, or by his own enemies, or
perhaps by the hand that first set it down. Names were weapons with handles hidden inside them.
Ignatz stepped into the chamber.
“Leave us,” he told Ossric.
Ossric remained beside the table. “I was ordered to deliver the ledgers.”
“You have delivered them.”
“That is not the same as being dismissed.”
Ignatz’s gaze shifted to him. “You have become precise.”
“I have always been precise.”
“Then you have become brave.”
The quartermaster said nothing. Isolde watched the silence pass between them. It had the brittle quality of
ice over deep water.

Ignatz moved to the table. His gloved finger rested on the map, near the Pale Coast.
“Gloamreach,” he said.
The word seemed to draw the room inward.
Gloamreach lay on the Pale Coast, quarantined behind its own silence. Its garrison numbered 2,483. The
number had been written in red, then circled twice, as if arithmetic could serve as a ward. No ships were to
make harbor there. No message was to leave without inspection. No dead were to be carried beyond its
sealed roads.
“Gloamreach is still closed,” Isolde said.
“It is a core location.”
“So the ledgers claim.”
“The ledgers claim many things.”
Ignatz looked at them. Beneath the calm of his face, something moved and vanished. A thought. A
calculation. Isolde could smell wet wool and the faint metallic tang of chain beneath his mantle.
He secretly sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel.
The knowledge had come to Isolde in pieces: a missing dispatch, a convoy diverted before its orders were
issued, a seal broken and pressed shut again with wax too smooth to trust. Ignatz had made a career of
guarding thresholds. It was almost elegant that he had learned to profit from opening them.
“Why bring me here?” Isolde asked.
“Because you fought at Blackport.”
“I did more than fight.”
“That is what the record says.”
“The record is shy.”
Ossric glanced at the ledgers. “The record says Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven fought in The Purge of
Blackport, fighting for House Morvain.”
The exactness of it struck harder than accusation.
For an instant, Isolde saw the face of their liege as it had been in the last chamber: astonished, not afraid.
That had been the worst of it. Fear could have been forgiven. Surprise had no such mercy.
They had plotted the death of their own liege.
The secret had lived beneath every oath they spoke afterward, warm as a buried coal.
Isolde pressed the silver knife into the map until its point pierced the parchment.
“Read the rest,” they said.
Ossric hesitated.
Ignatz did not. “The War of Drowned Light began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS, with 64617 casualties.
The conflict collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals. The Silent Choir is recorded as the victor.”

“The spark was secretly staged by The Silent Choir,” Isolde said.
Rain tapped the windows.
The old war entered the room without opening the door: drowned radiance, broken banners, triumph
stripped of all triumph. The Silent Choir had won, according to the record. The dead had not received the
victory. They had received reprisals, then more reprisals, until every surviving account sounded like a
confession spoken through a mouthful of mud.
Ignatz studied the map. “You know the figures.”
“I know what they buried under them.”
“64617.”
“Numbers are coffins with no bodies inside.”
Ossric’s fingers moved over the nearest ledger. “Cindermere Hold appears in the old garrison rolls.”
“Cindermere Hold was founded in 246 AS among The High Spires,” Ignatz said. “Its garrison once
numbered 8878.”
“Now it is abandoned,” Isolde said.
“And not a core holding,” Ossric added.
The quartermaster spoke as though reciting inventory. Isolde wondered what it meant to carry ruin in
columns: eight thousand eight hundred and seventy-eight absent from a fortress; two thousand four
hundred and eighty-three sealed behind quarantine; sixty-four thousand six hundred and seventeen
reduced to a line no clerk would dare smudge.
“Why show me this?” Isolde asked.
Ignatz unfolded a narrow strip of parchment. It bore no seal.
“Because someone has altered the Blackport account.”
Isolde felt the room grow colder.
“Altered how?”
“A name removed. A command reassigned. A company moved from one street to another.”
“Companies do not move on paper.”
“People do. Then paper follows.”
“Whose name?”
Ignatz did not answer.
Beyond him, Ossric’s face had gone still. The quartermaster knew something, or feared that he did. His
eyes remained fixed on the parchment.
Isolde reached for it.
Ignatz’s hand closed over the strip first.
The motion was fast enough to be an insult.

Blood stirred beneath Isolde’s skin. It rose in their veins with the familiar eager pressure, answering the
sudden heat in their anger. A drop welled at the base of their thumb where the glove seam had split. It
hung there, dark and shining.
Ignatz noticed.
“Do not,” he said.
“I have done worse.”
“Yes.”
The word carried no accusation. That made it worse.
The lamp flame bent toward Isolde. Shadows climbed the walls. In the wavering light, the maps seemed to
breathe: coastlines flexing, mountain ranges opening and closing like ribs.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched would want the rolls because lineage was a kind of battlefield,
and forged blood could be defended only by making every other bloodline look uncertain. Born in 289 AS,
Malchior wore sanctity like a garment tailored by a liar. The Arch-Prelate had forged their own lineage
papers. Isolde had seen the old seals. They had seen where the ink had been made to imitate age.
The five powers watched one another through the cracks of the realm: the Ashen Vanguard, House
Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown. Each claimed to be holding back
the dark. Each kept one hand inside it.
Ignatz released the parchment.
“Read it,” he said.
Isolde took the strip.
The writing was cramped. The ink had bled at the edges, but one line remained clear.
Their name.
Not their title. Not Unforgiven.
Isolde Fellgard.
A mark followed it, shaped like a hook driven through a circle.
They knew that mark.
The blood in their glove began to move.
Ossric whispered, “What does it mean?”
Isolde held the parchment closer to the lamp. The hook seemed to twist, becoming almost a letter, almost a
wound.
Behind the walls, something knocked once.
Then again.
Ignatz reached for his sword.
Isolde did not move. They were listening to the blood, to the old cisterns, to Blackport calling across the
years with the drowned patience of the dead. The mark on the parchment opened like an eye, and from

somewhere beneath the floor came a voice that was not a voice—
“Your liege,” it said, and the lamp went out.
The darkness did not fall. It thickened.
Isolde felt it gather against their face, warm as breath. Ignatz’s sword came free with a dry whisper, and
Ossric made a small sound behind them—the involuntary noise of a man discovering that his body had
betrayed him before his mind could choose courage.
“Hold,” Isolde said.
Their voice returned from beneath the floor.
Hold.
The blood in their glove tightened. It crawled along the seams, seeking the pulse in their wrist. Every drop
remembered the mark. Every drop had become an ear.
Ignatz shifted. “What is below us?”
“A question,” said Isolde.
“No.”
The word came from the dark at their feet.
Not the voice beneath the floor. Ignatz’s voice.
Isolde turned toward him. They could not see his face, but they felt the scrape of his breath, controlled and
shallow. A Warden-Commander did not fear darkness. A Warden-Commander feared what darkness
might reveal.
“Put away the sword,” Isolde said.
“You heard it.”
“I heard you.”
“I did not speak.”
“Not with your mouth.”
Something moved below them. The flagstones groaned in their sockets. Ossric stumbled against the table,
and glass shattered under his heel.
“I was born in 333 AS,” he said, too quickly, as if reciting an inventory might preserve him. “I have no
part in this. I am a quartermaster. I keep stores. I count grain. I do not open—”
The floor knocked once.
Ossric swallowed the rest.
Isolde knelt. Cold seeped through their trousers. Beneath the stone, water whispered through old channels.
They remembered the cisterns under Blackport: drowned masonry, silted steps, the pale hands that had
risen where no living bodies remained. Their blood remembered more than they did. That was the curse of
it. Blood kept every door it had ever touched.
A thin red thread slipped from their glove and crept between the stones.

The voice beneath them spoke again.
“Your liege.”
Isolde laid two fingers against the crack.
The answer came as pain.
They saw a chamber lit by six candles, though none burned with flame. They saw a hand signing a decree.
They saw the ring on that hand, dull with old blood. They saw their own fingers close around the throat
beneath it.
No face. No name.
Only the pressure.
The memory was not theirs. Or it was theirs, and the darkness had stripped away the mercy of recognition.
Ignatz caught their shoulder. “What did you see?”
Isolde rose slowly. “A door.”
“To where?”
“To the part of you that you sell.”
His grip tightened.
Ossric breathed, “Commander?”
Ignatz let Isolde go. “You are speaking madness.”
“Am I?”
The darkness seemed to lean toward him.
Isolde could smell iron now—not blood, not exactly, but the mineral scent of wet chains. Somewhere far
beneath the hold, a lock turned. The sound traveled through the stone with patient intimacy.
They remembered the first time Ignatz had come to them with a sealed packet and a warning not to ask
who had paid for its contents. He had called it necessity. Men with command called every betrayal by that
name. They built their honor around the wound and asked everyone else to admire the scar.
“Tell me,” Isolde said, “what does the Iron-Ring Cartel buy from you?”
Ossric went still.
Ignatz did not.
A blade of darkness seemed to pass between them.
“You have mistaken me for someone who can be threatened.”
“No,” Isolde said. “I have mistaken you for someone who still believes threats are necessary.”
The flagstones shuddered.
This time the voice did not come from beneath them. It breathed directly against Isolde’s ear.
Your liege.

The blood in their glove burst through the leather.
It spilled in a red crescent across the parchment. The hook-and-circle mark drank it. For a moment, the
symbol became bright enough to see. The parchment curled inward, not burning but folding around an
absence.
A face emerged in the black.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched.
Isolde knew the image though they had never trusted the person. The Arch-Prelate’s sanctified authority
had always seemed to strain against the shape of its own lie. The face blurred at the edges. Beneath it,
letters surfaced and dissolved.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched, born in 289 AS.
Then the image changed.
A hand lifted a document toward candlelight. The seal was perfect. The ink was old. The lineage was
false.
“He forged his own lineage papers,” Isolde whispered.
Ignatz’s sword lowered by a fraction. “What?”
The parchment showed another hand writing over the first. The letters crawled like insects.
Forged.
Then the face vanished.
Ossric pressed himself against the wall. “Who is your liege?”
Isolde looked at him. “You heard the voice.”
“I heard a word.”
“A word can be a chain.”
The floor opened.
Not wide. Not enough for a body. A seam appeared between the stones, and from it rose a breath of
drowned air. The chamber filled with the smell of black water and old ash. Isolde’s stomach clenched.
Their blood-thread vanished into the crack.
Below, something scraped upward.
Ignatz stepped in front of Ossric.
It was almost noble.
That was what made it obscene.
Isolde watched him take the stance of a guardian, watched the old reflex settle across his body like armor.
Yet beneath the coat, beneath the insignia, beneath every oath he had worn until it frayed, the Iron-Ring
Cartel waited with its open hand. Intelligence was a kind of blood. Once sold, it did not return to the vein.
“How much?” Isolde asked.

Ignatz’s face remained invisible.
“How much what?”
“For the names. The routes. The positions of men who believed your office meant safety.”
The scraping stopped.
He said, “You know nothing.”
“I know you secretly sell intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
Ossric gasped.
The sound was swallowed by the crack.
Ignatz’s sword came up.
Isolde did not move. Their blood slid from the torn glove and hung in the air between them, a dark red
filament trembling toward the blade.
“Put it away,” they said.
“You should not have said that name.”
“Which name? The Cartel’s? Or yours?”
The darkness behind Ignatz stirred. A second figure took shape there—not seen, only inferred from the
way the air bent around it. The voice spoke through his shadow.
“Your liege.”
Ignatz turned.
For the first time, command abandoned him.
Isolde saw the opening and understood that all betrayals were made of such openings: a breath withheld, a
hand unguarded, a man facing the wrong direction.
They had plotted the death of their own liege.
The knowledge rose in them without shame and without pardon. It had not been an impulse, nor an
accident born of war. It had been plotted. Considered. Nurtured in silence until the deed became inevitable
enough to resemble fate.
Their liege had been a door, too.
Perhaps every throne was.
“Isolde,” Ignatz said.
Their name sounded like an accusation in his mouth.
“No,” they answered. “Not tonight.”
The seam widened. Black water pushed through, carrying scraps of parchment and pale threads that
caught on the stones. One fragment struck Isolde’s boot. They bent and lifted it.
A map.

The coast had been drawn in faded ink. Along the margin, a single notation remained legible.
Gloamreach.
The name was followed by three words: Pale Coast. Quarantined. Core.
Then, beneath them:
Garrison: 2,483.
Ossric leaned closer despite himself. “Gloamreach.”
“Do not touch it,” Isolde said.
“I have not.”
“You are thinking about it.”
“I am a quartermaster.”
“As you keep reminding us.”
The map darkened where Isolde’s blood touched it. A second location appeared farther inland, elevated
above a jagged line of peaks.
Cindermere Hold.
Founded in 246 AS among The High Spires.
Garrison once numbered 8878.
Abandoned. Not a core holding.
The ink bled down the parchment like tears. The hold’s silhouette rose in the center of the map: blackened
towers, empty embrasures, a ruin lifted beyond reach. Immense strength hollowed into stone.
Ignatz stared at it. “Why show us this?”
“Because it wants to be remembered,” Isolde said.
“What does?”
“Everything.”
For an instant, another image came: banners drowned in pale radiance, fields split by old trenches, soldiers
moving beneath a light that had no sun behind it. The vision bore a name, etched across the dark in letters
of salt.
The War of Drowned Light.
It began in 225 AS.
It ended in 235 AS.
64617 casualties.
The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor.
But behind the banners, behind the drowned radiance and broken standards, veiled hands arranged the first
spark. The war’s spark had been secretly staged by The Silent Choir. The victory was only the cleanest lie

left standing after the reprisals.
