Isolde tasted ash.
“The Silent Choir,” Ignatz said, reading the name as it formed.
“Their war,” said Isolde. “Their victory. Their spark.”
Ossric’s eyes shone in the dark. “How can a dead war speak?”
“It never died.”
The vision collapsed.
The five powers seemed to gather at the edge of thought: The Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, The
Silent Choir, The Iron-Ring Cartel, and The Bleeding Crown. Their names did not appear on the
parchment, yet the blood made room for them. They pressed against one another in the darkness,
contending over ruins that had outlived the hands that first claimed them.
A drop fell from above.
It struck Isolde’s cheek.
They wiped it away and smelled iron.
Ignatz’s sword arm began to tremble.
“Commander,” Ossric whispered.
“I know.”
“No,” Isolde said. “You do not.”
From the open seam, a hand emerged.
It was not flesh. It was a shape made of wet shadow, fingers long and jointed, the nails packed with silt. It
reached toward Isolde’s glove.
The blood leapt to meet it.
Pain went through them so violently their knees struck the floor. Their mouth filled with copper. Beneath
their skin, every vein opened like a red road.
The hand touched their wrist.
And the voice, no longer beneath the floor, no longer inside the walls, spoke from within their own chest.
“Name your liege.”
Isolde saw Ignatz lift his sword.
They saw Ossric reach for the broken glass.
They saw the darkness turn its faceless attention toward the door.
Beyond it, footsteps approached—measured, unhurried, and familiar enough to make the blood in Isolde’s
glove begin to kneel.
The latch lifted.

Isolde’s blood tightened around their bones. The hand at their wrist withdrew, leaving a numbness that
was almost tenderness. Ignatz’s sword hung between them and the door, its edge trembling. Ossric
crouched beside the hearth with a shard of glass pinched in his fist, his breath coming in small, wet
catches.
The door opened inward.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched entered without haste.
The candlelight found the pale planes of their face and the dark fall of their vestments. Ash clung to the
hem as if the road had tried to bury them and failed. An Arch-Prelate should have carried the scent of oil,
incense, and clean stone. Malchior carried smoke. It threaded the chamber behind them.
The darkness beneath the floor went still.
“Name your liege,” it whispered from Isolde’s chest.
Malchior’s gaze settled on the glove, on the blood kneeling beneath its leather, and then on Isolde’s face.
“Do not,” Ignatz said.
It was not an order to Malchior. It was a plea addressed to whatever had entered with them.
Isolde rose slowly. Their knees had gone weak, but weakness was merely another form of exposure, and
they had survived too long by concealing both. The handprint on their wrist darkened. Five bruises
emerged beneath the skin, each one shaped like a narrow mouth.
“Your sword is drawn,” Malchior said.
Ignatz did not lower it. “Your presence was unannounced.”
“Doors are for those who believe themselves separate from what waits beyond them.”
Ossric swallowed. The glass trembled in his hand. He was a quartermaster; he knew the value of every
hinge, nail, ration, and blade in a room. He knew what could be counted. The thing below the floor had
made a ruin of counting.
Isolde looked at him and saw the fear he had tried to pack away like winter grain.
Then the voice spoke again.
“Name your liege.”
The word liege opened something behind their eyes.
They saw a table slick with wine. A seal broken under their thumb. A blade held not in anger but in
patience. The chamber where they had planned the death of their own liege had been colder than this one,
though no wind had touched it. They remembered the silence afterward—not grief, not triumph, but the
terrible relief of a door unbarred.
The secret had lived in them longer than any confession could survive.
Their blood knew it.
“Isolde,” Ignatz said.
There was warning in the name. Or recognition. With Ignatz, the two had become difficult to separate.

The blood under Isolde’s glove surged toward the sound.
Ignatz flinched.
A folded packet slipped from inside his coat and struck the floor.
The wax seal split.
Thin sheets slid across the stone. One came to rest against Isolde’s boot. The ink had been written in
several hands, neat as spear wounds. Cargo routes. Watch rotations. Names of stores and movements
reduced to marks. At the bottom of one page, the insignia of the Iron-Ring Cartel gleamed in black wax.
The chamber seemed to contract around it.
Ossric stared. “Warden-Commander.”
Ignatz’s sword lowered by a finger’s breadth.
“Do not mistake paper for treason.”
“Paper is how treason travels,” Isolde said.
His eyes found theirs. For the first time, command left his face. Beneath it was calculation, and beneath
calculation, the exhausted terror of a man who had sold pieces of the world and discovered that the world
kept receipts.
The darkness laughed softly inside Isolde’s ribs.
Malchior stepped over the papers. “The Iron-Ring Cartel buys information because information is cheaper
than armies.”
“You know their prices?” Isolde asked.
“I know the price of everything that claims to be sacred.”
There it was: the faint abrasion beneath the sanctity. The lineage papers. The forged ancestry hidden
beneath the Arch-Prelate’s robes, ink and seal fashioned into a bloodline where none could be proven.
Isolde had seen the uncertainty in Malchior’s gaze whenever old records were opened, the way their
fingers pressed flat against the pages as though touch might force falsehood to become inheritance.
The thing below knew it too.
“Name your liege,” it murmured.
Malchior’s mouth tightened.
“You are not the first priest to arrive carrying a counterfeit bloodline,” Isolde said.
Ossric made a sound like a cough.
Ignatz turned on them. “Enough.”
“No.” Isolde lifted the page with the toe of their boot. “We have all brought our hidden ledgers into this
room.”
Malchior’s eyes sharpened. “You speak as though yours is empty.”
Their wrist burned.

The blood on the glove pushed against the seams, eager to escape. In its red sheen, Isolde saw the old
campaign roads and the drowned banners. They saw The War of Drowned Light, which began in 225 AS
and ended in 235 AS, leaving 64617 casualties behind it. The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor. The
spark had been secretly staged by The Silent Choir, though the songs afterward had called it providence,
necessity, fate—any word that could wash blood from the hands of the living.
The war had not ended when the banners fell. It had collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals, each
killing remembered as an answer to another killing.
The thing beneath the floor stirred at the memory.
“Names,” it breathed. “All debts require names.”
A tremor ran through the stones.
Far below, something scraped its fingers along the underside of the world.
Isolde stepped toward the scattered papers. Their blood followed, a dark line moving through the cracks in
the floor.
“Why bring us here?” they asked.
Malchior did not look at the floor. “I did not.”
“Then why come?”
“Because the seal was broken.”
They meant the packet. Or perhaps something older.
Isolde bent to pick up another sheet. The ink blurred, then steadied. A location had been entered in the
margin: Cindermere Hold. Founded in 246 AS among The High Spires. Once its garrison had numbered
8878. Now abandoned, no longer a core holding. The figures stood together like a gravestone and an
accusation.
“Cindermere,” Ossric whispered.
Malchior looked at him.
He dropped the glass. It shattered across the floor, and the sound woke every shadow in the chamber.
“I have never been there,” Ossric said.
“No one asked,” Ignatz replied.
The quartermaster’s face had gone gray. “It is not a supply concern.”
“Everything is a supply concern,” Isolde said. “Even a ruin.”
Beneath them, the thing gave a slow, pleased pulse.
The page in Isolde’s hand warmed. Another entry surfaced beneath the first, as though the ink had been
waiting under the ink.
Gloamreach. Pale Coast. Quarantined. Garrison: 2,483.
The number was exact. The place felt exact too: sealed gates, pallid surf, watchfires kept behind walls,
every breath measured against what might enter with the tide.

Malchior’s hand moved toward the page.
Isolde burned it before they could touch it.
The parchment blackened without flame. Its ash climbed upward in a thin spiral and hung between them.
Malchior watched it rise.
“Blood-Mage,” they said.
The title was not accusation or praise. It was a door being tested.
“I have never hidden what I am.”
“No,” Malchior said. “Only why.”
Their words struck more deeply than they should have.
Isolde had been born in 286 AS. The fact had once been written in a registry beside a mark that meant
living, legitimate, and claimed. Now it felt like another piece of evidence against them. They had carried
grievance as others carried a family sword. Ambition had sharpened it. Betrayal had given it a handle.
Ignatz’s gaze flicked toward them. “You knew this place was awake.”
“I suspected.”
“And you brought us anyway.”
“I brought no one.”
The floor cracked.
A line opened from the hearth to the door. Red light shone inside it—not fire, not reflection, but the color
of blood held up to the sun. Ossric stumbled backward. Ignatz seized his collar and dragged him clear.
The voice rose through Isolde.
“Name your liege.”
Their teeth clicked together. The question had become a hook. It pulled at the place where obedience had
once lived.
House Morvain came to mind—not as liege, not as refuge, but as a banner beneath which they had fought
in The Purge of Blackport. The memory carried soot, iron, and the taste of men praying through broken
teeth. They had served a cause without surrendering the whole of themselves. That distinction had
mattered then.
It mattered less now.
Malchior came close enough for Isolde to smell the ash on their clothes.
“Say nothing,” the Arch-Prelate whispered.
“Why?”
“Because it is not asking you for allegiance.”
The red seam widened.
From somewhere beneath, a multitude drew breath.

Malchior’s expression changed. The sanctified mask slipped, revealing the person beneath it: not a fraud
exactly, but someone who had forged their own lineage papers and then lived long enough to fear the day
the forgery would acquire a voice.
“It is asking who owns the death you carry,” they said.
Isolde’s heart stopped.
The chamber vanished.
They were back at the table. Their hand was steady. The blade waited beneath the cloth. Their liege stood
on the other side, speaking of loyalty as though loyalty were a chain that grew stronger each time it cut the
skin.
Isolde had plotted the death. Not dreamed it. Not wished it in the privacy of hatred. Plotted it. Measured
the hour, the witnesses, the distance between mercy and suspicion.
The blood at their wrist opened its mouths.
“I own it,” Isolde said.
The darkness recoiled.
Every candle went out.
In the black, Ignatz swore. Ossric struck the wall. Malchior seized Isolde’s arm, but the touch sent a vision
through them: forged seals, a false descent, papers hidden beneath a vestment; a name built from ash and
forced into the shape of inheritance.
Then something below spoke with a voice that was no longer a whisper.
“Then kneel.”
The floor gave way beneath Isolde.
They fell only an inch before the blood caught them—every drop spilled in the chamber, every dark thread
beneath the stones, every buried memory with a pulse. Their body hung above the opening, suspended in a
red web.
Below waited a stair descending into absolute dark.
At its foot, far beneath the ruined hold, someone struck a bell.
Once.
Malchior’s grip tightened. Ignatz raised his sword. Ossric began to pray to a power he did not name.
Isolde looked into the darkness and understood that the footsteps beyond the door had never been
approaching them.
They had been ascending.

Chapter 15
The rain came down as ash.
It whispered against the shutters of the upper chamber, sifted through the cracks, and gathered in the
grooves of the table where the candles had burned low. Corvus Hollowmere the Pale watched the grey
flakes melt upon their glove. They became water, then vanished into the black leather.
The chamber had no windows large enough for a person to pass through. That was considered a comfort
by those who had built it. Corvus had never trusted comforts.
A single lamp burned beside the table. Its flame bent whenever the wind pressed against the walls.
Beneath it lay five seals impressed in wax: the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the
Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown. Five powers contending over what remained of the realm, each
calling its appetite by a different name.
A sixth seal lay broken.
Corvus touched the ragged wax with one finger.
“Who opened it?”
The door remained shut. Beyond it, footsteps paused, then resumed. Whoever had come had been taught
patience. That narrowed nothing. Patience was the first lesson of every court, every army, every
conspiracy that expected to survive its maker.
The latch lifted.
Hesper Wrenfield entered without haste, rain darkening the edges of their clothing. No insignia marked
them. No sword drew the eye. They carried only a leather tube beneath one arm.
“Outrider,” Corvus said.
“Hesper Wrenfield.” The reply was neither proud nor deferential. “You sent for me.”
“I sent for a report.”
“Then you sent for me.”
Corvus studied the young face before them and found no expression worth stealing. Hesper Wrenfield had
been born in 404 AS. The fact had been written in three ledgers, copied by three hands, and contradicted
by none. Their service as an Outrider had taken them through roads where men learned to lie with their
mouths closed.
“Put it down.”
Hesper placed the tube on the table.
It rolled through the ash and stopped against the broken seal.
Corvus did not open it. “You came from Gloamreach?”
“Yes.”
The word seemed to lower the temperature of the chamber.

Gloamreach lay on the Pale Coast, a core location sealed beneath quarantine. Its garrison numbered 2,483.
The number had been repeated so often that it had acquired the flat, bloodless sound of prayer. Two
thousand four hundred and eighty-three souls behind the barriers, while the coast watched them from
beyond the cordons and pretended not to listen for screaming.
“What did you see?”
“Nothing.”
“That is not a report.”
“It is the report.” Hesper’s gaze shifted to the lamp. “The gates remained closed. The quarantine remained
in force. No vessel left the shore. No messenger entered.”
“And yet you returned.”
“I was allowed to return.”
Corvus leaned back. The chair gave a dry complaint.
There were truths that arrived loudly, with horns and banners. They were rarely the dangerous ones. The
dangerous truths slipped beneath doors and waited for someone to notice that the room had begun to smell
of earth.
“Who allowed you?”
Hesper looked at the sealed tube. “The guard at the western gate.”
“Name?”
“I did not ask.”
For the first time, something moved in Hesper’s expression. Not fear. Perhaps the memory of a mistake.
Corvus opened the tube.
The parchment inside was narrow, folded twice, and stained at one corner with a dark residue. No script
marked the outer face. Inside, a sketch had been made in charcoal: a tower without a roof, a circle beneath

Cindermere Hold.
The hold had been founded in 246 AS among The High Spires. Its garrison had once numbered 8878.
Now it stood abandoned, no longer a core holding, its blackened silhouette lifted above the stone like the
corpse of some immense beast that had died upright.
Corvus placed the parchment flat.
“Where did you find this?”
“Gloamreach.”
“That was not my question.”
“It was under a floorstone in a guardroom.”
“Whose guardroom?”
“The western gate.”

The lamp flame shuddered.
Hesper continued. “The marks were fresh.”
“Fresh enough to be made by whom?”
“I saw no one.”
“No one is not a person.”
“No,” said Hesper. “It is what remained.”
Corvus let the silence thicken between them.
Under the floorstone, then. Beneath a gatehouse in a quarantined place. A drawing of Cindermere Hold,
though the abandoned hold was far from the Pale Coast, if distance still meant anything in the Ashen Era.
Roads had been broken by war, by flood, by old magic sleeping beneath the soil. Messages crossed the
realm by hands, by birds, by rumor, and sometimes by methods that left no corpse a priest could identify.
Corvus had been born in 351 AS. They remembered none of the world before their birth, but memory was
not required to inherit a wound. The old wars had entered every house like smoke.
“The War of Drowned Light began in 225 AS,” Corvus said.
Hesper did not answer.
“It ended in 235 AS. The records list 64617 casualties. Then the conflict collapsed into a decade of
guerrilla reprisals.” Corvus traced the charcoal circle. “The Silent Choir is recorded as the victor.”
“Recorded by whom?”
“By those who survived to write.”
“And the truth?”
Corvus looked at the broken seal bearing the Choir’s mark.
“The war’s spark was secretly staged by them.”
The words passed into the chamber and did not return.
Beneath their shirt, against the skin, the hidden oath tightened.
It had no metal clasp, no scar, no priestly witness. It lived in the architecture of silence: what Corvus did
not say, what they allowed others to believe, the names they buried before those names could become
evidence. The Silent Choir had not asked for worship. They had asked for obedience without consolation.
Corvus had sworn.
Hesper’s eyes remained on the parchment. “Then the drawing may be theirs.”
“Or someone wants us to believe it is.”
“Is that not the same thing?”
“No.” Corvus folded the parchment along its old crease. “Belief is a weapon. Ownership is merely a hand
around it.”
Hesper stood very still.

Outside, the ash-rain strengthened. It struck the shutters like fingernails.
Corvus opened the lowest drawer of the table. Within lay a square of winter-pale metal wrapped in dark

When the cloth was drawn back, the name had been etched along the metal in thin, severe letters:
The Sceptre of Final Winter.
It was a ward forged in 87 AS. Attunement to it costs 55.
Hesper drew a slow breath.
“You keep that here?”
“I keep many things.”
“That was not an answer.”
“It was the only one you were given.”
Corvus wrapped the ward again. The cold withdrew grudgingly, leaving the chamber clammy and close.
“The drawing,” they said. “Did it contain anything else?”
“A line of writing.”
“You omitted it.”
“I could not read it.”
“Show me.”
Hesper reached inside their coat and produced a scrap of cloth. It had been torn from something larger,
perhaps a banner, perhaps a sleeve. Upon it, stitched in thread the color of old blood, were four words.
Corvus read them once.
Then again.
The letters were not a command. They were a location without a name, a direction without a road. They
described the place where light failed beneath stone and where the dead were said to keep watch over the
living.
Corvus felt the oath turn beneath their ribs.
“What did you think it meant?” they asked.
“I did not think.”
“Everyone thinks.”
“Not when the wrong thought can be overheard.”
A useful answer. Perhaps an honest one.
Corvus rose. They were taller than Hesper by enough to make the difference inconvenient. The mirror on
the far wall returned a pale figure in a dark coat, the face sharpened by candlelight until it appeared carved

a hunger.
The five seals waited on the table.
The Ashen Vanguard would turn the drawing into a march.
House Morvain would turn it into a claim.
The Iron-Ring Cartel would turn it into a price.
The Bleeding Crown would turn it into a sentence.
The Silent Choir would turn it into silence.
Corvus lifted the parchment and held it over the lamp. The charcoal lines blurred. Beneath them, nearly
invisible, another mark surfaced where the heat touched the paper: a small black crescent pierced by a
vertical stroke.
Not a signature.
A summons.
Hesper saw it.
“You know that mark.”
Corvus let the parchment fall before the flame could take it.
“I know many marks.”
“Then tell me what this one says.”
The hidden oath tightened again, hard enough to make breathing an act of will.
Somewhere beyond the sealed chamber, the footsteps had stopped. The person outside was listening now.
Perhaps they had always been listening. Perhaps the walls had been built for that purpose.
Corvus turned toward the door.
“Hesper Wrenfield,” they said quietly, “when you left Gloamreach, did the western gate guard speak to
you?”
“No.”
“Did they watch you leave?”
“No.”
“Did they give you permission?”
Hesper’s silence became an answer.
Corvus reached for the latch.
From the corridor came a soft scrape, as if a fingernail had drawn a circle upon the wood.
The lamp guttered.
And from the other side of the door, a voice began to whisper the first words of the oath Corvus had
sworn—

The whisper did not falter.
“...and when the last ember drowns, the sworn hand shall—”
Corvus caught the latch.
Hesper Wrenfield moved behind them. Not quickly. Quickness belonged to panic, and panic was a
confession. The Outrider’s boots made no sound upon the rushes, but Corvus heard the leather draw tight
at the instep.
The voice beyond the door continued, soft as ash settling after a fire.
“—open what was sealed.”
Corvus’s hand remained on the iron.
A lesser fear would have been simpler. A knife beneath the ribs. A blade in a dark stairwell. Even poison
had the virtue of honesty: it entered the body and declared its purpose. This was worse. This was a hand
laid upon the hidden place inside them, fingers feeling for the knot.
The lamp smoked. Its flame leaned toward the door.
“Hesper,” Corvus said.
“Yes.”
“If I open this, do not speak.”
The Outrider breathed in. “Why?”
“Because whoever is there already knows too much.”
The voice stopped.
Silence pressed against the wood. In it, Corvus heard the small mortal noises of the room: oil ticking in the
lamp, Hesper’s breath held and released, the faint dry rasp of their own sleeve against the door. Beyond,
nothing. Not footsteps. Not the scrape of a weapon being drawn.
The absence was deliberate.
Corvus let the latch fall back into place.
A pale line showed beneath the door. Corridor light, thin and colourless, had found its way through the
gap. No shadow crossed it.
“Did you hear that oath before?” Corvus asked.
“No.”
“You recognized it.”
“I recognized you.”
The words struck more cleanly than accusation.
Corvus turned. Hesper stood near the table where the papers had been left in disorder, one hand resting
against the edge. The Outrider’s face was indistinct in the lamplight. That served them. Faces were
treacherous things; they invited the eye to search for innocence, and innocence was rarely present.

“You heard me swear it?” Corvus asked.
“I heard you say words.”
“Words are not an oath.”
“They were to you.”
For an instant, the chamber changed. The walls seemed to draw nearer, their old stone sweating a darkness
that the lamp could not warm. Corvus remembered a different room, though not its location, and a
darkness without walls. A voice had spoken then from within a silence deeper than sleep. No hand had
touched them. No blade had been held to their throat. They had knelt because the body understood certain
commands before the mind accepted them.
The Silent Choir had never demanded belief.
Only obedience.
Corvus had given it.
They moved away from the door and crossed to the table. The papers bore seals, routes, garrison marks,
small tidy lies arranged to look like administration. The Ashen Vanguard would call the arrangement
necessity. House Morvain would call it inheritance. The Iron-Ring Cartel would call it opportunity. The
Bleeding Crown had a word for everything, and none of those words made the dead less dead.
The Silent Choir did not name its hungers.
That was why the oath had survived.
“Why did you leave Gloamreach?” Corvus asked.
Hesper’s gaze shifted toward the door. “You asked me that already.”
“I am asking again.”
“Because I was ordered to carry a message.”
“By whom?”
“I was not told.”
“Who gave you the message?”
“I was not told.”
Corvus studied them. No tremor. No theatrical indignation. Hesper answered like someone who had
learned that the truth was not always a possession; sometimes it was merely the shape of the cage.
“And the message?”
“Burned.”
“By you?”
Hesper did not answer.
The voice beyond the door began again.
This time it did not speak the oath. It hummed.

The tune had no melody Corvus could have named. Three notes descending, then one held until the breath
should have failed. The sound was almost tender. That was the obscenity of it. The Silent Choir had
always understood that terror entered more deeply when offered gently.
Corvus saw, with unbearable clarity, the abandoned towers of Cindermere Hold rising among The High
Spires. Black stone against a bleached sky. Empty embrasures. Snow—or ash, or both—caught in the
teeth of the battlements. Once, its garrison had numbered 8878. Now the place held only wind, and
whatever remembered the men who had stood there.
The Winter Reckoning devastated Cindermere Hold in 271 AS.
The sentence surfaced whole, as if carved behind the eyes.
They had read it in a report whose ink had browned with age. The report had given no account of the
screams. No account of the cold. No account of what had been found beneath the keep, where the stone
had split into smooth black planes and every metal object had become too brittle to touch. It had recorded
devastation as a fact, then moved on.
Corvus had moved on as well.
They had been born in 351 AS, long after the Winter Reckoning, long after the War of Drowned Light had
become a wound used by every power according to appetite. Yet the past did not remain behind. It waited
in sealed rooms. It waited in oaths. It waited beneath the floorboards of every office where maps were
unfolded and redrawn.
Hesper watched them.
“You know the song,” the Outrider said.
“I know many songs.”
“That one?”
Corvus reached for a folded map. “It is not a song.”
The humming ceased.
A knock came at the door.
One touch.
Then another.
The lamp flame shrank until the room seemed to have been drowned in its own shadow.
“Spymaster,” said the voice outside.
The title was spoken without respect and without mockery. Simply placed between them.
Hesper straightened.
Corvus looked down at the map. Gloamreach had been marked along the Pale Coast in a blot of black ink.
The name was almost swallowed by the coastline, as though the parchment itself wished to close over it.
Quarantined. Isolated. Guarded against whatever the walls contained—or whatever wished to leave them.
“You should not have brought this here,” Corvus said.

“I did not bring it.”
“Then why did it follow you?”
Hesper’s mouth tightened. “You tell me.”
There it was: not fear. Not exactly. Something harder, less useful. Resentment perhaps, though Corvus
would not grant the feeling a name without proof.
Outside, the handle turned.
It stopped before the latch caught.
Corvus took the map and held it over the lamp. The parchment browned at once, curling inward. Hesper
stepped forward.
“What are you doing?”
“Removing a temptation.”
“You said it was only a map.”
“It was.”
The flame found the edge. Fire crawled across the inked coast, consuming the black mark of Gloamreach
first. The paper smelled of dust and bitter oil. Corvus watched the shape vanish. A place could be erased in
an instant. Not destroyed. Not changed. Only denied.
The door opened a finger’s width.
No face appeared in the gap.
A hand rested on the outer edge. Pale knuckles. Dark sleeve. No ring, no sigil, no sign by which allegiance
might be comfortably understood.
Corvus thrust the burning map into the basin.
The coals below exhaled sparks.
“Hesper,” they said, “when I tell you to run, you will go through the eastern passage.”
“There is no eastern passage.”
“There is now.”
The Outrider looked at them then—not at the door, not at the fire, but at Corvus. “You built one?”
“I arranged one.”
“That is not the same thing.”
“It is tonight.”
The hand beyond the door withdrew.
For one breath, nothing moved.
Then a voice spoke from the crack, so close that Corvus could hear the wetness in the throat.
“You swore to open what was sealed.”

Corvus felt the oath stir inside them. Not as memory. As command.
The hidden words had been buried beneath years of service, beneath reports carried through rain, beneath
the faces of the dead and the faces of those who had ordered their deaths. Corvus had believed
concealment was the same as mastery. A secret kept long enough became part of the keeper’s bones. It
could no longer be extracted without taking the skeleton with it.
The door opened wider.
The figure remained beyond the threshold, concealed by the angle of the corridor.
Hesper’s hand went to their weapon.
“Do not,” Corvus said.
The figure laughed softly.
It was not the laugh of a stranger.
Corvus knew that breath. Knew the measured pause before the final syllable. Knew the voice not by its
sound but by the wound it made in the mind.
The figure began the oath again.
This time, Corvus answered.
The first words left their mouth before permission could be denied, dry and quiet and perfectly formed.
Hesper recoiled.
The corridor light brightened. Somewhere beyond it, a second presence shifted. Then a third. The room’s
only door stood open now, and the darkness outside had gathered like an audience.
Corvus kept their eyes on the unseen speaker.
“What did you do with the message?” they asked.
The answer came as another line of the oath.
Hesper seized Corvus’s sleeve. “You know them.”
Corvus did not look down.
They knew the voice. They knew the cadence. They knew what waited at the end of the words, where the
oath became command and command became blood.
The Sceptre of Final Winter had been forged in 87 AS. Its ward still haunted every account of cold made
absolute, every instrument designed to end rather than protect. Corvus had spent years learning how men
concealed such things from one another. They had never learned how to conceal them from the Silent
Choir.
The unseen speaker whispered the next phrase.
Corvus felt the old obedience rise.
Their fingers tightened around the edge of the table until the wood bit through the glove.
“Run,” they said.

Hesper did not move.
“Now.”
The Outrider pulled the hidden latch beneath the table.
Stone groaned behind the wall.
The figure in the corridor stepped forward at last, and Corvus saw a pale mask where a face should have
been. No mark identified it. No emblem declared the hand behind it. Only the mouth showed through the
narrow opening, and the mouth was smiling.
Hesper vanished into the dark passage.
Corvus turned toward the mask.
The oath reached its final line.
And their own lips began to speak.
The final line passed through Corvus like a blade drawn slowly from the ribs.
“By drowned light, I open the door.”
The mask tilted.
Not surprise. Recognition.
Behind Corvus, the passage swallowed the sound of Hesper’s retreat. Stone settled with a deep, patient
thud. Dust sifted from the archway and silvered the black of Corvus’s gloves. They stood alone with the
pale face, the table between them, and the oath burning its old path through their mouth.
The figure lifted one hand.
A strip of dark cloth hung from its wrist. Upon the cloth, stitched in thread almost too dim to see, were
five broken marks: the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, the
Bleeding Crown. The powers had no common seal. No common law. Yet all of them had learned to fear a
door opened in darkness.
“You have delayed,” said the mask.
The voice was altered—not made deeper, not made higher, but emptied of the small warmth that proved a
living throat. It might have belonged to anyone. That was the point.
Corvus felt their pulse in the pale skin beneath their jaw.
“I have served,” they said.
“You have served yourself.”
The accusation found its mark because it was not wholly false.
Their service had worn many colors. They had bowed beneath the blackened banners of the Ashen
Vanguard, spoken honeyed poison into the courts of House Morvain, bought silence with the Iron-Ring
Cartel’s coin, and listened for the Bleeding Crown’s hunger beneath every proclamation. Yet the Silent
Choir had been the first voice beneath all voices. The hidden cadence. The hand that had taught them
obedience before they understood that obedience could be a chain.

They had sworn the oath in secret. They had kept it through years of ash, intrigue, and blood.
They had been born in 351 AS. The number had never seemed important until the Choir began counting
their life back toward them, year by year, as though a soul were only another ledger.
“I have served,” Corvus repeated.
The mask’s mouth smiled.
“Then serve now.”
A small object slid across the table.
It struck the wood with a sound no heavier than a fingernail.
Corvus did not touch it.
The object was wrapped in oilskin, bound with gray thread. Frost had formed along the edges despite the
room’s stale warmth. The cold moved over the table in a thin breath, raising the hairs along Corvus’s
wrists.
The Sceptre of Final Winter.
Even concealed, the ward announced itself. It had been forged in 87 AS, when the world was still learning
how to live inside the wound left by the Sundering. Attunement to it cost 55. Corvus had read the old

ice. The accounts had never agreed on what the ward protected. They agreed only on what it demanded.
The figure tapped the oilskin once.
“Take it to Gloamreach.”
Corvus’s gaze remained on the bundle. “Gloamreach is quarantined.”
“Yes.”
“Gloamreach lies on the Pale Coast.”
“Yes.”
“It is a core location.”
The mask did not answer.
Corvus heard the silence beneath the silence. They saw the bleak coast in their mind: pallid surf breaking
under a colorless sky, watchfires smothered behind walls, roads emptied by decree. Gloamreach’s garrison
numbered 2,483. Enough to make trespass costly. Not enough to make the quarantined place safe.
“And its garrison?” Corvus asked.
“2,483.”
The number entered the room and stayed there.
Corvus looked toward the sealed passage. Hesper Wrenfield had been born in 404 AS. An Outrider, young
enough that fear still showed itself in the body before discipline strangled it. Hesper had carried the
message because no courier sworn to any power could be trusted with it. An Outrider could cross a road
without becoming part of the road’s politics.

If Hesper reached the outer tunnels, they might live.
If the mask had anticipated the latch, they might already be dead.
“You sent the Outrider away,” Corvus said. “Why?”
“To make you choose.”
The cold around the bundle deepened.
Corvus had always believed that choice was merely obedience viewed from the other side. The Choir had
taught them that. Their oath had not been a chain, they had told themselves. It had been a blade placed in
their hand. The blade could be turned.
Outside, somewhere beyond the chamber, a horn sounded once.
The powers were moving.
The Ashen Vanguard would call it defense. House Morvain would call it inheritance. The Iron-Ring Cartel
would call it an opportunity. The Bleeding Crown would call it justice, if justice could be made to bleed in
public. And the Silent Choir would call nothing at all. It would let the others fill the air with their names
until every word became cover for the same quiet act.
Corvus reached for the bundle.
The oilskin was warm.
They stopped.
That warmth was worse than cold.
“Tell me what waits at Gloamreach.”
“The ward waits.”
“For whom?”
“For the hand that can bear its cost.”
“You said attunement costs 55.”
“I said nothing.”
“You did not need to.”
The mask leaned closer. A seam of darkness showed where cheek met throat. No skin. No breath. No
evidence that anything human inhabited the shell.
“The cost is not a number,” it said.
“Then why does the Choir preserve the number?”
“Because numbers comfort the living.”
The words struck an old place in Corvus, one they kept sealed beneath duty. They remembered ledgers
from the War of Drowned Light, their pages swollen with damp and red at the edges. The war had begun

when the ink did. The conflict had collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals, each killing answered by
another, each answer dressed as necessity.

The Silent Choir was recorded as the victor.
Corvus had once believed that victory meant a banner standing after all others fell. Later, they learned the
war’s spark had been secretly staged by the Silent Choir. The revelation had not come as thunder. It had
arrived in a folded report, a line without ornament, and the knowledge that thousands had died so the
Choir could prove that history was easiest to govern after it had been made afraid.
The memory turned their mouth dry.
“You staged the spark,” they said.
The mask remained still.
“Of the War of Drowned Light,” Corvus continued. “You began it, then let the reprisals consume what
remained.”
“Recorded history says the Silent Choir was the victor.”
“History says many things.”
“History is what survives the fire.”
The bundle waited beneath Corvus’s hand.
They thought of Cindermere Hold, founded in 246 AS among the High Spires. Once its garrison had
numbered 8878. The Winter Reckoning had devastated it in 271 AS, and now its towers stood empty
against the heights, blackened stone holding no core of power, no living claim worth defending. An
abandoned stronghold. A monument to the distance between a number and the bodies required to sustain
it.
Cindermere had seemed invincible until it became useful as a warning.
Gloamreach would not become another warning.
Not if Corvus could prevent it.
The oath tightened.
Their hand closed around the oilskin.
Frost crawled over the glove. Pain flashed through the fingers, then sank deeper, searching for bone. The
room narrowed to the bundle, the mask, the hidden passage, and the ancient command now waking under
their skin.
“Why me?” they asked.
For the first time, the figure seemed to hesitate.
Only the smallest motion. A pause in the smiling mouth.
Because Corvus was Spymaster. Because they were pale enough to be mistaken for a corpse in bad light.
Because they had survived every power that believed secrecy belonged to it. Because the Choir’s oath
lived inside them where no blade could cut it free.
The mask answered none of these.
“Because you have already touched the winter.”

Corvus looked down at the oilskin.
A thin white line had appeared across its surface. It resembled a crack in ice. Beneath it, something
breathed.
From beyond the wall came a muffled cry.
Hesper.
Corvus turned toward the passage.
The mask moved faster than thought. One gloved hand struck the table, and the wood split between them.
The impact flung dust into the air. Corvus stepped back, the bundle clutched against their chest, while the
hidden latch clicked again somewhere behind the stone.
Not opened.
Locked.
“Hesper,” Corvus whispered.
The name felt like a betrayal.
The mask reached for them.
Corvus raised the wrapped ward.
The frost exploded outward.
For one instant, the chamber filled with drowned radiance: white light without warmth, banners breaking
in a wind that did not exist, the black outline of Cindermere Hold suspended among the High Spires, its
empty windows burning with winter. Then the vision tore apart.
The bundle split.
Something beneath the oilskin pressed its length against Corvus’s palms.
The Sceptre of Final Winter did not look like a weapon. It looked like the memory of one: pale metal, a
narrow shaft, a head lost inside a crown of translucent thorns. Cold poured from it in waves.
The mask recoiled.
Corvus felt the ward enter them.
Not through the hands. Through the oath.
Their bones became hollow. Their blood slowed. Somewhere far away, in a place beneath language, a
choir began to sing without voices.
The cost was 55.
The number opened like a door.
Behind it waited the first memory Corvus had ever buried.
They heard Hesper strike the other side of the stone.
Once.
Twice.

Then silence.
Corvus turned the sceptre toward the masked figure.
The pale thorns opened.
And from within the ward, in Corvus’s own voice, the Silent Choir spoke the next command.
“Choose which door remains.”

left by the Sundering. Its doctrine is not custodial in the passive
sense. It defines containment as an active military obligation,
requiring militant discipline, controlled force, and uninterrupted
vigilance wherever dangerous remnants persist.

by the Sundering. Its authority derives from that oath, its appearance

bears the mark of that duty, and its conduct is governed by the
discipline required to enforce it. Vharenford remains the seat by which

stated purpose is restoration rather than accommodation.

its royalist claim is maintained.

The Iron-Ring Cartel
The Iron-Ring Cartel is a merchant cartel seated at Hollowreach. Its
doctrine is recorded as follows:
> The Iron-Ring Cartel — doctrine: Mercantile league running contraband
through the ruined trade roads.
The Cartel is a mercantile league organized around commerce conducted
across the remnants of the realm’s trade routes. Its operations concern
the movement, exchange, and concealment of contraband through roads
damaged or abandoned after the Sundering. The organization’s structure
is consequently commercial rather than feudal, with authority expressed
through control of trade, access, and passage.
Its visual identity is mercantile and hard-edged. Iron, sealed cargo,
marked ledgers, guarded wagons, and reinforced trade gear are
consistent with its cartel structure and contraband trade. These signs
are not ornamental. They indicate a faction whose public identity is
inseparable from the practical demands of commerce conducted beyond
lawful channels.
The Cartel’s demeanor is calculating and practical. It is comfortable
operating beyond lawful trade and does not present illegality as a
moral distinction requiring explanation. Decisions are assessed by
utility, risk, access, and return. Negotiation is therefore treated as
an instrument of commerce rather than a display of trust.

Office and Authority
The Silent Choir is a secretive priesthood whose religious authority is
exercised through control of the historical record. Its doctrine
assigns record, correction, suppression, and revision to a single
sacred function. History is therefore not treated as a fixed
inheritance. It is maintained as an instrument of order, subject to
examination and alteration by the Choir.
The Silent Choir records history. It censors history. It rewrites
history. These duties are not separate offices in the known account of
the faction, but expressions of one doctrine. The Choir’s authority
rests upon possession of the accepted version of events and upon the
restriction of competing versions.
The Silent Choir is seated at Vharencrag Fortress. Its seat is
associated with restrained religious practice, controlled access, and
the keeping of records. The visual identity of The Silent Choir is
priestly, restrained, and defined by secrecy and the keeping of
records. Its appearance communicates neither pageantry nor open force.
It presents the discipline of custody.
Conduct
The Choir is quiet, inscrutable, and deliberate in its handling of
truth. Statements are measured. Omissions are consequential. Disclosure
is treated as an act requiring the same care as inscription. The
faction’s silence is therefore not an absence of policy; it is a method
of policy.
Its custodians maintain a severe distinction between what may be
preserved, what may be concealed, and what may be rewritten. The

distinction is administered through religious authority rather than
public consent. For this reason, the Choir’s records possess both
archival and doctrinal weight.

remains a material consideration in all surviving accounts. Its victory
in The War of Drowned Light is therefore recorded as an established
factional result, while the form and interpretation of that result
remain subject to the Choir’s doctrine.

# **Transcript of the Inquiry into the Winter Reckoning**

*[The chamber is cold. Frost whitens the iron rails before the bench. A seal bearing the iron mark of the Iron-Ring Cartel hangs above the record table.]*

**CLERK:** Let the matter be entered: an inquiry concerning **The Winter Reckoning**.

**PRESIDING MAGISTRATE:** State the conflict under examination.

**CLERK:** The Winter Reckoning began in **270 AS** and ended in **283 AS**. It left **27,987 casualties**. The Iron-Ring Cartel was the victor.

**PRESIDING MAGISTRATE:** And why is the victor summoned before this bench?

**PROSECUTOR:** Because victory was not won by strength alone. It was decided by a betrayal at the eleventh hour.

**CARTEL ADVOCATE:** Objection. “Betrayal” is a word for mourners and tavern singers, not a finding.

**PRESIDING MAGISTRATE:** Overruled. The word may stand until proved false.

*[A witness is brought forward. Their hands are wrapped against the cold.]*

**PROSECUTOR:** You served among the allies of the Iron-Ring Cartel during the Winter Reckoning?

**WITNESS:** I served where I was ordered.

**PROSECUTOR:** Did the wells supplying those allies become poisoned?

**WITNESS:** They did.

**PROSECUTOR:** By whose hand?

**WITNESS:** The hand wore iron.

*[A stir passes through the chamber. The Cartel’s advocate rises sharply.]*

**CARTEL ADVOCATE:** This witness saw no face. The iron mark is worn by many.

**WITNESS:** Not as it was worn then. The mark was stamped on the barrels. A ring within a ring. The water tasted of bitter metal. Men drank, and afterward their tongues blackened.

**PROSECUTOR:** Were these wells behind enemy lines?

**WITNESS:** No.

**PROSECUTOR:** Whose wells?

**WITNESS:** Our allies’ wells.

*[Silence. Frost cracks somewhere beyond the shutters.]*

**PRESIDING MAGISTRATE:** Let the record show the concealed truth alleged: the victors poisoned the wells of their own allies.

**CARTEL ADVOCATE:** Alleged, yes. Concealed, perhaps. But the dead cannot testify to banners, orders, or intent.

**PROSECUTOR:** The dead testify in number.

**CLERK:** The recorded casualties are **27,987**.

**PRESIDING MAGISTRATE:** The court will not mistake arithmetic for innocence.

**CARTEL ADVOCATE:** Nor suspicion for judgment. The Iron-Ring Cartel won the conflict.

**PROSECUTOR:** Precisely. It won after its allies were weakened, at the eleventh hour, beneath the appearance of shared ruin.

*[The Magistrate studies the iron seal. No one speaks of removing it.]*

**PRESIDING MAGISTRATE:** The Winter Reckoning began in **270 AS** and ended in **283 AS**. Its outcome was decided by a betrayal at the eleventh hour. Whether victory excuses the poison, this court shall determine.

**CLERK:** Entered and sealed.

# Weeping Lurker (creature)

The **[[Weeping Lurker]]** is a nocturnal ambusher associated with concealed attacks in darkness. Its danger is expressed through waiting rather than open pursuit, and accounts describe it as mournful, patient, and unnervingly still. The creature has a hidden, indistinct form accompanied by the unmistakable image of weeping. The [[Weeping Lurker]] lairs in [[Embermarch]] and was unleashed in [[The Purge of Blackport]].

## History

The history of the [[Weeping Lurker]] is defined less by open activity than by concealed presence. It is a nocturnal ambusher, and its appearances are associated with darkness, waiting, and attacks that are difficult to anticipate. Rather than pursuing its victims openly, the creature allows danger to gather around its stillness. This quality has made the [[Weeping Lurker]] difficult to distinguish from the darkness in which it operates.

The [[Weeping Lurker]] lairs in [[Embermarch]]. This association is central to its known history, although the available record describes the creature’s lair only in general terms. Its hidden, indistinct form reinforces the impression that it belongs to places where visibility is uncertain and where an observer may sense a presence without clearly seeing its source.

The [[Weeping Lurker]] was unleashed in [[The Purge of Blackport]]. This event is the principal historical circumstance connected with the creature in the surviving record. The wording of the record identifies the creature as having been unleashed, while providing no further account of the circumstances surrounding that act. Its appearance in this context is consequently remembered through the same qualities that define the creature elsewhere: darkness, concealment, waiting, and the image of weeping.

No account presents the [[Weeping Lurker]] as a creature of open pursuit. Its danger lies in the interval before an attack, when it remains present but indistinct. The absence of visible movement is therefore not treated as evidence of absence. Instead, stillness forms part of the creature’s recognized behavior.

## Relationships & Affiliations

No relationship or affiliation is recorded for the [[Weeping Lurker]]. The creature is described through its habit, appearance, demeanor, lair, and historical association rather than through allegiance to any named power or group.

Its connection to [[Embermarch]] is geographical rather than an affiliation. The [[Weeping Lurker]] lairs in [[Embermarch]], but the record does not assign the creature to any household, order, settlement, or faction. Similarly, its unleashing in [[The Purge of Blackport]] establishes a historical association without identifying a lasting bond or allegiance.

This absence of recorded affiliation is consistent with the creature’s nature. A being whose presence is hidden and whose attacks are concealed does not present itself through banners, proclamations, or open advance. The [[Weeping Lurker]] is recognized by the signs surrounding its presence rather than by declared loyalties. Its mournful aspect, patience, and unnerving stillness form a more reliable means of identification than any association with an organized power.

The name itself does not establish a relationship with any other entity. It describes the image accompanying the creature’s indistinct form: unmistakable weeping perceived in connection with a presence that remains concealed. The record therefore treats the [[Weeping Lurker]] as an independent creature category rather than as a title, office, or known servant-name.

## Tactical Assessment

The primary danger of the [[Weeping Lurker]] is concealed attack in darkness. Its nocturnal ambusher habit places emphasis on timing and concealment rather than speed or visible aggression. The creature waits. That waiting is not incidental to its behavior; it is the principal expression of its threat.

The [[Weeping Lurker]]’s hidden, indistinct form complicates recognition. The appearance associated with it is not a clearly described body but the unmistakable image of weeping. This distinction is important in accounts of the creature. The observer may recognize the sign of grief while remaining unable to identify the form that produces it. The image of weeping consequently functions as the creature’s clearest visible indication, even though the creature itself remains indistinct.

Its demeanor is mournful, patient, and unnervingly still. These traits should be considered together. Mournfulness gives the creature its emotional character; patience describes its willingness to remain in place; stillness makes that patience unnerving. None of these qualities suggests open pursuit. Instead, they describe a threat that persists through silence and delay.

The known tactical pattern of the [[Weeping Lurker]] can therefore be summarized as concealment followed by waiting. Darkness provides the setting associated with its attacks, while stillness preserves the uncertainty surrounding its location. The creature’s danger is greatest where its presence cannot be clearly separated from the surrounding dark.

This assessment does not establish additional methods or capabilities beyond those recorded. The [[Weeping Lurker]] is known as a nocturnal ambusher whose concealed attacks are associated with darkness. Its defining advantage is the fear produced by an unseen, waiting presence, not any documented display of open pursuit.

## Legacy

The [[Weeping Lurker]] is remembered through a combination of place, event, and image. [[Embermarch]] provides its recorded lair, while [[The Purge of Blackport]] provides the historical event in which it was unleashed. Between these two associations stands the creature’s defining image: weeping perceived alongside an indistinct form in darkness.

Its legacy is consequently one of anticipation. The [[Weeping Lurker]] does not require a visible chase to inspire fear. The possibility that it is waiting is sufficient to make darkness significant. Because it is mournful rather than openly violent in its presentation, the creature carries an atmosphere of grief as well as danger.

The image of weeping also distinguishes the [[Weeping Lurker]] from a simple unseen attacker. Its presence is not merely hidden; it is accompanied by a recognizable emotional impression. The sorrow associated with that image does not lessen the threat. Instead, it makes the creature’s stillness more unsettling, joining grief to concealment and patience to attack.

In catalogues of creatures, the [[Weeping Lurker]] is therefore defined by what cannot be readily seen. Its form is hidden and indistinct, its movements are governed by waiting, and its attacks are concealed in darkness. The known record provides no need for open pursuit to explain its danger. The [[Weeping Lurker]] remains threatening precisely because it can be present without becoming plainly visible.
